Google review Read All Google Reviews Avondale Homes Remodeling Avondale&rsquo;s Homes, Old and New Most Avondale houses are 1990s and 2000s tract homes — the median home in the city was built in 2002, according to the Census Bureau&rsquo;s American Community Survey (2020–2024). Here is what that means for a kitchen or bath remodel in different parts of town. Old Town & Cashion Old Town, formerly the Historic Avondale District, runs along Western Ave. The city&rsquo;s General Plan names it, Cashion and Las Ligas as Avondale&rsquo;s oldest neighborhoods. County assessor records date some Cashion homes back to 1917, with a median build year around 1965. Older houses like these are more likely to need plumbing or electrical updates as part of a kitchen or bath remodel, and that work needs a City of Avondale permit, which we pull. Garden Lakes, Rancho Santa Fe & Westwind Most homes in Garden Lakes went up between 1988 and 1998, and most in Rancho Santa Fe and Westwind between 1995 and 1999. A kitchen or bathroom that has never been redone in one of these houses is now more than 25 years old. A tub-to-shower conversion , new cabinets and countertops , or a full remodel can bring it up to date without moving walls. Crystal Gardens, Corte Sierra, Coldwater Springs & Durango Park These neighborhoods were mostly built between 1999 and 2006, and about 42% of all Avondale homes date from the 2000s. If your home still has its original builder-grade cabinets, counters and fixtures, they are 20 years old or more. Semi-custom cabinets, quartz countertops and a walk-in shower are the upgrades that change these homes the most. Del Rio Ranch & Roosevelt Park Newer homes, mostly built from the mid-2000s on. Here a remodel is usually an upgrade rather than a repair: a larger shower, better storage, a kitchen island, or finishes you chose yourself in place of the builder&rsquo;s standard package. Built for Avondale&rsquo;s Water and Heat Avondale&rsquo;s tap water is very hard: the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report put city well water at about 21 grains per gallon. Scale builds up fast on faucets, shower valves and glass, so it pays to choose fixtures and surfaces that hold up to hard water . Summers are long, too — about 111 days a year reach 100&deg;F, based on National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals — which matters for outdoor kitchens and sun-facing rooms. If your home is in an HOA, check its rules before work starts; the city does not track HOA covenants. Home / Services / Accessible Remodeling Accessible Remodeling — Avondale, AZ Accessible Home Remodeling in Avondale, AZ Bathrooms and homes that keep working as the people in them change — planned at your Avondale home, with a free in-home consultation. Most remodeling is about how a room looks. This is about whether someone can still use it. In Avondale that is rarely a retirement question — it is a young city, with a median age of about 33 in the Census Bureau's 2020–2024 American Community Survey. The reasons here are usually different: making room for a parent, planning for three generations under one roof, recovering from an injury or surgery, living with a disability, or staying put in a house you have owned for years. It covers a range. At one end, a tub swapped for a low-threshold shower so nobody has to lift a leg over a wall to wash. At the other, a whole house reworked around a wheelchair. Most projects sit in between, and most start because something has changed — a fall, a diagnosis, a parent moving in, or simply the realisation that the bathroom is going to become a problem before the house does. We are not a walk-in tub company with a scripted pitch. We are a design-build remodeler that does this work properly, which mostly means telling you which changes are worth making and which are being sold to you. The four services Walk-In Showers Low-threshold and curbless showers that you step into rather than climb over. Tub-to-Shower Conversions Replacing a tub you can no longer step into, usually without moving plumbing. ADA-Style Bathrooms Bathrooms built to the clearances and reach ranges the ADA standard sets out. Aging-in-Place Remodeling Whole-home changes that let you stay in the house rather than move out of it. Not sure which applies? Curbless and zero-entry showers is the usual starting point, and the accessibility guides go through the decisions in detail. What the ADA standard does and does not require of your home This is the single most misrepresented thing in accessible remodeling, so it is worth being blunt about. The ADA Standards for Accessible Design govern public accommodations — businesses, government buildings, places open to the public. They do not apply to a private home. No homeowner is obliged to meet them, and any contractor implying you must be brought into compliance is selling you something. What the standard is genuinely useful for is as a set of tested dimensions. It is the most carefully researched answer available to "how much room does a wheelchair actually need", and we design to it because it works, not because anyone is compelled to. The figures we use are a 60-inch turning space (§304.3.1), a 32-inch clear width at a doorway (§404.2.3), and grab bars mounted 33 to 36 inches above the floor (§609.4), all verified against ADA.gov and the U.S. Access Board. For most households the honest answer is that you want some of it. A curbless entry and blocking in the walls, yes. Widening every doorway in the house, usually not. We will tell you which is which for your home rather than quoting the whole standard at you. The detail that has to happen before the walls close Blocking is the one thing that cannot be added later. It is the timber fixed between the studs behind the finished wall, and it is what a grab bar anchors into. Fitted during the remodel it costs almost nothing; retrofitted afterwards it means opening a finished wall, and a bar screwed into tile and drywall alone will not hold a fall. So we install blocking around the shower, beside the toilet and along the tub wall on accessible projects as a matter of course, whether or not a bar is going on it today. If the need arrives in ten years, the wall is already ready. This is the stage in our process where the difference gets made — see how a remodel runs . Accessible remodeling in Avondale: permits, HOAs and the house you have Most Avondale homes are newer than people expect. The median house in the city was built in 2002, and most neighborhoods are tract subdivisions from the 1980s through the 2000s. That usually helps: the framing is standard, and a tub-shower combination in a hall bath of that era tends to convert cleanly to a low-threshold shower. The city's oldest neighborhoods — Old Town, Cashion and Las Ligas — are a different job (Cashion's median house was built around 1965), with doorways and plumbing worth checking before a layout is set. Permits. Residential permits come from the City of Avondale's Building Services Division (Development Services Department, 11465 W. Civic Center Dr., (623) 333-4000), filed online through Accela. The city's code exempts finish work such as tiling, cabinets and countertops, but plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC changes are not exempt, and framing changes like a widened doorway are not on the exempt list either — we confirm the scope with Building Services before work starts. A rebuilt shower is inspected at the pre-slope and again at the shower liner test, before any tile goes on. We pull the City of Avondale permits for our work and book the inspections. HOAs. Exterior changes — a ramp, a wider entry, a new walkway — change how the front of the house looks, and the city does not track HOA covenants. It tells owners to check with their HOA before applying for a permit. If your street has an HOA, we put its review into the schedule at the start rather than finding out halfway through. Water and heat. Avondale has very hard water — about 21 grains per gallon for city well water in the city's 2022 water quality report — so handheld showers, thermostatic valves and linear drains get chosen for how easily they descale. Outdoors, National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals for the area put the July average high around 106&deg;F, with about 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or more. Ramp surfaces, handrails and thresholds that sit in full sun need materials that stay usable, and a zero-step entry needs drainage that copes with a monsoon storm (the season officially runs June 15 to September 30). Paying for it Accessible work is one of the few remodeling categories with funding attached to it. If the homeowner is a veteran, the VA administers home adaptation grants that can apply to exactly this kind of bathroom work — we have set out how that process generally runs on VA bathroom remodeling grants . For owner-occupied homes on City of Avondale water, the city's Home Repair Program (Neighborhood & Family Services, (623) 333-2703) lists ADA work — wider doors, grab bars, ramps — among the repairs it can help with. Eligibility rules apply, so ask the city what currently qualifies before you plan around it. Beyond that, the ordinary routes apply: see financing , and what a walk-in shower costs or what a tub-to-shower conversion costs for the ranges before anyone has seen your bathroom. We eliminate that problem entirely by handling every aspect of your project in-house: design, demolition, plumbing, electrical, tile, cabinetry, countertops, flooring, and finish work. This step pays for itself many times over by catching potential problems before they're built in. Every crew member who enters your home is background-checked and drug-tested. We carry general liability insurance and workers' compensation coverage on every job site — which means you're protected if anything unexpected happens during the project. In Arizona, contractor licensing is regulated by the Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC). You can verify any contractor's current license status at roc.az.gov. We encourage every homeowner in Avondale to verify this before signing a contract with any contractor — licensed or not. Unlicensed contractors may offer lower bids, but they offer no legal recourse if work is incomplete or substandard, and their work may create disclosure obligations when you sell your home. # Remodeling Financing Options in Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/financing.html
Section: Company & trust
Summary: How to finance your kitchen or bathroom remodel in Avondale, AZ. HELOC, personal loans, and FHA 203(k) options explained.
==============================================================================

Home / Financing Home Remodeling Financing How to Finance Your Remodel in Avondale, AZ By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 HELOC, home equity loans, personal loans, and contractor financing — your options explained clearly so you can make the decision that fits your situation. Financing Your Remodel You Have More Options Than You Think Most of our kitchen remodels run $25,000–$65,000, and a full master bath transformation runs $20,000–$65,000. For most homeowners, that's not a check you write out of savings — and you shouldn't have to. There are several financing routes available for home improvement projects, each with different rates, timelines, and qualification requirements. Infinity Kitchens and Baths is not a lender, and we don't markup our prices to cover financing costs. What we can do is explain the options clearly, help you understand what each involves, and connect you with lending partners we've worked with. This page is our honest, no-marketing-fluff guide to the most common ways homeowners finance kitchen and bathroom remodels. The best financing option depends on how much equity you have in your home, your credit profile, how quickly you need to start, and whether you prefer predictable payments or maximum flexibility. Read through the options below, then call or text us — we're happy to discuss what makes sense for your specific project and financial picture. Quick Comparison Option Best Rate? Equity Needed? Speed HELOC &#9733; Best Yes 2–6 weeks Home Equity Loan &#9733; Low Yes 2–6 weeks Personal Loan Moderate No 1–7 days Cash-Out Refi &#9733; Low Yes 4–8 weeks FHA 203(k) &#9733; Low No 45–90 days Your Options The Five Most Common Ways to Finance a Remodel 01 HELOC (Home Equity Line of Credit) A HELOC is a revolving line of credit secured by the equity in your home. It works like a credit card — you draw what you need, when you need it, and pay interest only on the amount drawn. Interest rates are typically variable and tied to the prime rate, but they're usually among the lowest available for home improvement financing because your home is the collateral. For a phased remodel — kitchen now, bathrooms next year — a HELOC is often the ideal tool. You open the line once, draw for the kitchen project, pay it down, then draw again for the next phase without applying for a new loan. Most Arizona lenders will approve a HELOC in two to six weeks. You'll generally need at least 20% equity in your home and a credit score of 620 or higher, though better rates start at 700+. The primary risk is that the rate is variable — if rates rise, your payment rises. This option is generally recommended for homeowners with meaningful equity and stable income. 02 Home Equity Loan (Second Mortgage) A home equity loan gives you a lump sum at a fixed interest rate, repaid over a set term — typically 5 to 20 years. Unlike a HELOC, the rate is locked at closing, so your monthly payment doesn't change. This predictability is valuable when you're budgeting a large, single-phase project like a complete kitchen overhaul or a master bath transformation. The trade-off: you borrow the full amount upfront, even if the project spans several months and you don't need all the cash immediately. Rates are typically slightly higher than HELOC draw rates but are fixed. Qualification requirements are similar: meaningful home equity, stable income, and a credit score of 620+. Home equity loans are best for homeowners who know their exact project cost, want payment certainty, and prefer not to manage a revolving line of credit. 03 Personal (Unsecured) Home Improvement Loan Personal loans for home improvement are unsecured — your home is not collateral. That means approval is faster (sometimes same-day through online lenders), and you don't need significant equity. The trade-off is higher interest rates: typically 8–25% APR depending on your credit, compared to 6–9% for equity-secured products. For a $25,000–$40,000 remodel, the rate difference can add up over a 5–10 year term. Personal loans make the most sense when you've owned your home less than five years and haven't built significant equity, or when you want to avoid putting your home up as collateral. They're also useful for smaller projects ($15,000–$25,000) where the rate premium is less significant in absolute dollars. Shop multiple lenders — rates and terms vary widely. Credit unions often offer competitive home improvement loan products for members. 04 Cash-Out Refinance A cash-out refinance replaces your existing mortgage with a new, larger mortgage and gives you the difference in cash. If you owe $200,000 on a home worth $350,000, you could refinance to a $260,000 mortgage and receive $60,000 in cash for renovations. The benefit: you pay mortgage rates on the remodel funds, which are the lowest available. The downside: you restart your mortgage term, pay closing costs (typically $3,000–$7,000), and extend the timeline significantly (4–8 weeks to close). Cash-out refinancing made the most sense during the 2020–2021 period of historically low rates. For homeowners who locked in sub-3% rates, using a cash-out refi today at current rates may not be financially optimal — you'd be repricing your entire mortgage balance at a higher rate. This option warrants a careful conversation with your lender about the long-term cost impact before proceeding. 05 FHA 203(k) Renovation Loan The FHA 203(k) is a government-backed mortgage that bundles home purchase and renovation costs into a single loan. It's primarily used when buying a fixer-upper property — you finance the purchase price plus the estimated renovation costs in one loan, and the contractor is paid directly from the loan escrow as work progresses. For existing homeowners, there's a limited version (Standard vs. Streamline) that can fund renovation work. The FHA 203(k) has lower down payment requirements and is accessible to borrowers with credit scores as low as 580. The drawback is complexity and time — the program requires a HUD-approved consultant, specific contractor documentation, a lengthy underwriting process (45–90 days minimum), and work must meet FHA requirements. It's a powerful tool in the right circumstances, but for a straightforward kitchen or bathroom remodel on a home you already own, simpler options are usually faster and less restrictive. City of Avondale Programs Two City Programs Worth Checking First Low-flow plumbing rebates. If you are a City of Avondale water customer replacing higher-use fixtures, the city&rsquo;s Low Flow Plumbing Rebate pays $75 per toilet (1.6 gallons per flush or less) and $25 per showerhead (under 2.6 gallons per minute). You apply within one year of purchase with a dated receipt, and funds are first come, first served. Call the city&rsquo;s water conservation line at (623) 333-4400 for the current application. Home Repair Program. The city&rsquo;s Neighborhood & Family Services department runs a Home Repair Program for owner-occupied homes on City of Avondale water. It covers emergency or substantial repairs — roofs, water heaters, plumbing leaks, electrical — and accessibility work such as grab bars, wider doors, and accessible showers or tubs. Eligibility rules apply; call (623) 333-2703 to ask. This is a city program, not one we run, but it is worth a call before you budget for a repair-driven remodel. Through Infinity Contractor Financing Partners Infinity Kitchens and Baths works with third-party home improvement lending partners to offer financing directly through our company for qualified applicants. This means you can get approved and start your project without a separate trip to a bank or credit union. Our lending partners offer fixed-rate installment loans for home improvement projects typically ranging from $5,000 to $100,000, with terms of 24 to 144 months. Rates vary based on credit profile and loan amount. Same-day decisions are available in many cases. This is not in-house financing — we connect you with the lender and you deal directly with them for the life of the loan. Ask about financing options during your free consultation. We'll provide you with information on current programs, and you can apply with no impact to your credit score during the initial check. If you're approved, you can start your project immediately — no waiting on a bank's appraisal or underwriting timeline. Tips Before You Borrow &#10003; Get your full project cost first. Apply for financing based on a real contractor quote, not an estimate. Our free consultation gives you a real number before you approach a lender. &#10003; Add a 10% contingency. Unexpected conditions behind walls are real. A 10% buffer in your financing amount prevents the project from stalling mid-build. &#10003; Shop two or three lenders. Rates vary meaningfully. Even 1.5% APR difference on a $40,000 loan over 10 years is roughly $3,000. &#10003; Understand the draw schedule. Contractors typically require a down payment and progress draws — not a single upfront payment. Your lender should align the draw schedule with the project milestones. &#10003; Check your home equity before you start. If you have 30%+ equity and good credit, a HELOC is likely your cheapest option and worth the 3–4 week wait. Common Questions Remodel Financing FAQ Can I finance a kitchen remodel with no equity? Yes — through an unsecured personal loan or contractor financing. Rates will be higher than equity-based products, but you don't need home equity to qualify. Many online lenders offer home improvement loans up to $50,000 with same-day approvals based on creditworthiness alone. If you've owned your home less than three years or bought at a high price with a small down payment, this is likely your primary non-cash option. What credit score do I need to finance a remodel? For equity-based products (HELOC, home equity loan), most lenders want a minimum of 620, with better rates starting at 700+. For personal loans, 640 and above is generally required for reasonable rates; below 640 you'll face higher rates or may need a co-signer. FHA 203(k) is accessible down to 580. Contractor financing programs vary — some accept 580, others require 640+. Pull your credit report at AnnualCreditReport.com before shopping lenders so you know where you stand. Does Infinity offer payment plans directly? Infinity Kitchens and Baths does not extend in-house credit. We work with third-party lending partners who offer home improvement financing programs, which we can facilitate during the consultation process. We do not charge a fee for connecting you with a lending partner. Our standard contract requires a down payment at signing and progress payments at defined project milestones, which aligns with how most home improvement loan draw schedules work. Is financing a remodel a good financial decision? It depends on the project and the option. Kitchen and master bathroom remodels typically return 60–80% of their cost in added home value — not a full return, but meaningful. If you're financing at 7–9% on a well-planned project, and the alternative is living in a dysfunctional kitchen or bathroom for years, the decision often makes both financial and quality-of-life sense. What doesn't make sense is financing a remodel at 18–25% interest on an unsecured loan for cosmetic changes — the carrying cost outweighs the value gain. Talk to us about your specific project and we'll give you an honest read on the value math. Start with a Real Project Quote The first step to financing any remodel is knowing the real number. Schedule your free consultation and we'll give you a detailed, itemized quote — so you can approach a lender with a real project cost, not a guess. # Licensing, Bonding & Insurance | Infinity Kitchens & Baths
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/licensing-insurance.html
Section: Company & trust
Summary: Infinity Kitchens and Baths of Avondale, AZ is licensed (AZ ROC #339999), bonded, and fully insured. Verify our license at roc.az.gov.

Home / About Us / Licensing & Insurance Trust & Credentials Licensing, Bonding & Insurance By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Licensed, bonded and insured for kitchen and bath remodeling in Avondale, Arizona. Choosing a remodeling contractor in Arizona requires more than comparing quotes. Understanding a contractor's licensing, bonding, and insurance is one of the most important steps you can take to protect your home, your finances, and your legal standing. Here's what our credentials mean and how to verify them independently. Our Credentials at a Glance #339999 AZ ROC License Bonded Surety Bond Active Insured General Liability Workers' Comp Coverage Active What the AZ ROC License Means The Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC) is the state agency that licenses and regulates contractors. To obtain a license, a contractor must pass a trade exam, pass a business management exam, submit to a background check, and maintain active bonding and insurance. The license must be renewed regularly and remains in good standing only when the contractor meets ongoing requirements. Our license number is AZ ROC #339999 . This is a General Contractor license, which authorizes us to perform kitchen and bathroom remodeling, structural modifications, additions, and related residential work across Arizona. How to Verify Our License We encourage every homeowner to verify any contractor's license before signing a contract. Here's how to verify ours: Go to roc.az.gov (the official Arizona Registrar of Contractors website) Click "License Lookup" in the navigation Search by license number 339999 or by company name "Infinity Kitchens and Baths" The result will show license status, license type, bond amounts, and any complaint history A license in "Active" status with no unresolved complaints is what you want to see. You can verify any Arizona contractor the same way before hiring. What "Bonded" Means A contractor bond — also called a surety bond — is a financial guarantee issued by a bonding company. It protects you as the homeowner if the contractor fails to complete the contracted work, abandons a project, or causes financial harm through improper performance. In Arizona, the ROC requires all licensed contractors to maintain a bond as a condition of licensure. The bond amount varies by license class and is set by the ROC. The bond is not insurance on our behalf — it is a protection mechanism for the homeowner and the public. If a contractor is unlicensed, they cannot legally hold a bond under the ROC system — which means you have no financial protection if something goes wrong. What Insurance Covers We carry two types of insurance that matter to you as a homeowner: General Liability Insurance General liability insurance covers accidental property damage caused by our crew during the project. If a worker drops a tool through your floor, damages a wall beyond the project scope, or causes an accidental water leak — general liability insurance covers the repair costs. Without this, you as the homeowner could be left absorbing those costs, or forced into a dispute with an uninsured contractor. We can provide a Certificate of Insurance (COI) upon request before the project begins. Workers' Compensation Insurance Workers' compensation is often overlooked by homeowners, but it's critical. If one of our workers is injured while working in your home, workers' comp covers their medical costs and lost wages. Without workers' comp on the contractor's policy, you as the homeowner may be held liable for an injured worker's medical expenses and legal costs under Arizona law. This is one of the most significant risks of hiring an uninsured contractor — and one of the most commonly misunderstood by homeowners. The Risks of Hiring an Unlicensed Contractor Unlicensed contractors frequently offer lower prices. That lower price reflects, in part, the absence of the overhead that exists to protect you. Here's what you give up when you hire unlicensed: Protection Licensed (ROC #339999) Unlicensed Contractor ROC complaint & remediation process &#10003; Available &#10007; Not available Bond protection if work abandoned &#10003; Available &#10007; Not available Homeowner's insurance claim support &#10003; Supported &#10007; May be denied Ability to pull permits &#10003; Yes &#10007; No Worker injury liability &#10003; Covered by workers' comp &#10007; May fall to homeowner 5 Questions to Ask Before Hiring Any Contractor Whether you hire us or someone else, these five questions protect you from the most common contractor pitfalls in Arizona: Are you licensed with the AZ ROC? — Ask for the license number and verify it yourself at roc.az.gov. Active status = good standing. Are you bonded and insured? — Ask for a Certificate of Insurance naming you (the homeowner) as an additional insured for the project duration. Will you pull the required permits? — In Avondale, structural changes and plumbing, electrical, gas or HVAC work beyond minor repairs need a permit from the City of Avondale&rsquo;s Building Services Division. If a contractor discourages permits, that's a significant red flag. Do you provide a written contract with scope, timeline, and payment schedule? — Never pay more than 10% or $1,000 (whichever is less) as a deposit without a signed contract. Do you provide a written workmanship warranty? — Verbal promises are not enforceable. Get coverage terms in writing before work begins. Frequently Asked Questions How do I verify Infinity Kitchens and Baths' license? Visit roc.az.gov , click "License Lookup," and search for license number 339999 or company name "Infinity Kitchens and Baths." The result will confirm our license type, active status, bond information, and any complaint history. We encourage you to check before signing any contract — with us or anyone else. What if I have a problem with a licensed contractor's work? If a complaint cannot be resolved directly with the contractor, homeowners can file a formal complaint with the Arizona Registrar of Contractors. The ROC investigates complaints, can order remediation, and can suspend or revoke a contractor's license for unresolved issues. This process is only available when the contractor is licensed — unlicensed contractors fall outside the ROC's jurisdiction. Does your insurance cover my belongings if they're damaged? General liability insurance covers accidental property damage caused by our crew during the project — including damage to your home's structure, fixtures, and surfaces within the work area. Coverage for personal belongings (furniture, electronics, artwork) is typically excluded from contractor liability policies and is better covered under your homeowner's insurance. We take care to protect your home during every project. Why do some contractors charge significantly less? Contractors who skip licensing, bonding, workers' compensation, and insurance have meaningfully lower overhead — and they pass some of that to you in the form of a lower bid. But those costs exist because the protections they buy are real. The unlicensed contractor who's 20% cheaper carries 100% of the risk back onto you if something goes wrong. Ready to Work With a Contractor You Can Trust? Licensed, bonded, and insured, and family-owned since 2011. Request a free consultation and we'll walk you through our process, our credentials, and exactly what to expect. Home / About / Our Process Our Process How Your Remodel Actually Runs Five stages, from the first free in-home visit to the written warranty — and what happens at each one. Most remodeling anxiety is not about the finished room. It is about the middle — how long the house is unusable, who is in it, what happens when something unexpected turns up behind a wall, and whether the price at the end resembles the price at the start. This page answers that before you call anyone, ours or otherwise. We are a design-build contractor, which means the people who draw your project and the people who build it work for the same company. There is no handoff between a designer and a general contractor, and no gap for a problem to fall into. What design-build means covers why that matters. Stage 01 Free In-Home Consultation & Home Assessment We meet at your home — not a showroom — for a no-pressure conversation about what you want to change, what is not working, and what your budget expectations are. We walk the space together, take field measurements, and note the structural constraints that will shape what is realistic. This is a design conversation, not a sales call, and there is never any pressure to sign the same day. It is free and carries no obligation. Stage 02 Concept Design & 3D CAD Presentation We take the measurements and your wish list back to the studio and develop scaled 2D floor plans — usually two or three layout alternatives so you can compare the trade-offs — then a photorealistic 3D rendering of the preferred layout with your selected finishes applied. You see the tile, the vanity placement, the shower layout and the fixtures before anyone touches a wall. This is the stage that prevents expensive mid-project changes. Stage 03 Final Selections, Itemised Scope & Contract Once the layout is approved we finalise every material selection — countertop slab, cabinet door profile, tile, hardware, plumbing fixtures and lighting — against a coordinated material board, so you are not hoping things match when they arrive. Then we produce an itemised scope of work with firm pricing: demo, framing, plumbing rough-in, electrical, tile, cabinetry, countertops and finish work each listed with its cost before you sign a construction contract. Nothing is vague, and nothing is left to be discovered later. Stage 04 Permits, Scheduling & Construction We pull the required permits, coordinate material deliveries, and manage every trade on a written schedule. Materials are ordered, verified and staged before the project starts, so your timeline is not waiting on a backorder. You get regular progress updates and a single point of contact for the whole build. If something is found behind a wall — moisture, dry rot, an old repair — it is raised and approved with you before work continues, never buried in a change order afterwards. Stage 05 Final Walkthrough, Punch List & Warranty When construction is complete we walk the finished space with you and document every punch-list item. All of them are resolved before we consider the project closed. The work is backed by a written workmanship warranty — the details are on our warranties page . Permits in Avondale: what needs one, and who issues it We handle the permit, but it is worth knowing how it works, because it is the part of a remodel homeowners are most often surprised by. In Avondale, residential permits come from the City of Avondale&rsquo;s Building Services Division, part of the Development Services Department at 11465 W. Civic Center Dr., and applications are filed online through the city&rsquo;s Accela portal. See Avondale remodeling permits . Not every job needs one. The city&rsquo;s code exempts finish work — painting, tiling, carpeting, cabinets and countertops. Plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC work beyond minor repairs is not exempt, so moving a sink, adding a circuit or replacing a shower valve means a permit and inspections. For a tiled shower, the city&rsquo;s inspections include a pre-slope and shower liner test before the tile goes on. If your home is in an HOA, check its rules as well. The city does not track HOA covenants and tells owners to check with their HOA before applying for a permit. We do not publish permit fees or review timelines here. Both change, and a stale number on a live page is worse than no number — we give you the current figures for your address at the consult. What changes by project type The five stages hold for every project, but the middle of the build differs. A bathroom lives or dies on the waterproofing — membranes on every shower pan and wall, a floor sloped to the drain at the required quarter-inch-per-foot, all of it tested before a single tile goes on. The full sequence is on bathroom remodeling . A kitchen is a sequencing problem instead: layout sets the cabinets, cabinets set the counters, and the counters cannot be templated until the cabinets are actually hung. See kitchen remodeling , or whole-house remodeling when several rooms move at once. Accessibility work has a stage the others do not — blocking has to go into the walls before they close up, and a grab bar added afterwards is never as strong. That is covered on accessible & aging-in-place remodeling . One thing we will tell you up front We do not send a sales team out to quote a backsplash on its own. If that is the whole job, we will point you at a tile installer who does that work, and we would rather say so now than waste your afternoon. Backsplash within a kitchen remodel is a different matter and is part of what we do — see kitchen backsplashes . Before you commit to anyone Whether or not you call us, verify the licence. Arizona contractors are registered with the Arizona Registrar of Contractors, and the register is public and free to search. Ours is AZ ROC #339999 , and the rest of our licensing and insurance is set out on licensing & insurance . How Remodel Costs Work in Avondale, AZ Remodeling cost comes down to three things: the size of the space, the quality of the materials and finishes you choose, and what the project uncovers behind the walls. # Our Warranty & Workmanship Guarantee
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/warranties.html
Section: Company & trust
Summary: Infinity Kitchens and Baths stands behind every project with a workmanship warranty and material guarantees.
==============================================================================

Home / About Us / Warranties Our Promise Warranties & Workmanship Guarantee By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Workmanship and manufacturer warranties for kitchen and bath remodels in Avondale, Arizona. When you invest in a kitchen or bathroom remodel, you're trusting a contractor with your home, your budget, and your time. At Infinity Kitchens and Baths, we believe that trust needs to be backed by a written commitment. Every project we complete comes with a workmanship warranty on labor and access to manufacturer warranties on materials — so your investment is protected long after we leave the job site. Our Workmanship Warranty We stand behind the quality of our installation work. Our workmanship warranty covers labor defects for 2 years from the date of project completion. If something we installed fails because of how it was installed — not because of a product defect or owner-caused damage — we will return and make it right at no cost to you. Covered under our workmanship warranty: Tile work — cracked grout lines (not caused by settling or movement), loose tiles, improperly sealed surfaces Cabinet installation — misaligned doors, improperly secured boxes, drawer hardware failures due to installation error Countertop installation — failed seams, unsecured edges, improper cutouts for undermount sinks Fixture installation — leaks at supply line connections caused by improper fitting, loose drain assemblies Flooring installation — lifting planks, gapping at seams, squeaking from improper subfloor prep Shower systems — grout or caulk failure at control and shower head penetrations, improperly seated shower bases Our warranty is included in every written contract. You receive documentation at project completion specifying the warranty period and how to submit a claim. What Is Not Covered A warranty is only meaningful when it's honest about its limits. The following are not covered under our workmanship warranty: Normal wear and tear — grout discoloration from use, minor scratches, fading from sun exposure Owner-caused damage — cracks from impact, staining from improper cleaning products, damage from modifications you make after project completion Manufacturer product defects — if the product itself is defective (not the installation), that claim goes to the manufacturer under their product warranty Structural movement — cracks caused by foundation settling or seismic activity beyond our control Deferred maintenance — damage resulting from failure to maintain sealed surfaces, re-caulk annual wear areas, or follow care instructions we provide If you're ever unsure whether an issue is covered, call us at 602-885-6998 — we'll assess honestly. Manufacturer & Product Warranties In addition to our workmanship warranty, most of the products we install carry separate manufacturer warranties. These vary by brand and product category. Below are typical coverage terms for the products we commonly install: Product Category Typical Warranty Notes Semi-custom cabinets 1–5 years Varies by manufacturer; covers finish and box integrity Custom cabinets Limited lifetime Most major custom cabinet lines offer lifetime warranty on box construction Quartz countertops 10 years to limited lifetime Silestone, Cambria, MSI, and similar brands; covers manufacturing defects Granite / natural stone Varies by supplier Natural materials have limited product warranties; fabrication quality is key Plumbing fixtures Lifetime limited (Delta, Moen, Kohler) Finish warranty typically 1–5 years; function warranty often lifetime LVP / luxury vinyl flooring 15–25 years (residential) COREtec, Shaw, Mohawk; wear layer warranty on residential use Solid surface shower systems Limited lifetime (product) Covers manufacturing defects in solid surface panels and bases Specific warranty terms are provided in writing at project completion for every product installed. Ask us for documentation on any product before we begin. How to Make a Warranty Claim Making a warranty claim with Infinity Kitchens and Baths is straightforward. Here's what to do: Call or text us at 602-885-6998 and describe the issue. Photos help us assess before we arrive. We schedule a site visit — usually within 5–7 business days for non-emergency issues, sooner if there's active water damage. We assess the cause — we'll honestly determine whether the issue is a workmanship defect, a product defect, or something outside warranty coverage. We repair or remediate — if covered under our workmanship warranty, we repair or replace at no charge. If it's a manufacturer defect, we assist you in filing the product warranty claim. We do not charge a service call fee to assess warranty claims during the warranty period. Why Warranty Matters When Choosing a Contractor A warranty is only as good as the contractor standing behind it. Unlicensed contractors and cash-only operations have no formal accountability — if the work fails, you have no recourse. When you hire a licensed, bonded, and insured contractor like Infinity Kitchens and Baths (AZ ROC #339999), there is a regulatory framework that holds us accountable. Key differences when hiring a licensed vs. unlicensed contractor: Licensed contractors must maintain active bonding and insurance as a condition of licensure Homeowners can file complaints with the AZ Registrar of Contractors if a licensed contractor fails to honor warranty work Permits pulled by a licensed contractor are inspected — giving you an independent third-party verification of work quality A written contract with a licensed contractor is enforceable; a verbal agreement with an unlicensed operator is not Before signing any remodeling contract, ask for the warranty in writing, confirm the ROC license number, and verify it at roc.az.gov . Frequently Asked Questions How long is your workmanship warranty? Our workmanship warranty covers labor defects for 2 years from the date of project completion. This is in addition to any applicable manufacturer or product warranties, which may extend coverage further depending on the product. Does the warranty transfer if I sell my home? The workmanship warranty applies to the work performed at the property. If you sell your home within the warranty period, you can provide the new owner with the warranty documentation. Manufacturer warranties vary — some are transferable, some are not. We'll provide clear documentation for each product so you have the details you need. What if a product fails but the installation was correct? If the product itself is defective — for example, a quartz slab with a manufacturing flaw — that's a manufacturer warranty claim, not a workmanship claim. We'll help you navigate the process with the manufacturer or supplier, including providing our installation documentation to support the claim. Do you provide warranty documentation in writing? Yes. Every project contract includes warranty terms. At project completion, we provide a summary document outlining the workmanship warranty period, the scope covered, and the process for submitting a claim. You receive this along with any manufacturer warranty cards or registration information for the products installed. Questions About Your Warranty Coverage? Our team is happy to walk you through what's covered before, during, and after your project. Call us directly or request a free consultation. # Accessibility Statement | Infinity Kitchens and Baths
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/accessibility.html
Section: Legal & accessibility
Summary: How we make our site usable for everyone: WCAG 2.1 AA conformance status, the measures in place, known limitations, and how to report a barrier.
==============================================================================

Home / Accessibility Legal Accessibility Statement Last reviewed: July 29, 2026 — Infinity Kitchens and Baths, LLC Infinity Kitchens and Baths, LLC is committed to making infinitykitchenandbathllc.com usable by as many people as possible, regardless of ability or the technology they browse with. A large share of the work we do — walk-in showers , ADA bathrooms , and aging-in-place remodels — exists to help people stay independent in their own homes. It would be inconsistent of us to build accessible bathrooms behind an inaccessible website. Conformance Status We aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA . This site is currently partially conformant with WCAG 2.1 Level AA. &ldquo;Partially conformant&rdquo; means most of the site meets the standard, but we know of some areas that do not yet, and those are listed below. We publish this honestly rather than claiming full conformance. Accessibility is not a one-time project: every time we add pages or change the site, we can introduce new barriers, so we treat this as ongoing maintenance. What We Have Done Measures currently in place across the site: Keyboard access. Every interactive control — navigation, buttons, forms, the estimate panel — can be reached and operated with a keyboard alone, and the currently focused element is shown with a clearly visible outline. Skip to main content. A skip link is the first item on every page, so keyboard and screen-reader users can jump past the navigation menu. Page structure. Pages use real landmarks and a single, ordered heading hierarchy, so assistive technology can navigate by region and by heading. Labelled forms. Every form field has a programmatic label, and submitting a form announces its result — success or failure — rather than only changing a button's appearance. Text contrast. Body text, links, and small print are checked against the 4.5:1 minimum contrast ratio. Text alternatives. Images that carry meaning have descriptive alternative text; purely decorative images are marked so screen readers skip them instead of reading out filenames. Reduced motion. If your device is set to reduce motion, our scroll and hover animations are switched off. Resizing and zoom. The layout reflows down to small screens and up to 200% browser zoom without loss of content or horizontal scrolling. Known Limitations We are aware of the following and are working on them: Embedded Google Maps. Some pages embed a map from Google. We do not control that embed's internal accessibility. Our address is always given as plain text alongside it, and you can call us for directions. Older project photography. Some alternative text on older gallery images is more generic than we would like. We are rewriting these as we revisit each page. Third-party content. Reviews and other content served from outside platforms may not fully meet the standard. Assistive Technology and Browsers The site is built to work with current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and with the screen readers and magnification tools built into those platforms. If you use an older browser or a specific assistive tool and something does not work, please tell us — that is genuinely useful information. If Something Is Not Accessible to You We want to hear about it, and we would rather over-hear than under-hear. If any part of this site blocks you, or if you need information from it in a different format — read to you over the phone, sent as large-print or plain text, or gone through in person — contact us: Phone: 602-885-6998 Email: info@infinitykitchenandbathllc.com Mail: Infinity Kitchens and Baths, LLC, 316 N Central Ave, Avondale, AZ 85323 Or use our contact form . Please tell us the page address and what went wrong, and include how you would like us to reply. We aim to respond within two business days. If we cannot fix something quickly, we will tell you what we are doing about it and give you another way to get the information you need in the meantime. Nothing on this site should ever be the only way to reach us or to get a quote. We offer free in-home consultations throughout Avondale, and you are always welcome to simply call. How We Test We assess this site by a combination of automated testing and manual review, including navigating pages by keyboard alone, checking heading and landmark structure, and verifying color contrast ratios against the WCAG formula. Automated tools catch only part of the picture, so manual checks are part of every review. Formal Approval and Review This statement was prepared on July 29, 2026 and applies to infinitykitchenandbathllc.com . It is approved by the ownership of Infinity Kitchens and Baths, LLC (AZ ROC #339999). We review it at least annually and whenever we make substantial changes to the site. # Accessibility & Aging-in-Place Guides | Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/accessibility-guides.html
Section: Guide categories
Summary: Guides to curbless showers, walk-in shower costs, grab bars and VA grants for accessible, aging-in-place bathroom remodels in Avondale, AZ.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Accessibility & Aging-in-Place Guides Avondale Remodeling Guides Accessibility & Aging-in-Place Guides Guides to curbless showers, walk-in shower costs, grab bars and VA grants for accessible, aging-in-place bathroom remodels in Avondale, AZ. Accessibility work is the part of remodeling where getting the details right matters most, and where the marketing is least reliable. These guides cover what actually changes a room's usability — threshold height, blocking in the walls, doorway clear width — and what the ADA standard does and does not require of a private home. What the ADA standard actually covers The 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design govern public accommodations and commercial facilities. A private home is neither, and no inspector will hold your bathroom to them. Any contractor implying your house must comply is selling something. The figures are still the best guidance available, because they came from testing how people using walkers and wheelchairs actually move. The three that matter most in a house are a 60-inch diameter turning space (§304.3.1), a 32-inch minimum clear doorway width (§404.2.3), and grab bars mounted 33 to 36 inches above the finished floor (§609.4). In a house those are targets. Plenty of existing bathrooms cannot produce a 60-inch turning circle without taking space from a bedroom, and a T-shaped turning space or a redirected door swing often solves the same practical problem. The order that matters more than the list Accessibility work is almost never done all at once, and the sequence matters more than the scope. The risk in a house is not evenly distributed. The bathroom is first, every time. It is the wettest room, holds the highest step, and is where most falls happen. A low-threshold or curbless shower with blocking in the walls addresses more real risk than any other single change. Then everything underfoot elsewhere: threshold strips between flooring types, a step into a sunken room, poor lighting on a hallway or stair. These are cheap and disproportionately dangerous to leave. Then the kitchen, where the issue is reach rather than danger — deep base cabinets, unreachable wall cabinets, and a single ceiling fixture leaving the counter in shadow. Build for it before you need it The cheapest accessibility work is the work done while a wall is already open. Adding blocking behind new tile costs very little and means a grab bar can be mounted into solid material a decade later without touching the tile. Retrofitting into a tiled wall with nothing behind it is possible and never as good. The same logic covers doorway width during any framing work, a comfort-height toilet when one is being replaced anyway, and an extra lighting circuit while a ceiling is open. None of it requires believing you will need it soon — only that you do not close the wall without thinking about it. If cost is what stands in the way, two routes are worth checking. Veterans should start with the VA bathroom grant guide . And the City of Avondale&rsquo;s Home Repair Program, run by Neighborhood & Family Services at (623) 333-2703, lists accessibility work such as wider doors, grab bars and ramps among the repairs it can help with for owner-occupied homes on city water. The eligibility rules are the city&rsquo;s, so ask them first. # Bathroom Design & Planning Guides | Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/bathroom-guides.html
Section: Guide categories
Summary: Bathroom layout, vanity, flooring, lighting and ventilation guides for planning a bathroom remodel in Avondale, AZ.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Bathroom Design & Planning Guides Avondale Remodeling Guides Bathroom Design & Planning Guides Bathroom layout, vanity, flooring, lighting and ventilation guides for planning a bathroom remodel in Avondale, AZ. Bathrooms are the smallest rooms with the most systems in them. These guides cover layout, fixtures and the finishes that survive a wet room, with an eye on what still works ten years in. The smallest room with the most systems in it A bathroom packs supply, drain, vent, electrical and mechanical ventilation into the smallest floor area in the house, usually with a wet zone in the middle of it. That density is why bathroom remodels have less tolerance for improvisation than any other room. It is also why the order of work is fixed. Demolition, then rough-in and inspection, then waterproofing, then surfaces. When a new shower pan is built, the City of Avondale&rsquo;s inspection list includes a pre-slope check and a shower liner test before anything is covered. A schedule that promises tile before an inspection has passed is describing something other than a permitted job. Ventilation is the most ignored decision Almost nobody chooses a bathroom for its extractor, and almost every bathroom problem that is not a leak traces back to one. Moisture that is not removed condenses, and condensation is what grows mold behind a vanity and lifts paint off a ceiling. Two things matter: that the fan is sized for the room rather than for the box it came in, and that it exhausts outside rather than into a roof space. Venting into an attic is common in older housing and simply relocates the problem to somewhere you will not notice it for years. Choosing finishes that survive a wet room The failure modes in a bathroom are specific: standing water at the vanity, splash at the tub, steam everywhere, and hard-water mineral deposits on everything. Materials that shrug at three of those and fail at the fourth still fail. In Avondale the fourth is the one to plan around: the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report put city well water at about 21 grains per gallon, which the report&rsquo;s own scale calls very hard. Practically that means sealed or engineered surfaces at the vanity rather than porous ones, flooring rated for wet areas rather than merely water-resistant, and a realistic view of how much cleaning the finishes you like will demand. Larger-format tile with fewer grout joints is the single easiest maintenance decision available. # How to Choose a Remodeling Contractor in Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/choosing-a-contractor.html
Section: Guide categories
Summary: How to evaluate kitchen, bathroom, cabinet and accessibility contractors in Avondale, AZ: license and insurance checks, permits, and the questions to ask.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Choosing a Remodeling Contractor Guides Choosing a Remodeling Contractor in Avondale How to evaluate kitchen, bathroom, cabinet and accessibility contractors for your Avondale, AZ home. These are checklists for judging a contractor, not rankings of one. Each covers what to ask, what to verify, and what a straight answer sounds like — including how to check a license with the Arizona Registrar of Contractors before anyone starts work. These are checklists, not rankings Every guide in this category is written as a way to judge a contractor, not as a league table of them. We are a remodeling company; a list from us ranking our competitors would be worth exactly nothing to you, and we are not going to publish one. What we can usefully offer is the set of questions that separate a company that will finish your project well from one that will not — including the questions we would rather you asked us. The checks worth doing before anyone quotes Verify the license yourself. The Arizona Registrar of Contractors publishes license status, classification and complaint history at no cost. Confirm the number is current and that the classification actually covers your work. Ours is AZ ROC #339999. Confirm insurance directly with the insurer, not from a certificate emailed to you. Certificates are easy to produce and easy to have lapsed since. Ask who is actually on site. There is a real difference between a company running its own crews and one subcontracting every trade to whoever is available that week. Neither is disqualifying; not getting a straight answer is. What a good answer sounds like Ask what they expect to find behind your walls. A contractor who has looked will describe what is likely given the age of your house and say how they would handle it. One who has not will reassure you. Ask what is excluded from the quote. Every quote excludes something, and a company that can name its exclusions immediately has thought about them. A quote with no exclusions listed is not a more complete quote — it is a less specific one. Ask what happens if the schedule slips. The answer you want is a process, not a promise that it will not. Questions that matter for an Avondale remodel Who pulls the permit? Permits for Avondale homes come from the City of Avondale&rsquo;s Building Services Division and are filed online. Painting, tiling, carpeting, cabinets and countertops need no building permit; plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC changes do. The city&rsquo;s permit application also says contractors must hold an ROC license unless the owner qualifies as an owner-builder — so a contractor who asks you to pull the permit in your own name is asking you to take on their responsibility. Who schedules the inspections? City inspections run Monday through Thursday, work has to pass before it is covered (a shower gets a pre-slope inspection and a shower liner test before tile), and a permit expires if no inspection is approved within 180 days. A good contractor builds that into the schedule without being asked. Have you checked with the HOA? The city doesn&rsquo;t track HOA covenants and tells owners to check with their HOA before applying for a permit. Ask whether the contractor expects the project to need HOA approval, and who will handle the paperwork. What do you expect to find in a house this age? The median Avondale home was built in 2002, and most are 1980s–2000s construction, with older homes around Old Town and in Cashion. A contractor who has looked at your house should be able to tell you what that age usually means for its plumbing, wiring and subfloor. On older homes, ask too about asbestos: the city&rsquo;s permit application notes that regulated renovation needs a NESHAP notice to Maricopa County 10 business days ahead. For the full rundown, see our guide to Avondale remodeling permits and our step-by-step contractor checklist . Home / Guides / Material & Product Comparisons Avondale Remodeling Guides Material & Product Comparisons Side-by-side comparisons — quartz vs. granite, porcelain vs. ceramic, refacing vs. replacing — with a clear pick for Avondale, AZ kitchens and baths. These are the decisions that stall a project. Each guide takes one pairing, sets out where each option genuinely wins, and says which we would specify in which situation rather than leaving you with a balanced shrug. Why most comparisons refuse to pick a winner Most material comparisons you will find online end in a shrug: both are great, it depends on your needs, talk to a professional. That is technically true and practically useless, and it usually means the writer has no installation experience to draw on. These guides take a position. Where one option is genuinely better for a specific situation, we say which and why. Where the honest answer really is that it depends, we say what it depends on in terms you can check against your own house rather than leaving you with a balanced paragraph. The questions that settle most material decisions Who is going to clean it? This decides more material choices than aesthetics do. Textured surfaces, small-format tile with many grout joints, clear glass and polished chrome all look excellent and all demand upkeep. In Avondale, where the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report put city well water at about 21 grains per gallon, that upkeep is not optional. How long are you staying? A five-year horizon and a twenty-year horizon justify genuinely different specifications. Trend-forward finishes are a reasonable choice if you will enjoy them and move; they are a worse choice if you will still be living with them in 2045. What is the room actually exposed to? A material that performs beautifully on a bathroom wall may be the wrong answer on a shower floor, and a counter that suits a guest bathroom may not suit a working kitchen. Comparisons that ignore the application produce confident, wrong recommendations. Where comparisons stop being useful At some point the remaining differences are small enough that the decision is aesthetic, and reading another comparison will not resolve it. That point arrives sooner than most people expect — usually once you have narrowed to two options in the same tier. When you get there, stop reading and go handle samples in daylight. Photographs misrepresent stone and tile more than any other building material, and the difference between two quartz patterns on a screen bears little relation to the difference in a room. # Remodeling Cost Guides & Pricing | Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/cost-guides.html
Section: Guide categories
Summary: Typical kitchen, bathroom, cabinet and countertop remodel costs from an Avondale, AZ remodeler: what moves a quote within its range, ROI and financing.

Home / Guides / Remodeling Cost Guides Avondale Remodeling Guides Remodeling Cost Guides Typical kitchen, bathroom, cabinet and countertop remodel costs from an Avondale, AZ remodeler: what moves a quote within its range, ROI and financing. Every figure in these guides is a range, because that is what an honest cost answer looks like before anyone has seen your house. The useful part is not the number — it is what moves you within the range: the age of the plumbing, whether walls move, and the material tier you choose. How to read a remodeling cost range Every honest cost answer is a range, and the width of that range is information rather than evasion. A contractor who gives you a single number before seeing the room is either guessing or has decided in advance what they will leave out. What a range does not tell you is where in it you sit. That is decided by three things, roughly in order of impact: whether anything moves, what condition the systems behind the walls are in, and which material tier you choose. Layout changes and plumbing relocations move a project between ranges. Finish selections move it within one. So the useful way to read these guides is backwards. Start from the low end and ask what would have to be true for your project to land there — usually that nothing moves and the rough-in is sound. Then read the high end the same way. Your quote will explain which of those two stories your house tells. The three things that move a number most Whether walls or plumbing move. Replacing fixtures where they already are is a different category of work from relocating a drain. In a slab-on-grade house, moving a drain means cutting concrete — that is a line item, not a detail. What is behind the walls. A 1960s bathroom and a 2010 bathroom can look equally tired and cost very differently to remodel, because one may need supply lines, venting and a circuit addressed while the wall is open and the other will not. This is the single biggest source of variance between an estimate and an invoice, and it is why we survey before quoting. Avondale has both kinds of house: the median home was built in 2002, but older neighborhoods such as Cashion include houses from the 1960s and earlier. Material tier. This is the part homeowners think decides the budget, and it is genuinely the smallest of the three. The gap between a mid-range and a premium counter is real but it is rarely what turns a project from one range into another. Which guide to start with If you are early and want a shape rather than a number, start with the whole-project cost guide for the room you are doing. If you already know the scope and are choosing between materials, the individual material and comparison guides will be more useful. If your question is really about affordability rather than price, the financing guide covers the options without the sales framing. And if you want a figure specific to your house rather than to the market, that is what the free in-home consultation produces — measured, written, and with the survey behind it. Why a local guide beats a national one Almost every remodeling article online is written to be read anywhere, which means it is written to be true nowhere in particular. That is fine for deciding whether you like a shaker door. It is close to useless once you start making decisions that interact with the building, the climate and the water coming out of the tap. Three things make Avondale different, and they run through most of what we have written. The first is water chemistry. Avondale&rsquo;s tap water is a blend of city well water and Colorado River water, and the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report put city well water at about 21 grains per gallon — very hard on the report&rsquo;s own scale. That changes which shower glass coating is worth paying for, how grout and natural stone weather, and how quickly a polished fixture finish stops looking polished. A guide that never mentions it will steer you toward finishes that look wrong within a couple of seasons. The second is heat. Avondale sits in the low desert at about 1,000 feet. National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals for the area put the July average high near 106&deg;F, with roughly 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or more, and the monsoon officially runs from June 15 to September 30, bringing dust and sudden storms. That combination is hard on anything installed outdoors and hard on anything that depends on a sealant joint. It also affects scheduling — some work is simply better done in some months than others, which is why timing your remodel is its own guide rather than a footnote. The third is that this is permitted work under a specific jurisdiction. The City of Avondale&rsquo;s Building Services Division has its own exemptions — cabinets, countertops and tiling need no building permit, while plumbing, electrical and gas changes do — and its own inspection sequence, including a pre-slope check and a shower liner test on new showers. The planning guides deal with that directly, and the Avondale permit guide is the place to start rather than a generic explainer. What a guide can tell you, and where it stops A cost guide gives you a range and, more usefully, the reasons a project lands at one end of that range instead of the other. Whether the layout moves. Whether the plumbing moves with it. What is behind the wall once it is open. Those variables are worth far more to you than a single headline number, because they are the ones you can still make decisions about. What a guide cannot do is price your house. Nobody can quote a remodel responsibly without standing in the room, and any figure produced without that is a guess wearing a decimal point. We publish ranges so you can sanity-check a bid and plan a budget; we produce actual numbers after a measured, in-person visit. If a contractor gives you a firm price over the phone before seeing the space, that is information about the contractor. The same applies to schedule. A timeline guide can tell you the order operations have to happen in and which steps cannot start until an inspection has passed. It cannot tell you when your particular job will finish, because that depends on scope, selections, and how quickly decisions get made once work is underway. How most people work through this library There is a rough order that tends to work. People start in the comparisons , because the first real question is usually a material one — quartz or granite, refacing or replacing, tile or a solid surface. Comparisons are the easiest place to form an opinion, and they are low stakes to change your mind about. From there the question becomes what it costs, which is where the cost guides come in, and then how it actually runs, which is process and planning . The room-specific libraries — kitchen , bathroom and showers and tile — are worth reading last, once you know roughly what you are building, because that is when layout advice becomes concrete instead of abstract. The accessibility guides sit slightly outside that sequence. If anyone in the household is planning to stay in the home long term, read them first rather than last — the decisions that make a bathroom work later, like blocking behind the walls for grab bars and getting a curbless entry right, are cheap while the wall is open and expensive once it is closed. If you would rather skip the reading, that is a legitimate option too. Home / Guides / Kitchen Design & Planning Guides Avondale Remodeling Guides Kitchen Design & Planning Guides Kitchen layout, cabinet, island, lighting, storage and backsplash guides for planning a kitchen remodel in Avondale, AZ. Kitchen decisions compound: the layout sets the cabinets, the cabinets set the counters, and the counters set the budget. These guides work through them in roughly the order you will face them. Kitchen decisions compound Kitchen choices are not independent, which is why the order you make them in matters. The layout sets what cabinets are possible. The cabinets set the counter runs. The counter runs set a large part of the budget. Changing the layout late unwinds all three. So the sequence worth following is: settle how the room works before you choose anything you can see. Where the sink, the range and the refrigerator sit relative to each other decides whether the kitchen is pleasant to cook in. No finish selection rescues a bad triangle. Where the money actually goes Cabinets are almost always the largest line. They dominate the budget in most kitchen projects, which is why the custom-versus-semi-custom-versus-stock decision has more financial weight than any other single choice. Moving plumbing or gas is the biggest hidden cost. An island that gains a sink is a different project from an island that does not. Worth deciding early, because it is expensive to add late. Electrical is the most commonly underestimated. Modern kitchens need more circuits than older houses have, and countertop receptacle requirements, dedicated appliance runs and range ventilation are the parts that most often need permit review. Permits follow the systems, not the finishes. Avondale&rsquo;s building code exempts cabinets, countertops, tiling and painting from a building permit. New circuits, moved plumbing and gas changes are not exempt and go through the City of Avondale&rsquo;s Building Services Division. Our Avondale permit guide covers what needs one. The upgrades people are most glad they made Consistently, in our experience: pull-out shelving in base cabinets rather than fixed shelves, layered lighting instead of one ceiling fixture, and drawers instead of doors below the counter. None of them photograph well. All of them change daily use. Equally consistently, the regret is under-specifying storage while over-specifying a feature — a statement backsplash in a kitchen with nowhere to put the mixer. # Remodeling Process & Planning Guides | Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/planning-guides.html

Summary: Timelines, City of Avondale permits, contractor selection and common mistakes: how a kitchen or bath remodel actually runs in Avondale, AZ.

Home / Guides / Remodeling Process & Planning Avondale Remodeling Guides Remodeling Process & Planning Timelines, City of Avondale permits, contractor selection and common mistakes: how a kitchen or bath remodel actually runs in Avondale, AZ. The questions that come before any material decision: how long it takes, who pulls the permit, what goes wrong, and how to tell a good contractor from a confident one. What actually determines how long a remodel takes Homeowners usually assume the timeline is set by the size of the job. More often it is set by two things that have nothing to do with size: whether the materials are on site before demolition starts, and how many inspection points the scope creates. City of Avondale building inspections run Monday through Thursday, and a request made by 3 PM is booked for the next business day, so every inspection point is a step the schedule has to wait for. A project that begins before the pan, the tile and the vanity have arrived will stall, and it will stall with your bathroom in pieces. We order and stage first and demolish second, which occasionally makes our start date later and reliably makes our finish date sooner. Permits are not optional, and who pulls them tells you something Any scope that moves plumbing, alters framing or adds circuits is the kind of work that gets reviewed. In Avondale that review belongs to the Building Services Division of the city&rsquo;s Development Services Department, and applications are filed online. Painting, tiling, cabinets and countertops need no building permit; plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC changes do. The city does not track HOA rules, so check with your HOA before anything is submitted. Our Avondale permit guide covers the details. The more useful signal is who offers to pull it. A contractor who suggests skipping a permit on work that needs one is telling you how they handle the things you cannot verify. It also creates a real problem at resale, when unpermitted work surfaces during a disclosure. The mistakes that repeat Deciding scope during demolition. Changes made once walls are open cost multiples of the same change made on paper. Settle the layout before anything is torn out. Choosing a contractor on price alone. The cheapest quote is frequently the one that has left something out, and the omission surfaces as a change order after you are committed. Not verifying the license. The Arizona Registrar of Contractors publishes license status and complaint history free. It takes two minutes and it is the highest-value check available to a homeowner. # Shower & Tile Design Guides | Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/shower-guides.html
Section: Guide categories
Summary: Shower design, tile, grout, waterproofing and glass guides for bathroom remodels in Avondale, AZ, where very hard water decides which finishes last.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Shower & Tile Guides Avondale Remodeling Guides Shower & Tile Guides Shower design, tile, grout, waterproofing and glass guides for bathroom remodels in Avondale, AZ, where very hard water decides which finishes last. A shower is the most demanding assembly in a house: it has to shed water for decades behind a surface nobody can inspect. These guides cover the parts that decide whether it does — waterproofing, slope, grout and glass. The part of a shower nobody can inspect A shower is the most demanding assembly in a house. It has to shed water continuously for decades, and almost everything that determines whether it does is buried behind a surface you cannot see once the job is finished. That asymmetry is the reason showers are where corner-cutting concentrates. Tile is visible and gets attention. Waterproofing, slope and the pan beneath it are invisible and are where a bad job hides. A shower that leaks rarely does so immediately — it does so quietly, into a wall, for a year or two before anything shows. So when you read these guides, notice how much of the content is about what goes in before the tile. That is not padding. That is the part that decides whether the shower is still sound in fifteen years. Slope, waterproofing, and grout are three different things Slope is what moves water to the drain. A flat or wrongly-sloped pan ponds, and in a curbless shower it ponds onto your bathroom floor. Linear drains make consistent slope easier on large or curbless showers because the floor only falls in one direction. Waterproofing is the membrane or coating behind the tile. It — not the tile, and not the grout — is what keeps water inside the shower. Tile is a wear surface. Grout is a filler between tiles and is not, and has never been, waterproof. Grout that needs sealing, cleaning or occasional repair is grout behaving normally. Grout blamed for a leak is usually covering for a waterproofing failure underneath. On a permitted job in Avondale, the city&rsquo;s inspection list includes a pre-slope inspection and a shower liner test before tile covers them — one of the few times anyone besides the installer sees that layer. Hard water changes the specification Avondale&rsquo;s water is very hard — the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report put city well water at about 21 grains per gallon — and it decides which finishes stay looking good. Clear glass and polished chrome show mineral spotting within days. Larger-format tile with fewer joints, treated or lightly textured glass, and brushed rather than polished metal all age better with less work. None of that is a reason to avoid the finishes you want. It is a reason to choose them knowing who will be maintaining them and how often.
