# Best Accessible Kitchen Features for Aging in Place (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-accessible-kitchen-features-for-aging-in-place.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Eleven accessible kitchen features for aging in place in Avondale, AZ: drawer bases, pull-down shelves, D-pulls, a lower counter, knee space and wall ovens.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Accessible Kitchen Features Aging in Place Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Accessible Kitchen Features for Aging in Place (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: The accessible kitchen features that do the most are the ones that stop bending and reaching: full-extension drawer bases instead of doors, pull-down upper shelves, a wall oven at waist height and a counter section at 32–34 inches. Add easy-grip hardware and faucets, good task lighting, a slip-resistant floor and enough clear floor space to turn around. Most of it looks like any well-planned kitchen remodel . The bathroom gets most of the attention in aging-in-place remodeling , and for good reason: it is where the falls happen. But the kitchen is where independence is quietly lost. It is the pot on the bottom shelf that becomes too much trouble, the upper cabinet that needs a step stool, the oven door that means bending while holding something hot. The features below are ranked by how much daily strain they remove for the money and disruption. Where we quote a clearance, it comes from the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design. Private homes do not have to meet the ADA; it governs public places. We use it as a benchmark because its dimensions are well tested, and we apply as much of it as the kitchen and the household actually need. The list Full-Extension Drawer Base Cabinets Pull-Down Shelves in Upper Cabinets D-Pull and Loop Hardware Lever, Touch and Touchless Faucets A Lower Counter Section Knee Space Under the Sink or Cooktop Wall Ovens, Side-Opening Doors and Appliances at Reach Induction Cooktop With Front Controls Layered Task Lighting Slip-Resistant Flooring Wider Aisles and Clear Floor Space 1 Full-Extension Drawer Base Cabinets Best single change for any kitchen A standard base cabinet is a door and a shelf: to reach the back you kneel, lean in and dig. Replace it with full-extension drawers and the whole contents come out to you, visible from above, whether you are standing or seated. Deep drawers hold pots and small appliances; shallow ones hold utensils and spices. This is the upgrade we recommend first, because it helps everyone in the household and never looks like an accessibility feature. Soft-close slides stop a heavy drawer from slamming back into fingers. See our kitchen cabinets page for construction options. Pros No kneeling or reaching into the back Works standing or seated Watch-outs Costs more per cabinet than a door and shelf 2 Pull-Down Shelves in Upper Cabinets Best for keeping upper cabinets usable Upper cabinets are the first storage to go out of reach, and the top shelf is where step stools — and falls — come in. A pull-down shelf is a mechanism installed inside the upper cabinet: you pull a handle and the shelf unit swings out and down to counter height, then lifts back into place. They reduce usable space a little and have a weight limit, so they suit everyday dishes and glasses rather than heavy serving pieces. In base cabinets that stay as doors, the counterpart is a pull-out shelf, which rolls the contents forward. Both can be added to many existing cabinet boxes, no full remodel needed. Pros Brings upper storage down to reach Often retrofittable Watch-outs Loses some cabinet space Weight limits on the mechanism 3 D-Pull and Loop Hardware Best for arthritic hands Small round knobs need a pinch and a twist, which is exactly the grip arthritis takes away first. D-shaped pulls, bar pulls and loop handles can be opened with a closed fist, a hooked finger or even a forearm when your hands are full. This is the cheapest item on the list and the easiest to add at any time. Choose pulls with enough space behind the bar for four fingers, and put them where a hand falls naturally: near the top of base drawers, near the bottom of upper doors. Pros Inexpensive Usable with a fist or forearm Watch-outs Long bar pulls can catch clothing in narrow aisles 4 Lever, Touch and Touchless Faucets Best at the main sink A single-lever faucet sets flow and temperature with one push of the hand, with no grip or twist needed. Touch and touchless faucets go further: a tap of the wrist or a wave of the hand turns the water on, which helps when hands are full, stiff or covered in raw food. Touchless faucets are one of the kitchen changes listed on our aging-in-place page. Pair any of them with a pull-down spray head so a pot can be filled on the counter instead of lifted out of the sink. Avondale&rsquo;s water is very hard — about 21 grains per gallon for city well water in the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report — and that scale is hard on sensor windows and aerators, so choose a model you can clean and service easily. Pros No gripping or twisting Pull-down spray reduces lifting Watch-outs Sensor faucets need batteries or power and occasional cleaning 5 A Lower Counter Section Best for seated prep and shorter cooks Standard counters sit at 36 inches, which is right for a standing adult of average height and too high for someone seated or much shorter. A counter section at 32–34 inches, as we set out in our aging-in-place guide , lets a person prep food while seated. The 2010 ADA Standards (&sect;902.3) put accessible work surfaces between 28 and 34 inches above the floor. It does not have to look like an afterthought. An island with a dropped end, or a baking counter set lower than the rest, reads as a design choice. Our kitchen island ideas show how a split-level island works in practice. Pros Seated prep becomes practical Easy to design in as a baking station Watch-outs Needs planning at layout stage, not afterward 6 Knee Space Under the Sink or Cooktop Best for wheelchair users and anyone who needs to sit An open space under the sink lets a person roll or sit right up to it instead of reaching sideways. The 2010 ADA Standards (&sect;306.3) call for knee clearance at least 27 inches high, and &sect;606.3 keeps a sink rim no higher than 34 inches. The drain pipes need insulating or covering so they cannot burn or scrape legs, the same detail we use on roll-under vanities on our ADA bathroom page. If nobody needs it yet, removable cabinet fronts can close off the space and come out later. A shallower sink bowl helps too, since a deep bowl eats into knee room. Pros Sink usable from a seated position Removable fronts keep storage for now Watch-outs Gives up sink-base storage once open 7 Wall Ovens, Side-Opening Doors and Appliances at Reach Best for anyone who dreads bending with hot pans A range oven puts the hottest, heaviest lift in the kitchen at knee height. A wall oven mounted so its rack sits around counter level turns that into a sideways slide. Side-hinged oven doors, which swing open like a cabinet, let a seated cook get closer to the rack than a drop-down door allows. Put a heat-safe landing counter right beside it. The same logic applies elsewhere. Our guide recommends raising the dishwasher 12–18 inches on a platform to cut bending, and a side-by-side or French-door refrigerator for easier access. Microwave drawers set below the counter avoid lifting hot liquids from above head height. Pros Removes the worst lift in the kitchen Works standing or seated Watch-outs Needs cabinet space for a tall oven tower 8 Induction Cooktop With Front Controls Best for burn and fire safety Induction heats the pan directly through a magnetic field; the glass only gets hot from contact with the pan. There is no open flame to catch a sleeve and no red-hot element after the pan comes off. Many models also stop heating when no pan is detected, and most have timers and lock functions. Choose one with controls at the front or side, so nobody reaches over a hot pot to adjust it. Two practical notes: induction needs magnetic cookware (a magnet that sticks to the base is the test), and anyone with a pacemaker or implanted device should check the manufacturer&rsquo;s guidance before switching. A cooktop set into a counter can also have knee space beneath it for seated cooking. Pros No flame, no glowing element Automatic shutoff on many models Watch-outs May require new cookware Check with a doctor if anyone has an implanted device 9 Layered Task Lighting Best for aging eyes Older eyes need more light and are more bothered by glare. Under-cabinet lighting puts light on the counter where the knife is, rather than behind your head where a ceiling fixture casts your own shadow onto the work. Add light inside deep pantries, too. Controls matter as much as fixtures. Our aging-in-place page puts outlets at 18–24 inches and switches at 42–48 inches to reduce bending and reaching, with large rocker switches that work with an elbow. Our kitchen lighting ideas cover fixture choices in detail. Pros Shadow-free counters Rocker switches work with full hands Watch-outs Best wired during a remodel 10 Slip-Resistant Flooring Best for spills and walkers Kitchen floors get wet in small, unexpected ways: a dropped ice cube, a drip from the sink, a splash from the dog bowl. Choose a matte or lightly textured surface over polished stone or glossy tile. Luxury vinyl plank is slightly softer underfoot, quiet and forgiving on dropped dishes; matte porcelain from our tile flooring range holds up to heavy traffic and hard water. Keep the floor level from room to room, with no raised thresholds for a walker wheel or a shuffling foot to catch. If the floor must change material, a color-contrasting edge makes the change visible. Our LVP vs. tile comparison sets the two side by side. Pros Fewer slips on spills Level transitions for walkers Watch-outs Heavily textured tile is harder to clean 11 Wider Aisles and Clear Floor Space Best for walkers, wheelchairs and two cooks Everything above depends on being able to get to it. The 2010 ADA Standards set a 60-inch turning space (&sect;304.3) and a 30 by 48 inch clear floor space in front of each fixture or appliance (&sect;305.3). For kitchens, &sect;804.2 calls for at least 40 inches between opposing counters in a pass-through kitchen and 60 inches in a U-shaped one. Not every home can reach those numbers, and not every household needs them. We use them as the target and tell you where your floor plan falls short. Opening a wall or moving an island is sometimes the change that makes everything else work; our small kitchen remodeling page covers how we find room in tight layouts. Pros Room for a walker, wheelchair or helper Two people can cook at once Watch-outs Can mean moving walls or an island The ADA kitchen benchmarks, in one table A private home does not have to meet the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design. They cover public accommodations. These are the figures we plan toward when a household wants a kitchen that will work with a walker or wheelchair. Requirement 2010 ADA Standards figure Section Turning space 60 in. diameter circle &sect;304.3 Clear floor space at a fixture or appliance 30 in. by 48 in. &sect;305.3 Knee clearance height 27 in. minimum &sect;306.3 Work surface height 28 to 34 in. &sect;902.3 Sink rim height 34 in. maximum &sect;606.3 Clearance between opposing counters 40 in. (pass-through) / 60 in. (U-shaped) &sect;804.2 What to do now, and what to plan for Some of this list can happen any weekend: D-pulls, a new faucet, pull-out shelves in existing cabinets, brighter under-cabinet lights. The rest belongs in a remodel, because it depends on layout, plumbing and wiring: drawer bases, a lower counter, knee space, a wall oven, wider aisles and a level floor. If you are remodeling anyway, it costs little extra to plan the second group now, even if nobody needs them yet. Our accessible remodeling page explains how we decide what is worth doing in a particular home, and the aging-in-place guide walks through the rest of the house. Planning an accessible kitchen in Avondale, AZ Accessible kitchens are not only for later life. Avondale is a young, family-heavy city, and the reasons for these features are usually closer to home: a parent moving in, a multigenerational household sharing one kitchen, recovery after surgery or an injury, a family member with a disability, or long-term owners who intend to stay put. The list above works the same way in each case — start with the changes that stop bending and reaching, then plan the ones that depend on layout, plumbing and wiring. Permits. The City of Avondale&rsquo;s code says cabinets and countertops need no building permit, so drawer bases, pull-down shelves, new hardware and a lower counter section usually go in without one. Moving the sink, adding a circuit for a wall oven or induction cooktop, or changing a gas line is plumbing, electrical or gas work, which is not on the city&rsquo;s exempt list. That part of a remodel goes through the Building Services Division of the Development Services Department (11465 W. Civic Center Dr., (623) 333-4000), with applications filed online through Accela. We confirm what your scope needs with Building Services and pull the City of Avondale permits for our work; see our Avondale remodeling permits guide for the details. Heat and hard water. National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals for the area show roughly 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or more, so an induction cooktop has one more advantage here: it puts less waste heat into a kitchen the air conditioner is already working to cool. The very hard water noted above also shapes fixture choice — we favor faucets with replaceable aerators and sensor windows you can wipe clean. Help with the cost. The City of Avondale&rsquo;s Home Repair Program (Neighborhood & Family Services, (623) 333-2703) lists ADA work such as grab bars, wider doors and ramps for eligible owner-occupied homes on City of Avondale water. It is not a kitchen program, but if a wider doorway is part of the plan, ask the city about current eligibility before you budget. Our Avondale location at 316 N Central Ave is open by appointment. We come to your Avondale home for a free in-home consultation and can plan the kitchen and the bathroom at the same visit. Frequently Asked Questions What is the most important accessible kitchen feature? For most households it is replacing door-and-shelf base cabinets with full-extension drawers. Everything in the drawer comes out to you, so there is no kneeling or reaching into the back of a dark cabinet, and it works for a standing or seated cook. It also looks like any well-planned kitchen, so nobody reads it as an accessibility feature. What counter height is best for aging in place? Standard counters are 36 inches. We suggest keeping most of the kitchen at that height and adding one section at 32 to 34 inches for seated prep. The 2010 ADA Standards put accessible work surfaces between 28 and 34 inches. A dropped end on an island or a lower baking counter is the usual way to fit it in without it looking out of place. Is an induction cooktop safer for seniors? In several ways, yes. There is no flame to catch clothing, the glass only gets hot from contact with the pan, and many models stop heating when no pan is detected. Choose one with front or side controls so nobody reaches over a hot pot. It needs magnetic cookware, and anyone with a pacemaker should check the manufacturer&rsquo;s guidance first. How much space does a wheelchair need in a kitchen? The 2010 ADA Standards set a 60-inch turning space and a 30 by 48 inch clear floor space in front of each appliance or fixture. They also call for at least 40 inches between opposing counters in a pass-through kitchen and 60 inches in a U-shaped one. Homes do not have to meet the ADA, but these are the targets we plan toward. Can I make my kitchen more accessible without a full remodel? Yes. D-shaped pulls, a lever or touchless faucet, pull-out and pull-down shelves in existing cabinets and better under-cabinet lighting can all be added to a working kitchen. Drawer bases, a lower counter, knee space, a wall oven and wider aisles depend on layout, plumbing and wiring, so they are best planned as part of a remodel. Do I need a permit for an accessible kitchen remodel in Avondale? Not for every part of it. The City of Avondale&rsquo;s code says cabinets and countertops need no building permit, so drawer bases, pull-down shelves, new hardware and a lower counter section usually go in without one. Moving plumbing, adding a circuit for a wall oven or induction cooktop, or changing a gas line is not exempt and goes through the city&rsquo;s Building Services Division. We confirm the scope with Building Services and pull the permits for our work. # Best Bathroom Storage Ideas (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-bathroom-storage-ideas.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: The best bathroom storage ideas for 2026: drawer vanities, recessed medicine cabinets, linen towers, over-toilet cabinets, shower niches and floating vanities.

Home / Blog / Bathroom Storage Ideas Bathroom Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Bathroom Storage Ideas (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: The best bathroom storage comes from building into the walls and upward instead of out onto the floor. Start with a vanity that uses drawers instead of doors, add a recessed medicine cabinet and a recessed shower niche, then use tall, narrow cabinetry such as a linen tower or over-toilet cabinet for bulk items. Plan it all during a remodel, when walls are open. Our bathroom vanities page shows the vanity options we install. Most bathrooms do not lack square footage so much as they waste it. A sink base with two doors and one shelf, a surface-mounted mirror, and a wire caddy in the shower are three storage decisions that each leave usable space on the table. These are the storage ideas we recommend most in our bathroom remodels, ordered by how much they change daily use. A few, like recessed cabinets and niches, only make sense while the walls are open. That is the main reason to decide storage early in a bathroom remodel , before tile and drywall lock in the layout. The list Vanity Drawers Instead of Doors Recessed Medicine Cabinet Linen Tower or Side Cabinet Over-Toilet Cabinet Recessed Shower Niche Floating Vanity With Drawers Drawer Organizers and Pull-Outs Double Vanity or a Long Single Vanity In-Drawer Outlet (Electrician and Permit Required) 1 Vanity Drawers Instead of Doors Best single storage upgrade If you change one thing, make the vanity mostly drawers. Deep drawers keep everyday items visible and reachable, while a door-and-shelf base turns into a pile you dig through on your knees. Drawers also hide the clutter that makes a bathroom look old fast. Doors still have a place. Tall bottles, a hair dryer, and cleaning supplies fit better behind a door than in a shallow drawer. A good split is drawers on the sides with a door or U-shaped drawer at the sink, where the drain trap sits. Our bathroom vanity guide walks through the configurations. Pros Everything visible at a glance No kneeling to reach the back Watch-outs Drawer under the sink must be notched around plumbing 2 Recessed Medicine Cabinet Best for small bathrooms A medicine cabinet set into the wall cavity between the studs adds real storage with essentially zero footprint, and it doubles as your mirror. It is one of the few upgrades that makes a small bath feel both bigger and more organized at the same time. Feasibility depends on the wall. Before we confirm a recessed unit, we check the wall cavity depth and look for obstructions such as plumbing vents, supply lines, and wiring. If the wall behind the vanity is a plumbing wall, a surface-mounted cabinet or a recessed unit on a side wall may be the better answer. Either way, a medicine cabinet above the vanity roughly doubles usable storage at the sink. Pros Storage with no floor or counter footprint Replaces the mirror Watch-outs Wall must be clear of pipes and wiring 3 Linen Tower or Side Cabinet Best for towels and bulk supplies A tall linen tower beside the vanity handles what the vanity cannot: towels, extra toilet paper, and backup supplies. In a primary bath with a long vanity wall, a tower at one end can match the vanity cabinetry so it reads as one built-in piece. The caution is scale. The most common small-bath mistake is trying to fit a full tub, a separate shower, a double vanity, and a linen tower into a room with space for two of them. A slim tower is worth it if the width allows; if it pinches the walkway, skip it and put that storage into the vanity and the walls instead. Pros Holds bulky items the vanity cannot Can match vanity cabinetry Watch-outs Needs spare wall width 4 Over-Toilet Cabinet Best use of dead wall space The wall above the toilet is usually empty. A shallow wall cabinet there uses vertical space that would otherwise go to waste and keeps spare supplies close without cluttering the counter. Keep it shallow and high enough that nobody hits their head standing at the toilet, and anchor it into studs or blocking. Closed doors look calmer than open shelves in a small room; open shelves are fine for rolled towels if you like the look and do not mind dusting. In a remodel we match the finish to the vanity so it looks planned rather than bought separately. Pros Uses space nothing else can Inexpensive to include in a remodel Watch-outs Must be shallow to stay out of the way 5 Recessed Shower Niche Best for shower storage A tiled niche built into the shower wall holds bottles without a protruding caddy and gives you a clean spot for an accent tile. One larger niche is more useful than several small ones, and a shelf inside the opening doubles the tiers. The niche must sit inside the shower&rsquo;s waterproofing, with its bottom pitched so water drains out, which is why it has to be planned before the walls are closed. Our shower niche and bench ideas page covers sizing, placement, and how the niche fits between studs. Pros No caddy, no clutter Works in any size shower Watch-outs Only practical during a shower remodel 6 Floating Vanity With Drawers Best for making a small bath feel bigger A wall-mounted vanity leaves the floor visible underneath, which makes a small room read larger and makes mopping easier. With drawers instead of doors, it can still hold a surprising amount. The trade-off is that a floating vanity gives slightly less storage than a floor-standing one of the same width, because there is no toe kick or base below. It also needs solid wall framing; we typically add a horizontal ledger or blocking between the studs to carry the load. A floating vanity lets you choose the height instead of accepting the standard 32-inch floor-mounted height. See the styles on our bathroom vanities page. Standard floor-mounted height 32 in. Support Ledger or blocking between studs Pros Open floor looks larger Height set to suit you Watch-outs Slightly less storage than floor-standing Needs blocking in the wall 7 Drawer Organizers and Pull-Outs Best low-cost add-on A deep drawer without dividers becomes a junk drawer. Drawer dividers, a pull-out shelf in a door base, and a tray for small items turn the same cabinet into organized storage. They cost little when ordered with the vanity and are awkward to retrofit to odd drawer sizes later. Think about who uses which drawer. In a shared primary bath, each person getting their own stack of drawers usually ends more arguments than a larger mirror does. Pros Cheap when specified up front Makes deep drawers usable 8 Double Vanity or a Long Single Vanity Best for shared primary baths In a primary bath, a double vanity at 60 to 72 inches or more gives each person a sink and their own storage. Keep at least a 30-inch clear path between fixtures so the room still works. If the wall is shorter, a longer single vanity with more drawers and counter can be more useful than squeezing in two sinks, especially if only one person uses the bathroom at a time. Our master bathroom ideas guide covers the layout side, and small bathroom ideas covers the opposite problem. Double vanity width 60–72+ in. Clear path between fixtures At least 30 in. 9 In-Drawer Outlet (Electrician and Permit Required) Best for hair tools, if you plan it properly An outlet inside a vanity drawer lets a hair dryer or trimmer stay plugged in and out of sight. It is a nice idea, but it is electrical work, not cabinetry. It needs a licensed electrician, GFCI protection, a product listed for in-drawer use, and in most cases a permit and inspection as part of the remodel. In Avondale, only like-for-like swaps such as replacing a receptacle are exempt from a building permit; a new outlet or circuit goes through the City of Avondale&rsquo;s Building Services Division. Treat this as something to raise at design, not a gadget to add later. Running a new circuit or relocating a box is straightforward while the walls are open and difficult once they are closed. If the electrical work is not in scope, a drawer with a heat-safe liner for tools is a simpler option. Pros Tools stay plugged in and hidden Watch-outs Requires a licensed electrician and usually a permit Must use a listed in-drawer product Which Storage Ideas Fit Your Bathroom Bathroom Start with Then add Small hall or guest bath Floating vanity with drawers Recessed medicine cabinet, over-toilet cabinet Primary bath Double or long single vanity, drawers over doors Linen tower, large shower niche Shared kids&rsquo; bath Drawer stacks for each person Shower niche instead of caddies Aging-in-place bath Drawers at an easy height Niche within reach of a shower seat Plan Storage Before Demolition The storage ideas that make the biggest difference live inside walls: a recessed medicine cabinet, a shower niche, blocking for a floating vanity, and wiring for an in-drawer outlet. All of them are straightforward when the walls are open and expensive or impossible once they are closed. At Infinity Kitchens and Baths we design storage alongside the layout during the free in-home consultation, then build it in during rough-in. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best way to add storage to a small bathroom? Build into the walls and upward instead of onto the floor. A recessed medicine cabinet and a recessed shower niche add storage with no footprint, a floating vanity with drawers keeps everyday items organized, and a slim linen tower or over-toilet cabinet uses vertical space that would otherwise go to waste. Are drawers or doors better in a bathroom vanity? Drawers are better for most everyday items because everything is visible and reachable without kneeling. Doors still work for tall bottles, a hair dryer, and cleaning supplies. A common layout is drawer stacks on the sides with a door or U-shaped drawer at the sink to clear the plumbing. Can any wall take a recessed medicine cabinet? No. The wall cavity has to be deep enough and free of obstructions such as plumbing vents, supply lines, and wiring. We check the wall before confirming a recessed unit. If the wall behind the sink is a plumbing wall, a side wall or a surface-mounted cabinet may be the better choice. Do floating vanities have less storage? Slightly less than a floor-standing vanity of the same width, because there is no base below the cabinet. Choosing drawers instead of doors makes up much of the difference. A floating vanity also needs solid blocking or a ledger in the wall, which is easiest to add during a remodel. Can I put an outlet inside a bathroom drawer? It can be done, but it is electrical work that needs a licensed electrician, GFCI protection, a product listed for in-drawer use, and usually a permit and inspection. It is best planned during a bathroom remodel while the walls are open, not added afterward. # Best Bathroom Ventilation & Moisture Fixes (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-bathroom-ventilation-and-moisture-fixes.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: The best bathroom ventilation and moisture fixes for 2026: fan sizing by CFM, humidity-sensing fans, exterior ducting, quiet sone ratings and waterproofing.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Bathroom Ventilation Fixes Bathroom Planning Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Bathroom Ventilation and Moisture Fixes (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: The best bathroom moisture fix is an exhaust fan sized for the room and ducted to the outside, not into the attic. The Home Ventilating Institute (HVI) guideline is 1 CFM per square foot of floor for bathrooms up to 100 square feet. Add a humidity sensor or timer so the fan runs long enough, choose a quiet sone rating so people actually use it, and protect everything behind the tile with a continuous waterproofing membrane. We handle all of this as part of a bathroom remodel . Arizona&rsquo;s dry air gives a false sense of security. A bathroom still produces a lot of steam every time someone showers, and if that moisture is not removed it condenses on the ceiling, behind the vanity, and inside the walls. That is where mold, peeling paint, failing grout, and swollen cabinet edges come from. This list covers the ventilation and moisture fixes we build into our bathroom remodels, from the fan itself to what sits behind the tile. We do not sell standalone fan swaps; these are the details we get right when we are already rebuilding the room, and the questions worth asking any contractor who remodels yours. The list Size the Fan by CFM, Not by the Box Duct It to the Exterior, Never the Attic Humidity-Sensing Fan Timer Switch A Quiet Sone Rating Fan Placement Near the Shower Continuous Waterproofing Membrane Behind the Tile Seal Every Penetration Plan for Monsoon Humidity 1 Size the Fan by CFM, Not by the Box Best first fix for any bathroom The fan should be sized for the room rather than for whatever came in the box. The Home Ventilating Institute&rsquo;s guideline for bathrooms up to 100 square feet is 1 CFM (cubic foot per minute) per square foot of floor area, so an 8&times;10-foot bath needs at least an 80 CFM fan. For bathrooms over 100 square feet, HVI recommends adding up the fixtures instead: 50 CFM each for a toilet, shower, and bathtub, and 100 CFM for a jetted tub. A primary bath with a separate toilet room may be better served by two fans than one large one. Much of Avondale&rsquo;s housing went up in the 1990s and 2000s (the city&rsquo;s median home was built in 2002), and a bathroom fan from that era is often a small, loud builder-grade unit that moves far less air than its label claims once it is pushing through a long duct. We check the existing fan during planning and replace it when it is undersized. Up to 100 sq ft (HVI) 1 CFM per sq ft of floor Over 100 sq ft (HVI) 50 CFM per toilet, shower, tub; 100 CFM per jetted tub 2 Duct It to the Exterior, Never the Attic Best fix for hidden moisture damage A fan that dumps into the attic does not remove moisture from the house; it moves it somewhere you will not notice for years. Venting into an attic is common in older housing and it is a code violation. The warm, wet air soaks into the insulation and condenses on roof sheathing and framing on cooler nights, and the damage shows up long after the bathroom looks fine. The duct should run to a roof or wall cap with a damper so outside air, and monsoon dust, does not blow back in. Keep the run as short and straight as practical, use smooth or rigid duct where possible, and slope it so condensation does not drain back into the fan housing. Ask any remodeler exactly where the duct terminates. Pros Moisture actually leaves the house Protects attic framing and insulation Watch-outs May need a new roof or wall penetration 3 Humidity-Sensing Fan Best for households that forget the switch The most common ventilation failure is not the fan; it is people turning it off as they walk out, while the room is still full of steam. A humidity-sensing fan turns itself on when moisture rises and runs until the room is back down. No one has to remember anything. These are especially useful in guest baths, kids&rsquo; baths, and rentals, and for homeowners who do not want to think about it. Most let you adjust the trigger level. In our dry climate, a sensor set too high may rarely trigger, so we set it based on how the room is used. Pros Runs when needed without anyone thinking about it Watch-outs Sensor setting needs tuning for a dry climate 4 Timer Switch Best simple, low-cost control If a humidity sensor is more than you want, a countdown timer switch does most of the job. You turn it on when you shower, and it keeps running for a set period after you leave. It stops the fan from being switched off too early and stops it from running all day because someone forgot. A timer is also a good fit where the fan is on its own switch separate from the lights, which we generally recommend. It is a small detail that is simple to add during a remodel while the electrician is already rewiring the room. Pros Inexpensive Easy for everyone to understand 5 A Quiet Sone Rating Best for making sure the fan gets used Sones measure how loud a fan is, and lower is quieter. A noisy fan is a fan people turn off. A quiet one can run long enough to clear the room without anyone noticing it. Compare the sone rating on the HVI-certified label when you choose a fan, alongside the CFM. Two fans with the same airflow can sound very different. Paying a little more for a quiet, well-built unit is money well spent; as we note in our bathroom remodel mistakes guide, a $150–$300 quality exhaust fan is not the place to cut costs in a remodel. What to compare CFM and sones on the HVI-certified label Quality fan (our cost guide) $150–$300 Pros People leave it running Better daily comfort 6 Fan Placement Near the Shower Best for clearing steam at the source A properly sized fan in the wrong spot still leaves a damp room. Put the fan close to the shower or tub, where steam starts, rather than in the middle of the ceiling or over the vanity. If the fan sits inside or directly over the shower, it must be a unit rated for that location and wired with the protection the code requires. Air also needs a way in. A gap under the door or a transfer grille lets replacement air flow into the room so the fan can do its job. A fan in a sealed room moves far less air than its rating. Pros Clears steam before it spreads Watch-outs Over-shower units must be rated for the location 7 Continuous Waterproofing Membrane Behind the Tile Best protection for walls and floor Ventilation handles the air; waterproofing handles the water. Tile and grout are not waterproof on their own. The membrane underneath is what keeps water out of the walls and subfloor. We apply a continuous waterproofing membrane to all wet areas, including shower walls, shower floor, and tub deck, before any tile is set, and slope every shower floor toward the drain at 1/4 inch per foot. For curbless showers the membrane often extends a few feet past the shower. If you prefer fewer grout lines to maintain, groutless shower systems give you a non-porous wall surface as well. Shower floor slope 1/4 in. per foot to the drain 8 Seal Every Penetration Best fix for slow, hidden leaks The weak spots in a wet wall are the holes: the shower valve, the showerhead arm, the tub spout, and any niche or bench. Each needs a proper seal or gasket tied into the waterproofing, not just caulk on the surface. The same goes for the fan housing and duct at the ceiling, where warm, moist air can leak into the attic around a poorly sealed box. These details are invisible once the room is finished, which is exactly why they get skipped. They are what separate a bathroom that lasts decades from one with a soft wall a few years later. Pros Stops leaks you would not see until damage appears 9 Plan for Monsoon Humidity Best for Arizona summers For most of the year the air in Avondale is dry. The monsoon, which officially runs June 15 through September 30, is the exception: indoor humidity climbs, bathrooms dry slowly, and a marginal fan that seemed fine in spring suddenly leaves mirrors fogged and towels damp. That is the season a correctly sized, exterior-ducted fan with a humidity sensor or timer earns its keep. It is also when poorly sealed penetrations and under-slope niches show themselves. Here the same storms arrive on top of desert heat and blowing dust, and the area averages about 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or hotter (National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals), so a bathroom that relies on an open window is working against the weather. Design the ventilation for the worst month, not the best. Moisture Problems and Their Usual Causes What you see Likely cause Fix during a remodel Mirror stays fogged after showers Undersized or poorly placed fan Size by CFM, move fan near the shower Peeling ceiling paint, mildew spots Fan turned off too early Humidity sensor or timer Stains or mold in the attic above the bath Fan ducted into the attic Duct to an exterior cap Soft wall or loose tile near the valve Unsealed penetration or missing membrane Rebuild with continuous waterproofing Dark grout in shower corners Standing water, slow drying Correct slope, better ventilation, fewer grout lines Why We Treat Ventilation as Part of the Remodel Almost nobody chooses a bathroom for its exhaust fan, yet almost every bathroom problem that is not a leak traces back to one. At Infinity Kitchens and Baths we check the existing fan, the duct route, and where it terminates during planning, and we replace or add ventilation as part of the bathroom remodel when it falls short. The fan goes in during rough-in along with the plumbing and electrical, so it can be inspected before the walls close. Frequently Asked Questions What size bathroom exhaust fan do I need? The Home Ventilating Institute guideline for bathrooms up to 100 square feet is 1 CFM per square foot of floor area, so an 80 square foot bath needs at least 80 CFM. For larger baths, HVI suggests adding 50 CFM for each toilet, shower, and tub, and 100 CFM for a jetted tub. Can a bathroom fan vent into the attic? No. Venting into the attic is a code violation and simply moves the moisture into the roof space, where it condenses on framing and sheathing. The duct should run to an exterior roof or wall cap with a damper. Ask any remodeler exactly where your fan duct ends. Are humidity-sensing bathroom fans worth it? For most households, yes. The usual failure is people switching the fan off too soon. A humidity-sensing fan turns on when moisture rises and runs until it drops, with no one having to remember. A countdown timer switch is a simpler, lower-cost alternative that solves most of the same problem. What is a good sone rating for a bathroom fan? Lower is quieter, and quieter fans get used. Compare the sone rating alongside the CFM on the HVI-certified label, since two fans with the same airflow can sound very different. A quiet fan can run long enough to clear the room without bothering anyone. Does Arizona dry air mean I do not need a bathroom fan? No. Showers still produce a lot of steam, and the monsoon, which officially runs June 15 through September 30, raises indoor humidity so bathrooms dry slowly. Without a properly sized fan ducted outside, moisture condenses on ceilings and inside walls, leading to mold, peeling paint, and failing grout. # Best Cabinet Colors (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-cabinet-colors.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: The best kitchen cabinet colors for 2026, from warm white and greige to sage, navy and natural wood, and how Arizona light and sun change each one.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Best Cabinet Colors Kitchen Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Cabinet Colors (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 8 min read Quick answer: The safest and most popular cabinet color for 2026 is a warm white or cream , followed by greige and natural light wood ; for a bolder look, sage or olive green , navy and warm charcoal work best on lower cabinets or an island. Cool, flat gray is fading. In Arizona, always judge samples in your own kitchen light, because strong sun warms and washes out colors, and keep dark or saturated colors away from cabinets that sit in direct afternoon sun. Cabinet color is the biggest single visual choice in a kitchen, and it is harder to change than hardware or a light fixture. The good news is that the palette has settled. After a decade of all-white and cool gray kitchens, what we are specifying in 2026 is warmer: creamy whites, earthy greens, deep blues and real wood. Our 2026 kitchen design trends guide covers the broader shift; this list ranks the individual colors and says where each one works. We describe colors generically on purpose. Every paint maker has dozens of near-identical warm whites, and the right one depends on your light, floors and counters, not a trending paint code. Bring big samples home and look at them morning and evening before you commit. The list Warm White and Cream Greige (Warm Gray-Beige) Sage and Olive Green Deep Forest Green Navy and Deep Blue Natural Light Wood (Oak and Maple Tones) Mid-Tone and Dark Wood (Walnut, Cherry) Warm Charcoal and Soft Black Cool Gray (Use With Care) 1 Warm White and Cream Best timeless choice for any kitchen A white with a slightly warm or creamy undertone is still the most requested cabinet color we paint or order, and it is the choice least likely to date. It reflects light, makes small kitchens feel bigger, and works with nearly every countertop, from white quartz to warm granite. The shift is away from stark, blue-leaning whites, which can read cold and clinical in strong, warm desert light. In a bright Avondale kitchen with west-facing windows, a cream can look almost yellow in afternoon sun, so test a large sample next to your countertop before you decide. Painted white shows scuffs on the lowers; a satin finish is easier to wipe than flat. Pros Never really goes out of style Brightens small or dark kitchens Pairs with any counter or metal Watch-outs Shows scuffs and grime on base cabinets Undertones shift a lot in strong sun 2 Greige (Warm Gray-Beige) Best for replacing a dated gray kitchen Greige sits between gray and beige, and it is where many homeowners land when they want something softer than white but still neutral. It hides everyday wear better than white, it looks right with both cool and warm counters, and it is the natural next step if your current kitchen is a cool gray that now feels dated. It works on a full kitchen, or as the perimeter color with a deeper island. Our two-tone cabinet guide lists greige perimeter with a charcoal island as one of the combinations we install most. The watch-out is going too beige: next to cream counters and tan tile floors, a warm greige can make the whole room look flat. Pros Hides wear better than white Bridges warm and cool finishes Watch-outs Can look muddy next to beige floors 3 Sage and Olive Green Best color for a calm, nature-forward kitchen Soft, gray-leaning greens are the color story of the last few years, and they bring a calm, natural note to a kitchen while pairing easily with wood, brass and warm whites. A muted sage is gentle enough for a whole kitchen; olive reads richer and is usually best on the lower cabinets or an island. Greens pair beautifully with warm metals, so this is where brushed or unlacquered brass hardware earns its place (see our cabinet hardware styles list). Keep counters calm, a warm white quartz or a soft natural stone, and let the cabinets be the color in the room. Pros Warm, current and still calm Works in craftsman and ranch homes Watch-outs Greens shift noticeably between morning and evening light 4 Deep Forest Green Best bold color for an island or lower cabinets A dark, saturated green is the dramatic cousin of sage. It looks tailored and expensive, especially on shaker doors with brass pulls, and it hides fingerprints better than any light color. We rarely put it on every cabinet in a small kitchen; it earns its keep on an island, the base cabinets under white uppers, or a single pantry wall. Deep colors carry more visual weight, so they need good lighting. Plan under-cabinet and ceiling light at the same time as the color (see kitchen lighting ideas ). Pros Rich, custom look Hides fingerprints and wear Watch-outs Makes a dim kitchen feel smaller Dark colors show dust on horizontal edges 5 Navy and Deep Blue Best classic accent color Navy has been a favorite island and base-cabinet color for years, and it has held up because it behaves like a neutral: it goes with white, cream, marble-look counters, wood floors and almost any metal. White uppers over navy lowers is one of the pairings on our 2026 trends list, and it reads classic rather than trendy. If you want blue but less contrast, look at slate blue or a blue-green; those softer, grayed blues are holding up better than flat gray. Brass hardware warms navy up; matte black or nickel keeps it crisp. Pros Classic, works with most finishes Good way to add color without going dark everywhere Watch-outs Very dark navies can read black at night 6 Natural Light Wood (Oak and Maple Tones) Best for warmth without paint Real wood is back, but not the orange oak of the 1990s. The look now is a light, natural or lightly washed oak or maple with visible grain and a matte finish. It adds warmth that paint can&rsquo;t, and wood lowers under light painted uppers is a combination that suits a wide range of homes. Stained wood also hides everyday wear better than paint, which our door style guide notes too. On slab doors, ask about grain matching across a run; on shaker doors, wood grain adds texture that keeps a simple door from looking plain. Pros Warm, natural, hides wear Pairs with nearly any painted color Watch-outs Wood color can change with long exposure to direct sun 7 Mid-Tone and Dark Wood (Walnut, Cherry) Best for traditional and craftsman homes Richer wood tones, walnut, cherry or a medium-brown stain, suit craftsman and traditional homes, and stained shaker in cherry or warm maple reads beautifully in that architecture. Many kitchens from the 1990s and 2000s were built with wood cabinets in these tones, and most Avondale homes date from that era (the city's median home was built in 2002, per Census Bureau survey data); if the boxes are sound and you only want a different look, our refinishing and refacing team can tell you whether a refinish or new doors makes more sense. Mid-tone wood is also a smart island color with painted perimeter cabinets, because it bridges a painted color and a wood floor. Pros Suits traditional architecture Hides wear very well Watch-outs Can darken a small kitchen Cherry naturally darkens over time 8 Warm Charcoal and Soft Black Best for a modern, grounded kitchen A warm charcoal (not a cool blue-gray) or a soft black gives a modern kitchen weight and drama. It is excellent on flat-panel doors, on an island paired with a light perimeter, or on lowers with white uppers. Charcoal with light counters and wood open shelving is a very Arizona-modern look. Two practical notes. Very dark finishes show dust, flour and hard-water spots near the sink more than mid-tones do. And an all-black kitchen needs more light than you think; most of the time we recommend using it on one element rather than every cabinet. Pros Strong, modern contrast Makes light counters and brass pop Watch-outs Shows dust and water spots Needs generous lighting 9 Cool Gray (Use With Care) Best only if it matches fixed finishes you are keeping We include cool gray because we still get asked about it. Flat, cool gray was the dominant cabinet color for roughly a decade, and it is now the color most likely to make a kitchen look dated. If you are keeping cool gray tile, gray counters or a gray floor, a cabinet color that works with them may still be the right call. If you are starting fresh, choose a greige, a slate blue or a blue-green instead; they give you the same restraint with more warmth. Pros Coordinates with existing gray finishes Watch-outs Most likely color to date a kitchen Can look cold in warm desert light Avondale Sun and Water: What They Do to Cabinet Color Avondale gets intense low-desert sun — the area averages about 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or hotter (National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals) — and very hard water, and both change how color looks and lasts: Strong, warm light shifts undertones. A white that looks neutral on a small chip under store lighting can read cream or yellow in a sunny kitchen, and greens and grays swing more than you expect. Test big samples on the actual wall, at the times of day you use the kitchen. Direct sun is hard on finishes. Painted and stained cabinets in a sunbeam from an unshaded west or south window can fade or change color unevenly over the years, and that shows most on dark and saturated colors. Window film or shades protect the cabinets as well as the floors. Hard water shows on dark finishes. Avondale's water is very hard (city well water averaged about 21 grains per gallon in the city's 2022 water quality report). Around the sink and dishwasher, dried splashes are more visible on charcoal, black and navy than on white or wood. Dry desert air makes solid wood move a little seasonally. A factory-applied finish holds up better than a brushed-on DIY coat. How to Choose Start with what is not changing: floors, counters, and the view. Pick the lighter color for the uppers and anything on the window wall, then decide whether you want one color or two; if two, our two-tone guide covers pairings, and shaker vs. flat-panel explains how door style changes the same color. If you are buying new cabinets, the color is chosen as part of the cabinet order . If you like your layout, a professional refinish is the budget route: our refinishing page lists $2,500–$7,000 for an average kitchen, done in 3–5 days. Frequently Asked Questions What is the most popular kitchen cabinet color in 2026? Warm white and cream remain the most popular cabinet colors, followed by greige and light natural wood. For accent cabinets and islands, sage and olive green, navy and warm charcoal are the colors we specify most. Cool, flat gray is the color most homeowners are moving away from. What cabinet color makes a small kitchen look bigger? Light colors such as warm white, cream and pale greige reflect light and make a small kitchen feel larger. Painting cabinets close to the wall color also helps the room read as one surface. If you want a darker color, put it on the lower cabinets or an island and keep the uppers light. Do cabinets fade in the Arizona sun? They can. Painted and stained cabinets that sit in direct sun from an unshaded window can fade or shift color unevenly over time, and the change is most visible on dark or saturated colors. Shades or window film help, and lighter colors hide gradual change better. Should upper or lower cabinets be the darker color? Keep the darker color on the lower cabinets or the island and the lighter color on the uppers. That grounds the room while keeping it bright, and it puts the bolder color on the pieces that are easiest to repaint later if your taste changes. Can I change my cabinet color without replacing cabinets? Yes. If the cabinet boxes are solid, a professional refinish removes the doors, cleans, sands, primes and sprays a new factory-grade finish. Our cabinet refinishing page lists a typical range of 2,500 to 7,000 dollars for an average kitchen, completed in 3 to 5 days. # Best Cabinet Hardware Styles (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-cabinet-hardware-styles.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Bar pulls, cup pulls, knobs, edge pulls or handleless? The best cabinet hardware styles and finishes for 2026, with sizing rules of thumb that work.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Best Cabinet Hardware Styles Kitchen Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Cabinet Hardware Styles (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 8 min read Quick answer: The best all-around cabinet hardware is a simple bar pull : it suits shaker and slab doors, it is easy to grip, and it works in every finish. Cup pulls and knobs suit traditional and farmhouse kitchens, while edge pulls and integrated or handleless fronts suit modern flat-panel cabinets. For finishes in 2026, warm brass and bronze are gaining on matte black and satin nickel. A common rule of thumb is a pull about one-third the width of the drawer. Hardware is the jewelry of a kitchen, and it is also the part you touch dozens of times a day. It is one of the cheaper pieces of a remodel and one of the easiest to change later, which is exactly why our 2026 trends guide suggests putting your trend-forward choices here rather than in the cabinets or counters. Below are the hardware styles we install most, ranked by how widely they work. The sizing notes are rules of thumb that designers use, not fixed standards; your door style and drawer sizes decide the final pick. Hardware goes on last in a remodel, after everything else is in place. The list Bar Pulls Cup (Bin) Pulls Round Knobs Knob-and-Pull Mix Edge (Tab) Pulls Integrated Channel (Handleless) Push-to-Open Hardware Appliance Pulls 1 Bar Pulls Best all-around choice for most kitchens A straight bar on two posts. It is the most versatile pull there is: on white shaker it reads clean and timeless, on slab doors it reads modern, and in brass on a green or navy cabinet it reads tailored. Bars are also easy to grab with a full hand, which matters for anyone with stiff fingers. Sizing is where bar pulls go right or wrong. The rule of thumb is a pull about one-third the width of the drawer, and on very wide drawers either a longer bar or two pulls. Common center-to-center sizes include 3 inches, 96 mm, 128 mm and 160 mm, so decide on one family of sizes before you order. Our door style guide pairs bar pulls with both shaker and flat panel. Pros Works with almost any door style Easy full-hand grip Available in every finish and length Watch-outs Sizing across many drawer widths takes planning 2 Cup (Bin) Pulls Best for farmhouse, traditional and craftsman drawers A half-moon cup you hook your fingers under. Cup pulls are the classic drawer pull for farmhouse and traditional kitchens, and they look especially good on stacked drawer banks. They are a natural pairing for shaker and raised-panel doors. They belong on drawers, not doors; the usual approach is cup pulls on drawers with knobs or small bar pulls on the doors. Cups have a small grip opening, so try them in person, and be aware that the inside of the cup collects crumbs in a baking zone. Pros Classic, warm look Great on drawer banks Watch-outs Tighter grip; harder with arthritis Drawers only 3 Round Knobs Best budget-friendly choice for cabinet doors A single-post knob is the simplest hardware there is: easy to install, small, and usually the least expensive per piece. Knobs are a traditional choice for doors, and small knobs on upper doors keep a kitchen from looking cluttered with hardware. The downside is grip. Turning or pinching a small knob is harder for aging hands than pulling a bar, and the 2010 ADA Standards (&sect;309.4) call for operable parts that work with one hand without tight grasping, pinching or twisting of the wrist. If anyone in the house has arthritis, lean toward pulls; see our aging-in-place remodeling page. Pros Simple and economical Low visual clutter on doors Watch-outs Harder to grip than a pull Can look dated on large drawers 4 Knob-and-Pull Mix Best for transitional kitchens The most common real-world scheme: knobs on doors, pulls on drawers, in one matching finish. It gives a kitchen rhythm, uses the more economical knob where it works well, and puts the easier-to-use pull on drawers, which you open far more and which carry more weight. Keep it to one finish and one design family so the mix looks intentional. If you want a single style everywhere, bar pulls on everything is the other clean option. Either way, lay the hardware out on the CAD drawing so every door and drawer is accounted for before you order. Pros Balanced, classic look Pull where it matters most Watch-outs Two part numbers to match and stock 5 Edge (Tab) Pulls Best for slim, modern flat-panel cabinets A thin metal lip that mounts to the top edge of a drawer or door, so the hardware is almost invisible from the front. Edge pulls keep flat-panel kitchens looking clean and uninterrupted, and they do not catch clothing in a tight galley, one of the reasons our small kitchen page suggests low-profile pulls. They need a door thick and solid enough to take the screws, and they suit full-overlay and frameless construction best. On lower drawers you are grabbing a small lip, so they suit hands that grip well. Pros Minimal, modern Nothing sticks out to catch hips or clothing Watch-outs Small grip surface Not every door material takes them well 6 Integrated Channel (Handleless) Best for a fully handleless European look Instead of hardware on the front, a finger channel is built into the top of the drawer or into a recessed rail in the cabinet box, so the fronts are completely flat. This is the cleanest look in cabinetry, and it is specified with the cabinets, not added afterward. It is typically paired with frameless construction and flat panel doors. Because it is designed into the boxes, it is harder to change later than surface hardware, and the channels need occasional wiping. It is a good choice for a modern kitchen you plan to live with for a long time. Pros Cleanest possible cabinet face Nothing to snag in narrow aisles Watch-outs Must be ordered with the cabinets Hard to change later 7 Push-to-Open Hardware Best for tall panels and appliance-matching fronts A mechanism inside the cabinet that pops the door or drawer open when you press the front. It gives a handleless look without a channel and works nicely on tall pantry doors, panels that hide appliances, and upper cabinets out of easy reach of a pull. Push-to-open fronts tend to collect fingerprints where you press, and some mechanisms do not pair with soft-close slides the same way. Ask to try the exact mechanism, and consider it for a few specific cabinets rather than the whole kitchen. Pros Handleless look on any flat door Useful on tall and panel-ready fronts Watch-outs Fingerprints at the press point Mechanisms add cost and adjustment 8 Appliance Pulls Best for panel-ready refrigerators and pantry doors A longer, sturdier pull designed for heavy doors. Panel-ready refrigerators, which our trends guide lists as a growing 2026 choice, need one that matches the rest of your hardware, as do tall pantry cabinets. Pick appliance pulls from the same collection as your cabinet pulls so the finish matches exactly; finishes vary between manufacturers even when they share a name. Confirm the mounting requirements with the appliance panel before ordering. Pros Strong grip on heavy doors Ties panel-ready appliances into the cabinetry Watch-outs Need to match finish to the cabinet hardware Hardware Finishes for 2026 Finish Look Pairs well with Watch-outs Brushed / satin brass Warm, current Green, navy, white, wood Check that tones match across pieces Unlacquered brass Warm, develops a patina over time Traditional and craftsman kitchens Changes color by design; not for anyone who wants it to stay bright Matte black Graphic, modern White, wood, light greige Shows hard-water spots and oily fingerprints Satin nickel / stainless Clean, neutral White, gray, stainless appliances Very safe, less of a statement Oil-rubbed or warm bronze Rustic, traditional Wood tones, cream, raised panel Can read heavy on dark cabinets Polished chrome Bright, retro-classic White and blue kitchens Shows every water spot and fingerprint Our 2026 trends guide notes that brushed nickel dominance is softening, unlacquered and satin brass and warm bronze are gaining, and matte black on everything is cooling. Mixed metals are fine when they are deliberate, for example a matte black faucet with brass cabinet pulls. Avondale's water is very hard — city well water averaged about 21 grains per gallon in the city's 2022 water quality report — so finishes near the sink show mineral spots; brushed and satin textures hide them better than polished or flat black. Sizing and Placement Rules of Thumb Drawers: a pull about one-third the drawer width, centered; very wide drawers get a longer pull or two. Doors: knobs or pulls near the corner opposite the hinge; on base doors near the top, on upper doors near the bottom. Consistency: pick one or two lengths and repeat them, so drawers of similar width match. Test the grip: order one of each and live with them before buying the whole kitchen. Changing hardware is part of almost every kitchen remodel and every cabinet refinish or reface ; new pulls on existing cabinets is also a classic kitchen refresh move. If new hardware needs new holes, plan it with the refinish so old holes can be filled before the finish goes on. Frequently Asked Questions What size cabinet pulls should I use? A common rule of thumb is a pull about one-third the width of the drawer. On standard doors, a shorter pull or a knob works, and very wide drawers look best with a longer pull or two pulls. Pick one or two lengths and repeat them across the kitchen so the hardware looks consistent. Should I use knobs or pulls on kitchen cabinets? Pulls are easier to grip and work on both doors and drawers, so they are the safer choice, especially for anyone with arthritis. A popular approach is knobs on doors and pulls on drawers in one matching finish. Using bar pulls everywhere is the other clean option. What cabinet hardware finish is in style for 2026? Warm metals are gaining, including brushed and satin brass, unlacquered brass and warm bronze. Satin nickel stays a safe neutral, and matte black is still used but no longer on everything. Mixing metals is fine when it is deliberate, such as a black faucet with brass pulls. What hardware is best for seniors or people with arthritis? Choose bar or D-shaped pulls that you can grab with a whole hand rather than small knobs or tight cup pulls. The 2010 ADA Standards call for operable parts that work with one hand and without tight grasping, pinching or twisting of the wrist, which is a useful guide even in a private home. Can I change cabinet hardware without replacing my cabinets? Yes. New pulls and knobs are one of the easiest kitchen updates. If the new hardware uses different hole spacing, the old holes need to be filled and touched up, so it is best to change hardware at the same time as a refinish or reface. # Best Faucets and Fixtures for Hard Water (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-faucets-and-fixtures-for-hard-water.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: The best faucets and fixtures for hard water in 2026: finishes that hide spots, ceramic disc cartridges, rub-clean showerheads, handheld showers and aerators.

Home / Blog / Fixtures for Hard Water Fixture Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Faucets and Fixtures for Hard Water (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: For hard water, choose brushed or satin finishes over polished ones, because they hide mineral spots between cleanings. Inside the faucet, look for ceramic disc cartridges, which hold up to mineral grit better than older washer designs. In the shower, pick a showerhead with soft rub-clean nozzles and add a handheld on a slide bar for rinsing walls and glass. Simple shapes with fewer crevices and aerators you can remove and soak make routine cleaning quick. We help clients choose fixtures as part of every bathroom and kitchen remodel . Avondale has very hard water. The city&rsquo;s tap water is a blend of groundwater from city wells and Colorado River (CAP) water, and the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report put city-produced water at an average hardness of about 21 grains per gallon (357 mg/L), well past the report&rsquo;s own &ldquo;very hard&rdquo; line of 10.5 grains. Total dissolved solids averaged about 649 ppm in the same report. The result shows up in every bathroom and kitchen: white spotting on faucets and glass, crusty showerhead nozzles, and cartridges that stiffen over time. You cannot pick a fixture that is immune to hard water, but you can pick fixtures that hide it, shrug it off, and clean up in seconds. These are the choices we steer clients toward in our remodels, ordered by how much difference they make day to day. The list Brushed and Satin Finishes Over Polished Ceramic Disc Cartridges Showerheads With Rub-Clean Silicone Nozzles Handheld Shower on a Slide Bar Aerators You Can Remove and Clean Simple Shapes With Fewer Crevices Pull-Down Kitchen Faucet in a Forgiving Finish Non-Porous Surfaces Around the Fixtures A Water Softener or Filter (General Advice) 1 Brushed and Satin Finishes Over Polished Best for hiding water spots Finish choice does more to hide hard water than any other decision. Brushed nickel, brushed stainless, and satin or brushed brass have a fine texture that breaks up the look of dried water spots and fingerprints. Polished chrome and polished nickel look great the day they go in, but every dried droplet shows as a white dot. Warm metals such as brushed brass and champagne bronze have largely replaced polished chrome on faucets and hardware in the bathrooms we build, and in our water that trend works in your favor. Matte black hides fingerprints well, but be aware that light mineral film can show on a dark finish, so it still needs a regular wipe. Hides spots best Brushed nickel, brushed stainless, brushed or satin brass Shows spots most Polished chrome, polished nickel Pros Spots far less visible Pairs well with the warm palettes popular now Watch-outs Matte black can still show white mineral film 2 Ceramic Disc Cartridges Best inside the faucet What matters most in a faucet is the part you never see. A ceramic disc cartridge controls water with two hard, polished ceramic plates that slide against each other. Mineral grit has little to grab onto, so the handle keeps turning smoothly and the faucet resists drips far longer than older rubber-washer designs. Most quality faucets use ceramic disc cartridges today, but it is worth confirming on the spec sheet, especially on budget models. Also check that replacement cartridges are available from the manufacturer. In hard water, the day may come when a cartridge needs swapping, and a faucet with a readily available cartridge is a quick repair instead of a replacement. Pros Smooth handle action over time Resists drips Watch-outs Confirm replacement parts are available 3 Showerheads With Rub-Clean Silicone Nozzles Best for keeping full spray pressure Scale builds up in showerhead nozzles until the spray turns uneven or shoots sideways. Showerheads with soft silicone or rubber nozzles let you rub the buildup off with your thumb in a few seconds, with no soaking or tools. This is the single most useful shower feature for hard water, and many manufacturers offer it across their lines at different price points. Pair it with a rain head only if you are prepared to clean the larger face regularly; a large, flat rain head has more nozzles to keep clear. Our walk-in showers page covers head and valve layouts. Pros Clears scale in seconds No vinegar soaks needed Watch-outs Large rain heads have more nozzles to maintain 4 Handheld Shower on a Slide Bar Best for rinsing walls and glass A handheld shower on an adjustable slide bar is useful for everyone in the house, from rinsing a child to bathing while seated, and it is also a cleaning tool. After a shower, a quick rinse of the walls and glass with clean, warm water removes soap before it dries with the minerals into a film. Pair it with a squeegee and you remove most of the water that would otherwise dry into spots. In an accessible or aging-in-place design, place the handheld within reach of the shower seat. The aging-in-place bathroom guide covers placement. Pros Easy daily rinse of walls and glass Helps seated bathing 5 Aerators You Can Remove and Clean Best for restoring faucet flow When a faucet&rsquo;s flow gets weak or starts to spray sideways, the aerator at the tip is usually clogged with scale. Look for faucets where the aerator unscrews easily, either by hand or with the small key supplied with the faucet. Some hide the aerator inside the spout, which is tidy but harder to service. Cleaning is simple: unscrew it, soak it in white vinegar to dissolve the mineral buildup, rinse, and reinstall. Doing this a few times a year keeps flow strong. Keep the key in a drawer where you will find it again. Pros Restores flow without replacing anything Watch-outs Hidden aerators need the right key 6 Simple Shapes With Fewer Crevices Best for fast cleaning Every joint, groove, and decorative detail is a place for mineral film to collect. A single-handle faucet with smooth, simple lines is quicker to wipe down than a three-piece widespread set with ornate handles and a separate base plate. That does not mean you have to give up style. Clean-lined designs come in every finish and price range. It is just worth running your hand over a faucet at the store and asking yourself where the white crust will end up. The same goes for the base: a faucet that mounts directly to the counter, without a deck plate, leaves fewer seams for water to sit in. Pros Wipes clean in one pass Watch-outs Fewer ornate style options 7 Pull-Down Kitchen Faucet in a Forgiving Finish Best for kitchens The kitchen faucet gets more use than any bathroom fixture. A pull-down or pull-out sprayer with a ceramic disc cartridge, a brushed or stainless finish, and rub-clean spray nozzles checks every hard-water box at once. Choose one with a solid docking mechanism, since a sprayer that will not stay parked is a common complaint. Consider the sink and counter as a set. A non-porous countertop like quartz wipes clean of mineral spots, which matters more here than in most markets. Our kitchen remodeling page covers how faucets, sinks, and counters come together in a remodel. Pros Handles daily use and hard water well Watch-outs Cheap docking mechanisms wear out 8 Non-Porous Surfaces Around the Fixtures Best for the whole wet area A good fixture surrounded by surfaces that trap scale still looks bad. Around the shower, a groutless shower system gives you smooth, non-porous walls where hard-water deposits stay on the surface and wipe away. With tile, large-format porcelain means fewer grout lines to clean, and a darker or mid-tone grout hides scale better than white. For shower glass, ask about glass coatings that resist mineral spotting and make cleaning easier. At the vanity, quartz tops never need sealing, so hard water has nothing to etch into. Pros Makes the fixtures look clean too Watch-outs White grout shows scale quickly 9 A Water Softener or Filter (General Advice) Best for treating the cause Every idea above manages the symptoms. A whole-house water softener or conditioning system treats the water itself, reducing scale on fixtures, glass, and inside appliances and water heaters. Point-of-use filters at the kitchen sink address taste and some contaminants but do little for scale elsewhere. Water treatment is its own specialty. It is not something we sell or install, and the right system depends on your water, whether you are on city water or a well, and household use. A water-test from a licensed plumber or water-treatment specialist is the place to start. Plan any loop or space for the equipment before the remodel so it is easy to add. Watch-outs Separate trade; get your water tested first Finish Comparison for Hard Water Finish Hides water spots Hides fingerprints Notes Brushed nickel / stainless Very well Well The safest all-around pick Brushed or satin brass Well Well Warm tone that suits current palettes Champagne bronze Well Well Soft warm metal Matte black Fair Very well Mineral film can show white Polished chrome / nickel Poorly Poorly Looks best but needs the most wiping How We Handle Fixtures in a Remodel At Infinity Kitchens and Baths, fixtures are chosen during design alongside tile, counters, and glass, so the finish, the cartridge, and the surfaces around them all suit local water. Plumbing fixtures, including faucets, showerheads, valves, and drain trim, are installed to manufacturer specifications and tested before we call the job complete. If your remodel replaces an older toilet or showerhead and you are a City of Avondale water customer, check the city&rsquo;s Low Flow Plumbing Rebate: $75 per toilet that uses 1.6 gallons per flush or less, and $25 per showerhead that flows under 2.6 gallons per minute. Apply within a year of the purchase with a dated receipt; the program is first come, first served. Frequently Asked Questions What faucet finish is best for hard water? Brushed nickel, brushed stainless, and brushed or satin brass hide water spots best, because their fine texture breaks up the look of dried mineral droplets. Polished chrome and polished nickel show every spot. Matte black hides fingerprints but can still show white mineral film. Do ceramic disc cartridges help with hard water? Yes. Ceramic disc cartridges use two hard, polished plates that mineral grit has little effect on, so the handle stays smooth and the faucet resists drips longer than older washer designs. Check that replacement cartridges are available from the manufacturer in case one is ever needed. How do I keep a showerhead from clogging with hard water? Choose a showerhead with soft silicone or rubber nozzles that you can rub clean with your thumb. For heads without them, remove the head and soak it in white vinegar to dissolve the scale, then rinse. Cleaning a few times a year keeps the spray even. How do I clean a faucet aerator? Unscrew the aerator from the tip of the spout by hand or with the small key that came with the faucet, soak it in white vinegar to dissolve the mineral buildup, rinse it, and screw it back on. Weak or sideways flow is usually a sign the aerator needs cleaning. Should I get a water softener before remodeling? It is worth considering, since a softener treats the cause of scale rather than the symptoms. The right system depends on your water and whether you are on a well, so start with a water test from a licensed plumber or water-treatment specialist, and leave space for equipment in your remodel plan.
