# Best Grab Bars That Don&rsquo;t Look Clinical (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-grab-bars-that-dont-look-clinical.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Nine grab bar types that pass for good bathroom hardware in Avondale, AZ homes: towel-bar combos, fold-down and vertical bars, finish-matched metals.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Grab Bars That Don&rsquo;t Look Clinical Accessible Bathroom Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Grab Bars That Don&rsquo;t Look Clinical (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: The grab bars that look least clinical are the ones that do a second job: a towel bar, a toilet-paper holder or a shower shelf that is also a rated grab bar. Finish-matched metals, fold-down bars and a single vertical bar at the shower entry cover most homes. None of it works without solid blocking in the wall — see our ADA bathroom remodeling page for how we install it. Most people who resist grab bars are not resisting safety. They are resisting the look — the stainless-steel tube from a hospital corridor, screwed to the wall at an odd height, announcing that somebody in the house has a problem. It is a fair objection we hear in most aging-in-place consultations, and an outdated one. The bars below are the types we actually install and recommend, ranked by how well they disappear into a finished bathroom while still holding a person who slips. We have not named brands; product lines change yearly, and what matters is the type, the rating and what is behind the wall. Where we quote a dimension, it comes from the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, §609. Your home does not legally have to meet that standard, but it is the best-tested benchmark available, and we design to it. The list Towel Bar / Grab Bar Combinations Toilet-Paper-Holder Grab Bars Shower Shelf Grab Bars Finish-Matched Bars (Brushed Brass, Matte Black, Nickel, Bronze) Textured-Grip Bars Fold-Down (Flip-Up) Grab Bars Vertical Entry Bars Slide Bar / Grab Bar Combinations Concealed-Flange Bars 1 Towel Bar / Grab Bar Combinations Best for bathrooms where nobody wants a grab bar yet This is the type that converts skeptics. It looks like a towel bar, it holds towels like a towel bar, and it is built, rated and anchored like a grab bar. Hung beside the shower or the tub, it sits exactly where a person naturally reaches when they lose their footing, and people grab towel bars in a fall whether or not they were designed for it. The catch is the word &ldquo;rated.&rdquo; An ordinary decorative towel bar, however heavy it feels, is held by small anchors and a thin mounting post. Buy one that is sold and labeled as a grab bar, and mount it into blocking. We install these in most aging-in-place bathrooms we build. Pros Reads as an ordinary towel bar Placed where hands actually go during a slip Watch-outs A towel draped over it hides the grip surface Decorative towel bars look identical and are not rated 2 Toilet-Paper-Holder Grab Bars Best beside the toilet in a small bathroom The wall next to the toilet is the single most useful spot for a grab bar and the one people most object to, because it is visible from the door. A combination unit puts the paper roll on or under the bar, so the wall carries one piece of hardware instead of two. Two cautions. First, the bar itself has to be the rated part; a roll holder with a decorative arm is not a grab bar. Second, the ADA standard wants nothing sitting within 12 inches above a grab bar and keeps the dispenser from blocking the grip, so some combination units put the roll in the way of a full-hand grip. At home that is a judgment call; we mock it up before we drill tile. The ADA side-wall bar is at least 42 inches long, longer than most combination units, so treat these as a compromise, not a full transfer bar. Pros One fixture instead of two Where people push up from the seat Watch-outs Shorter than a true side-wall transfer bar The roll can crowd the grip 3 Shower Shelf Grab Bars Best inside the shower, where a niche would otherwise go A shelf bar pairs a narrow shelf for shampoo and soap with a grab rail along its front edge. Inside a walk-in shower , where a bar is most needed and most visible, it earns its place twice. Once the shelf is loaded with bottles, the rail is partly blocked, and in a slip nobody has time to move a bottle. The ADA standard asks for 12 inches of clear space above a grab bar precisely because objects over a bar get in the way of a hand. Our rule: use a shelf bar as an extra grip point, and keep the main bar — usually a horizontal bar on the control wall — clear. It is the kind of detail we settle in the layout plan for any curbless shower . Pros Replaces a separate caddy or niche Adds a grip point inside the shower Watch-outs Bottles block the rail Not a substitute for a clear primary bar 4 Finish-Matched Bars (Brushed Brass, Matte Black, Nickel, Bronze) Best for any remodel with a defined fixture finish The fastest way to make a grab bar disappear is to stop it being the only brushed-stainless object in the room. Rated grab bars now come in the same finishes as faucets and shower trim — brushed nickel, matte black, oil-rubbed bronze, polished chrome and, increasingly, brushed and satin brass. When the bar matches the shower valve and the vanity faucet, the eye reads it as part of a set. Matte and brushed finishes also hide the water spots that Avondale&rsquo;s very hard water — about 21 grains per gallon for city well water in the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report — leaves on polished chrome. Brass tones vary between makers, so compare samples. We coordinate finishes across the whole room in our accessible bathroom remodels so the bars are specified with the fixtures, not added afterward. Pros Reads as part of the fixture package Brushed and matte finishes hide hard-water spotting Watch-outs Specialty finishes can cost more and take longer to arrive Brass tones vary between makers 5 Textured-Grip Bars Best for wet hands and arthritic grips A smooth, polished bar is slippery once it is wet and soapy, which is exactly when it gets used. Textured bars have a knurled, ribbed or lightly patterned grip surface over part or all of their length. The better ones use a fine texture that reads as a design detail. The 2010 ADA Standards (§609.2) set a round bar diameter of 1&frac14; to 2 inches. Within that range, most people with arthritis find the middle of the range easier to close a hand around than the thinnest bars, so try a bar in your hand before you choose. Inside the shower, where hands are always wet, this is the upgrade we suggest first. Pros Grips better with soap and water Fine textures look intentional Watch-outs Heavy knurling looks industrial and can collect residue 6 Fold-Down (Flip-Up) Grab Bars Best beside a toilet with no side wall Many toilets sit between a vanity and a tub, or in the open, with no wall on one side to take a bar. A fold-down bar mounts to the wall behind the toilet on a heavy hinge, drops down beside the seat when needed and folds up flat against the wall when it is not. Folded, it takes up little more visual space than a vertical towel bar. The mounting point carries the whole lever arm of the bar, so the blocking behind it has to be substantial — this is not a job for anchors in drywall. Check the manufacturer&rsquo;s load rating for the bar in its down position, and ask whether it locks in the up position so it cannot drop on its own. Pros Works where there is no side wall Folds out of sight when not needed Watch-outs Needs heavier blocking than a fixed bar Moving parts; check the lock 7 Vertical Entry Bars Best at the shower or tub entry One vertical bar at the shower entrance does more for the everyday act of stepping in and out than any other single bar. The hand slides up and down it as the body rises or lowers, so it works for tall and short users alike. A short, finish-matched vertical bar reads almost like a door pull. This is the bar we suggest when a client wants exactly one piece of hardware and no more. It is especially useful while a household is still using a tub; over the longer term, removing the step altogether through a tub-to-shower conversion is the bigger safety gain, and the vertical bar comes along to the new shower. Pros One bar, used by everyone Small and easy to style Watch-outs Supports stepping, not a seated transfer 8 Slide Bar / Grab Bar Combinations Best with a handheld shower A handheld shower on a slide bar lets a person shower seated or standing. Some slide bars are built as rated grab bars, with a heavier rail and anchoring meant to take body weight, so one fixture does two jobs. Ordinary slide bars are not rated and are held with light fasteners; a person who grabs one in a slip can pull it off the wall. The combination versions look nearly identical, so read the specification sheet for a grab bar rating and install it into blocking like any other bar. The same goes for glass-door handles: never treat one as a grab bar. Pros One fixture for the handheld and the grip Vertical, so it suits users of every height Watch-outs Look-alike slide bars are not rated 9 Concealed-Flange Bars Best for a clean, modern bathroom The exposed screws on a basic grab bar flange are a big part of the institutional look. Concealed-flange bars hide the fasteners under a snap-on or threaded cover, so the bar meets the wall with a plain round or square escutcheon, like a good towel bar. If you choose a non-round profile, check that it still gives a real grip: the ADA standard allows non-circular bars within set perimeter limits so a hand can close around them. The standard also sets 1&frac12; inches of clearance between the bar and the wall (§609.3), which is enough for knuckles but not enough for an arm to slip through behind the bar. Pros No visible screws Pairs with modern trim Watch-outs Some flat profiles are hard to grip The part nobody sees: blocking Every bar on this list is only as strong as what it is screwed into. Blocking is solid lumber or a backing plate installed between the studs before the walls close. Without it, a bar has to land on a stud, which is rarely where a hand needs it, or go into tile and drywall, which will not hold a fall. On accessible projects we install blocking around the shower, beside the toilet and along the tub wall whether or not a bar is going up that day; our accessible remodeling page explains why that is the one step that cannot be done cheaply later. The ADA benchmark, in one table A private home does not have to meet the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design. They govern public accommodations, not houses. We still use §609 as the benchmark for every bar we install, because it is the most carefully tested answer to how a grab bar should be sized and mounted. Requirement 2010 ADA Standards figure Section Round bar diameter 1&frac14; to 2 in. &sect;609.2.1 Space between bar and wall 1&frac12; in. &sect;609.3 Clear space above the bar 12 in. minimum &sect;609.3 Mounting height (top of gripping surface) 33 to 36 in. above the floor &sect;609.4 Strength 250 lb applied at any point, in any direction &sect;609.8 Toilet bars, side wall / rear wall length 42 in. / 36 in. minimum &sect;604.5 Why we will not install suction-cup bars Suction-cup bars are sold as portable and damage-free, and many are marketed as balance aids rather than support for body weight. Their grip depends on a perfectly smooth, clean, nonporous surface. Grout lines, textured tile, soap film and the mineral scale that hard water leaves behind all break the seal, and it can let go without warning. They feel solid when you test them by hand, which is the danger. If a bar is needed now and the remodel is months away, have a proper bar installed into a stud; a single grab-bar installation starts at about $300 on our aging-in-place page. Grab bars in Avondale homes: who needs them, permits and help with the cost Avondale is a young, family-heavy city, so the reason for a grab bar here is often not the homeowner&rsquo;s own age. It is a parent moving in, a multigenerational household sharing one hall bath, someone coming home after surgery or an injury, a family member with a disability, or long-term owners planning to stay in the house. The bars above suit all of them, and a bar that looks like good hardware is easier for the whole household to live with. Permits. Whether a bathroom project needs a City of Avondale permit depends on the rest of the scope. The city&rsquo;s code puts tiling on its exempt list, but plumbing, electrical and gas work beyond minor repairs is not exempt, so moving a shower valve, rebuilding a shower pan or adding a light circuit goes through the Building Services Division of the Development Services Department (11465 W. Civic Center Dr., (623) 333-4000), filed online through Accela. A rebuilt shower gets the city&rsquo;s pre-slope and shower liner test inspections, and the city inspects work before it is concealed — the same open-wall stage when we install blocking. We confirm what your scope needs with Building Services and pull the City of Avondale permits for our work. Our Avondale remodeling permits guide has more. Help with the cost. The City of Avondale&rsquo;s Home Repair Program (Neighborhood & Family Services, (623) 333-2703) lists ADA work such as grab bars, wider doors and ramps for eligible owner-occupied homes on City of Avondale water. Ask the city about current eligibility before you plan around it. Where to start For most homes the first three bars are a vertical bar at the shower entry, a horizontal bar on the shower control wall and a bar or fold-down beside the toilet. If you are remodeling, add blocking everywhere a bar might one day go. Infinity Kitchens and Baths plans this at a free in-home consultation — we come to your Avondale home, look at what is behind the walls and mock up bar positions. Veterans may be eligible for help with the cost; see VA bathroom remodeling grants . Frequently Asked Questions Can a towel bar be used as a grab bar? Only if it was made and rated as a grab bar and is anchored into blocking or studs. An ordinary towel bar is held by light anchors and will pull out of the wall under body weight. Combination towel bar and grab bar products look almost identical to decorative towel bars, so check the packaging or specification sheet for a grab bar rating before you rely on one. What height should grab bars be at home? The 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, section 609.4, put the top of the gripping surface 33 to 36 inches above the floor. Homes do not have to follow the ADA, but that range suits most adults. A vertical bar at the shower entry is placed so both short and tall users can slide a hand along it. We mock bars up at the user&rsquo;s own height before drilling tile. Are suction-cup grab bars safe? We do not recommend them for support. Their grip depends on a perfectly smooth, clean surface, and grout lines, textured tile, soap film and hard-water scale can all break the seal without warning. Many are sold as balance aids rather than support for body weight. A bar screwed into a stud or into blocking is the safe option, even as a stopgap before a remodel. Can grab bars be added after the tile is finished? Yes, if the bar can land on a stud or if the wall already has blocking behind it. If it has neither, the tile and drywall have to be opened to add blocking, because a bar anchored in tile and drywall alone will not hold a fall. That is why we put blocking in during every accessible remodel, whether or not a bar goes up that day. Does the City of Avondale help pay for grab bars? It may. The City of Avondale&rsquo;s Home Repair Program, run by Neighborhood & Family Services at (623) 333-2703, lists ADA work such as grab bars, wider doors and ramps for eligible owner-occupied homes that receive City of Avondale water. Eligibility and funding change, so ask the city about current eligibility before you plan around it. Veterans may also qualify for VA grants. # Best Kitchen Countertop Materials (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-kitchen-countertop-materials.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Nine kitchen countertop materials ranked for Avondale, AZ kitchens: quartz, granite, quartzite, porcelain and more, with typical installed prices and upkeep.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Best Countertop Materials Kitchen Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Kitchen Countertop Materials (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 10 min read Quick answer: For most Arizona kitchens, quartz is the best all-around countertop material: it is non-porous, never needs sealing, and shrugs off the spotting that Avondale's very hard water leaves behind. Granite is the best natural stone for heat and value, quartzite is the best choice if you want a marble look that holds up, and porcelain slab is the best pick for sun-exposed or outdoor counters. Installed prices on our projects typically run from about $8/sq ft (laminate) to $165+/sq ft (premium quartzite), per our countertop cost guide . Every week someone asks us which countertop is "best," and the honest answer is that it depends on how you cook, how much upkeep you will actually do, and how much sun and hard water your kitchen sees. A surface that is perfect for a weekend baker in a shaded kitchen can be the wrong call for a busy family with a west-facing window over the sink and an Avondale summer outside it. Below are the nine materials we template, fabricate, and install most often, ranked for everyday kitchen use in Arizona. Prices are the installed per-square-foot ranges from our countertop cost guide ; materials without a published range on our site get no number here, and we will quote them at your consult. For the head-to-heads, see quartz vs. granite , quartzite vs. quartz , butcher block vs. quartz , and granite vs. marble . The list Quartz (Engineered Stone) Granite Quartzite Porcelain Slab Sintered Stone Solid Surface Butcher Block Marble Laminate 1 Quartz (Engineered Stone) Best overall for busy kitchens Quartz is crushed natural quartz bound with resin, which makes it non-porous: it never needs sealing, and coffee, wine, and tomato sauce wipe off instead of soaking in. Patterns are consistent from slab to slab, so the sample you approve is what lands on your cabinets. That predictability is why quartz is the default we recommend for most households. Two cautions. Quartz is less heat-tolerant than natural stone, so use a trivet for hot pans. And strong direct sun over years can affect some colors, which matters for a counter under a big west window or in an outdoor kitchen. On hard water, quartz is a little easier to clean than granite because minerals sit on the surface rather than in pores. Our quartz vs. granite comparison goes deeper. Installed (typical) $55–$120/sq ft Sealing Never Heat Use trivets Pros No sealing, ever Consistent color and pattern Easy hard-water cleanup Watch-outs Hot pans can damage the resin Some colors can shift in strong direct sun 2 Granite Best natural stone for heat and value Granite is 100% natural stone, so no two slabs match. It is very hard, handles hot pots better than quartz, and resists stains well as long as it is sealed. At the entry level, domestic granite can actually come in under quartz, which makes it the value pick for homeowners who want real stone. The trade is maintenance: granite is porous and should be sealed annually. In hard-water homes, mineral deposits can build up around the faucet if the counter is left to air-dry, though unlike marble they do not chemically etch the surface. Because every slab is unique, pick your actual slab at the yard rather than approving a small sample. See granite vs. marble for how the two natural stones compare. Installed (typical) $45–$100/sq ft Sealing Annually Heat Very good Pros Excellent heat tolerance One-of-a-kind natural look Entry-level slabs are affordable Watch-outs Needs annual sealing Hand-select the slab; samples vary 3 Quartzite Best for a marble look that holds up Quartzite is not quartz. It is a natural metamorphic stone, sandstone transformed by heat and pressure into one of the hardest countertop materials available. It usually has the soft, flowing veining people love in marble, but it is far more durable and harder than granite. Like granite, it is porous and needs sealing about once a year. It also sits at the top of the price range, and some slabs sold as "quartzite" are softer stones, so buy from a fabricator who will test and stand behind the slab. If you want the look of Calacatta without babying it, this is the material. Our quartzite vs. quartz guide sorts out the naming confusion. Installed (typical) $85–$165/sq ft Sealing Annually Hardness Harder than granite Pros Marble-like veining Very hard and heat tolerant Every slab is unique Watch-outs Highest price tier Needs sealing 4 Porcelain Slab Best for sunny and outdoor counters Large-format porcelain slabs bring the look of stone with engineered performance. Porcelain is UV-stable, which is a real advantage in Arizona: it will not fade under a skylight, beside a sliding door, or in an outdoor kitchen . Maintenance is close to zero. Thin profiles allow waterfall edges and a crisp modern look that thicker stone cannot match. The flip side is fabrication: porcelain takes a skilled shop to cut cleanly, and edge profiles are more limited because the pattern is printed rather than running through the full body. Ask to see a mitered edge sample before you commit. We do not publish a per-square-foot range for porcelain, so we price it by the job at your consult. Sealing Never UV Stable Best use Sunny kitchens, outdoor kitchens Pros UV-stable in Arizona sun Near-zero maintenance Thin, modern profiles Watch-outs Needs a skilled fabricator Fewer edge options 5 Sintered Stone Best for serious cooks Sintered stone is made by compressing raw minerals under extreme heat and pressure. The result has zero porosity, excellent scratch resistance, and more heat tolerance than any resin-based surface, so hot pans and sharp knives are far less of a worry than on quartz. It shares porcelain's strengths (UV stability, no sealing) and its drawbacks: fabrication is specialized, chipped edges are hard to repair invisibly, and the color range is narrower than quartz. For a cook who wants a counter that performs as hard as it looks, it is worth a look. Like porcelain, we quote sintered stone per project. Sealing Never Heat Excellent Porosity Zero Pros Top-tier heat and scratch resistance No sealing Watch-outs Edge chips are hard to repair Specialized fabrication 6 Solid Surface Best for seamless sinks on a budget Solid surface is an acrylic-based material with the color running all the way through. Its best trick is the integrated sink: the bowl and counter can be one continuous piece with no seam or rim to trap grime, which is a genuine help with hard-water buildup around the drain. It is softer than stone, so it scratches and can scorch, but scratches can usually be sanded out and seams repaired so they nearly disappear. It is a smart choice for a budget build, a rental, or a secondary prep area, and less so for a showpiece island. We price solid surface by the job. Sealing Never Repairs Scratches sand out Heat Use trivets Pros Seamless integrated sinks Repairable surface Watch-outs Scratches and scorches more easily than stone 7 Butcher Block Best for warmth on an island Nothing warms up a kitchen like wood, and butcher block is a favorite for islands and baking stations in farmhouse and craftsman kitchens. It is also forgiving on knives and dishes. Dry desert air is hard on wood, and the Avondale area gets only about 7 to 8 inches of rain a year. Butcher block needs oiling every 3–6 months, should not sit under standing water, and can crack or warp near the sink or dishwasher if it is neglected. Many of our clients split the difference: quartz around the sink and cooktop, butcher block on a separate island. Our butcher block vs. quartz comparison walks through that combination. Installed (typical) $35–$65/sq ft Upkeep Oil every 3–6 months Pros Warm, natural look Kind to knives Watch-outs Dry air can crack it Risky around the sink 8 Marble Best for a statement baking station Marble is stunning and stays cool for rolling dough, which is why bakers love it. It is also the one material we always have a frank conversation about before recommending, because it etches: lemon juice, tomatoes, wine, and coffee leave dull marks that cleaning will not remove. Hard water makes it harder. Mineral deposits on unsealed marble can cloud and etch the surface over time, and marble should be sealed 2–4 times a year. If you cook a lot or have young kids, marble is the wrong main counter regardless of budget. As an accent on a baking station, it can be wonderful. Installed (typical) $75–$150/sq ft Sealing 2–4 times a year Etching Yes, from acids Pros Classic, timeless look Ideal pastry surface Watch-outs Etches from acids High upkeep in hard water 9 Laminate Best for the tightest budgets Laminate is the least expensive countertop by a wide margin, and modern patterns look far better than the laminate of past decades. It needs no sealing and is easy to clean. It scratches and chips easily, can be damaged by hot pans, and a standard laminate top generally works with a drop-in sink rather than an undermount. It makes sense for a rental, a laundry room, or a short-term refresh, but in a full kitchen remodel we usually steer clients toward entry-level granite or quartz for a longer life. Installed (typical) $8–$18/sq ft Sealing None Pros Lowest cost No sealing Watch-outs Scratches and chips easily Usually limited to drop-in sinks Countertop Materials Compared Material Installed (typical) Sealing Hard-water cleanup Quartz $55–$120/sq ft Never Easy Granite $45–$100/sq ft Annually Moderate Quartzite $85–$165/sq ft Annually Moderate Porcelain / sintered Quoted per job Never Easy Solid surface Quoted per job Never Easy Butcher block $35–$65/sq ft Oil every 3–6 months Wipe dry Marble $75–$150/sq ft 2–4 times a year Difficult (etches) Laminate $8–$18/sq ft None Easy Source: our countertop cost guide . Extras such as a sink cutout ($150–$300), specialty edges, and seams are listed there. Avondale Factors That Should Shape Your Choice Hard water. Avondale's water is very hard — city well water averaged about 21 grains per gallon in the city's 2022 water quality report — and it leaves calcium and magnesium spots wherever it air-dries. Non-porous surfaces (quartz, porcelain, sintered stone, solid surface) wipe clean; porous stone needs to stay sealed; marble can etch. Mid-tone, lightly patterned slabs hide spotting better than solid black or pure white. Sun. Arizona UV is intense, and the Avondale area averages about 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or hotter (National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals). If a counter sits in direct sun for hours a day, porcelain or natural stone is a safer bet than quartz or wood. Dry air. Low humidity is hard on wood, so butcher block needs a real oiling routine here. Permits. Under the City of Avondale's building code, replacing countertops is finish work that needs no building permit. If the new layout moves the sink, adds a cooktop, or needs new circuits, that plumbing, gas, or electrical work does — and we pull City of Avondale permits for our work. We can look at slabs with you as part of a kitchen remodel or a standalone countertop replacement , and we fabricate and install in-house. Frequently Asked Questions What is the most durable kitchen countertop material? For everyday kitchen use, quartzite and sintered stone are the hardest and most heat tolerant, and granite is close behind. Quartz is extremely stain and scratch resistant but less tolerant of hot pans. For most families, quartz or granite gives the best mix of durability and low upkeep. Which countertop is best for hard water in Arizona? Non-porous surfaces are easiest: quartz, porcelain slab, sintered stone, and solid surface all let mineral spots sit on top where a damp cloth removes them. Sealed granite does well too. Marble is the hardest to live with, because hard-water deposits can cloud and etch it over time. How much do kitchen countertops cost? According to our countertop cost guide, installed prices on our projects typically run about $8 to $18 per square foot for laminate, $45 to $100 for granite, $55 to $120 for quartz, and $85 to $165 for quartzite. Most full kitchens in popular quartz, granite, or quartzite land between $6,000 and $10,000 installed. Is quartz or granite better for a kitchen? Quartz is better if you want zero maintenance and consistent color, since it never needs sealing. Granite is better if you want a one-of-a-kind natural slab and more heat tolerance, and you do not mind sealing it once a year. Entry-level granite can cost slightly less than entry-level quartz. Can quartz countertops go in direct sunlight? Indoors, most quartz is fine, but strong direct sun over years can affect some colors because of the resin binder. For a counter under a large sunny window or in an outdoor kitchen, porcelain slab or natural stone is the safer choice in Arizona. # Best Kitchen Flooring Options (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-kitchen-flooring-options.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Eight kitchen flooring options ranked for Avondale, AZ homes: LVP, porcelain, wood-look tile, hardwood and more, judged on water, heat, sun, pets and comfort.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Best Kitchen Flooring Kitchen Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Kitchen Flooring Options (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 10 min read Quick answer: For most Arizona kitchens, the two best floors are rigid-core luxury vinyl plank (LVP) and porcelain tile . LVP is 100% waterproof, softer and warmer underfoot, and handles Avondale's dry air and summer heat without cupping when it is installed with proper expansion gaps; porcelain is the most durable and water-resistant floor you can buy and the best partner for radiant heat. Solid hardwood and standard laminate are the riskiest choices near a sink in our climate. See LVP vs. tile for the head-to-head. A kitchen floor takes more abuse than any other surface in the house: dropped pans, dishwasher leaks, pet bowls, sand tracked in from the yard, and hours of standing at the counter. In Avondale it also has to cope with very dry air, serious summer heat — the area averages about 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or hotter (National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals) — monsoon dust tracked in at the back door, and strong sun pouring through west-facing patio doors. These are the eight kitchen floors we see most, ranked by how well they hold up in real Arizona kitchens. We install luxury vinyl plank and tile flooring as part of our kitchen remodels, so the top of the list reflects what we trust in our own clients' homes. Because our pages quote installed flooring prices in more than one place, we have left dollar figures off this list; the LVP vs. tile cost breakdown has current numbers for the two front-runners. The list Rigid-Core Luxury Vinyl Plank (SPC) Porcelain Tile Wood-Look Porcelain Plank Ceramic Tile Natural Stone Tile (Slate, Travertine) Engineered Hardwood Solid Hardwood Laminate 1 Rigid-Core Luxury Vinyl Plank (SPC) Best overall for busy kitchens Rigid-core LVP is 100% waterproof all the way through the plank, so a spilled pot or a slow dishwasher leak will not swell or delaminate it. It is noticeably softer and warmer underfoot than tile, which your back will appreciate after a long day of cooking, and the best products are hard to tell from real wood. In dry desert air, solid hardwood can cup and gap; quality SPC stays far more stable. It still expands with heat, though, so in a kitchen with a big west-facing slider, insist on proper expansion gaps and use window coverings, because strong afternoon sun can heat a run of planks well above room temperature. Skip standard LVP in a garage or other space that isn't air-conditioned. Most click-lock products can float over an existing floor, and a single room usually goes in in one day. For homes with kids or dogs, do not go below a 12 mil wear layer, and step up to 20 mil for multiple large dogs. More on our LVP flooring page . Water 100% waterproof core Wear layer 12 mil minimum; 20 mil for heavy use Relative cost Low to moderate Pros Waterproof Comfortable underfoot Stable in dry air Watch-outs Can dent under very heavy point loads Some products fade in strong direct sun 2 Porcelain Tile Best for durability and radiant heat Porcelain is clay fired at very high temperatures, with water absorption below 0.5%, which is the ANSI definition of porcelain. It is harder and denser than ceramic, resists stains without sealing, and does not expand or contract meaningfully with temperature. Pick a matte or textured finish for a kitchen; polished tile looks sleek but gets slippery when wet. The trade-offs are comfort and installation. Tile is hard and cold underfoot, a dropped glass will not survive, and it needs a flat, properly prepared subfloor. Its cool surface is a plus through an Avondale summer, and porcelain is also the ideal partner for electric radiant heat if you want the chill off on winter mornings. Grout is the weak link, so ask about a stain-resistant grout and a mid-tone color. See our tile flooring service . Water absorption Below 0.5% (ANSI) Hardness PEI 3–5 Relative cost Moderate to high Pros Extremely durable Best with radiant heat No sealing on the tile itself Watch-outs Hard and cold underfoot Grout needs attention 3 Wood-Look Porcelain Plank Best for a wood look with zero water worries Wood-look porcelain plank gives you the long, grained boards of hardwood with all the durability of porcelain. It is a favorite in Arizona homes that run one floor from the kitchen through the living area and out toward the patio, because it does not care about sun, sand, water, or pet claws. Long planks demand a very flat subfloor and careful layout to avoid lippage, so installation takes longer than LVP, and it has the same hard, cool feel as any tile. A narrow grout joint in a color close to the tile keeps the wood illusion convincing. If you love the look of wood but live with dogs and a busy back door, this is the one we point you to. Our porcelain vs. ceramic guide covers the tile basics. Look Hardwood Water Waterproof tile body Relative cost Moderate to high Pros Wood look, tile toughness Handles sun and pets Watch-outs Needs a very flat subfloor Hard underfoot 4 Ceramic Tile Best budget tile Ceramic tile costs less than porcelain and comes in endless colors and patterns. For a kitchen floor, choose a floor-rated ceramic with a PEI rating of 3 or higher; lower ratings are meant for walls and light-traffic rooms. Ceramic absorbs more water than porcelain and has a softer body under the glaze, so a chip shows the clay color underneath. It works well in a lightly used kitchen or a budget refresh, but in a busy family kitchen we usually recommend porcelain because the cost difference is modest and it holds up better over decades. The full breakdown is in our porcelain vs. ceramic tile comparison . Floor rating PEI 3 or higher Relative cost Low to moderate Pros Lower cost than porcelain Huge design range Watch-outs Chips show the body color Less durable than porcelain 5 Natural Stone Tile (Slate, Travertine) Best for one-of-a-kind character Slate, travertine, and other natural stone tiles make dramatic floors that suit Southwest and rustic homes, and slate's cleft texture gives natural slip resistance. Stone handles Arizona's climate well, indoors and out. Natural stone is porous, so it must be sealed at installation and periodically after that, and softer stones such as travertine and marble can scratch and etch from acidic spills. That makes stone a higher-maintenance kitchen floor than porcelain. If you love it, slate is the more forgiving choice for a working kitchen. Sealing At install and periodically Relative cost High Pros Unique, natural character Slate is naturally grippy Watch-outs Needs sealing Travertine and marble can etch 6 Engineered Hardwood Best real wood for dry climates Engineered hardwood has a real wood top layer over a cross-laminated core, which makes it much more stable than solid wood in Arizona's very dry air. If you want genuine wood in an open-concept kitchen that flows into the living room, it is the better of the two wood options. It is still water-sensitive. Standing water at the sink or a dishwasher leak can damage it, and it needs on-site acclimation for several days before installation. Strong sun through big windows can also fade wood over the years. Many engineered products are rated for radiant heat, which solid hardwood usually is not. Water Sensitive Acclimation Several days on site Relative cost Moderate to high Pros Real wood surface More stable than solid wood Watch-outs Not waterproof Can fade in strong sun 7 Solid Hardwood Best for resale warmth, with care Nothing matches the warmth and character of solid hardwood, and it can be refinished more than once. Buyers love it. In our climate, though, solid hardwood is the floor we see fail most often. Desert air keeps indoor humidity low, and seasonal shifts make solid wood expand and contract, which leads to cupping, gapping, and splitting, and a kitchen adds spills and leaks to the mix. If you want it anyway, plan for steady indoor humidity (often a whole-home humidifier), wipe spills immediately, and consider engineered wood or wood-look porcelain near the sink. Water Sensitive Dry-air risk High Relative cost High Pros Classic warmth Can be refinished Watch-outs Moves with dry air Vulnerable to leaks 8 Laminate Best for bedrooms, not kitchens Laminate fuses a photographic wood-look layer over a dense fiberboard core under a tough wear layer. It is affordable, scratch resistant, and quick to install, and it does well in bedrooms and living areas. Its weakness is water: standard laminate's fiberboard core swells if moisture reaches the seams, so it is a poor choice for kitchens and baths. At a similar budget, rigid-core LVP is the better kitchen floor. We include laminate here mainly so you know why we will steer you away from it at the sink. Water Core swells if wet Relative cost Low Pros Affordable Scratch resistant Watch-outs Poor water resistance Not recommended for kitchens Kitchen Flooring at a Glance Floor Water Comfort Dry-air stability Relative cost Rigid-core LVP Waterproof Soft, warm Excellent Low–moderate Porcelain tile Waterproof tile, porous grout Hard, cool Excellent Moderate–high Wood-look porcelain Waterproof tile, porous grout Hard, cool Excellent Moderate–high Ceramic tile Good Hard, cool Excellent Low–moderate Natural stone Needs sealing Hard, cool Excellent High Engineered hardwood Sensitive Warm Good Moderate–high Solid hardwood Sensitive Warm Poor High Laminate Poor Moderate Good Low How to Choose for Your Kitchen Open plan? LVP runs from kitchen to living room without transitions and floats over many existing floors, which keeps doorway heights manageable. Summer heat? Porcelain stays cool underfoot and doesn't move with temperature. LVP does well indoors with proper expansion gaps, but keep it out of the garage and other spaces that aren't air-conditioned. Monsoon dust? Monsoon season runs June 15 to Sept. 30, and storms bring dust and mud to the back door. A mid-tone floor and grout hide it better than very light or very dark finishes, and a good mat at the patio door saves the floor. Chilly winter mornings? Winters here are mild, but porcelain with an electric radiant mat is the most comfortable tile floor you can own. Our bathroom flooring guide covers radiant heat in more detail, and the same systems work in kitchens. Big sunny windows? Arizona UV can fade wood, laminate, and some vinyl over the years. Porcelain does not fade; for other floors, plan on window treatments. Pets and kids? SPC vinyl with a thick wear layer and porcelain tile both shrug off claws far better than wood or laminate. Permits? Under the City of Avondale's building code, tiling, carpeting and similar floor finish work need no building permit on their own. If the remodel also moves plumbing or adds circuits, that work is permitted and inspected through the city, and we pull those permits for our work. We handle flooring as part of a full kitchen remodel , coordinated with cabinets and plumbing from day one, and floor choice often comes down to what sits next to it. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best flooring for a kitchen in Arizona? Rigid-core luxury vinyl plank and porcelain tile are the two best choices. LVP is waterproof, comfortable underfoot, and stable in dry air. Porcelain is the most durable and water-resistant option and pairs well with radiant heat. Solid hardwood and standard laminate are the riskiest near a kitchen sink. Is LVP or tile better for a kitchen? LVP is better if you want comfort underfoot, a faster install, and a lower cost. Porcelain tile is better if you want the longest possible life, radiant heat, or a floor that will never fade in the sun. Both are waterproof at the surface; with tile, the grout joints are the part that needs care. Can you put hardwood in an Avondale kitchen? You can, but it takes care. Avondale's desert air is very dry, and indoor humidity shifts between seasons, which makes solid hardwood expand and contract and can lead to cupping and gaps. Engineered hardwood is more stable, and wood-look porcelain or LVP gives a similar look with no water risk. What wear layer should kitchen LVP have? For a household with kids, dogs, or heavy traffic, do not go below a 12 mil wear layer. If you have multiple large dogs or want the floor to look new longer, choose a 20 mil commercial-grade product. Thicker wear layers resist scratches and scuffs longer. Is porcelain tile slippery in a kitchen? Polished porcelain can be slippery when wet. For kitchens, choose a matte or textured finish. For wet floor areas, look for a DCOF rating of 0.42 or higher under the ANSI A326.3 standard, which most textured porcelain floor tile meets. # Best Kitchen Layouts for Small Homes (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-kitchen-layouts-for-small-homes.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Galley, L-shape, one-wall, U-shape, peninsula or island? How to pick the best kitchen layout for a small home, with the clearances that decide it.

Home / Blog / Best Small-Home Kitchen Layouts Kitchen Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Kitchen Layouts for Small Homes (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: For most small homes the best kitchen layout is an L-shape (it opens to the living area and handles a corner well), followed by a well-planned galley when the room is long and narrow and a peninsula when you want seating but lack room for an island. Choose by clearance first: keep at least 42 inches between facing counters in a galley, and only add an island if you can hold at least 36 inches of walkway on every side. See our small kitchen remodeling page for the storage, lighting and appliance side of the job. In a small home the layout is the one decision you can&rsquo;t fix later with paint or hardware. It sets where the plumbing and gas run, how many people can work at once, how much counter you get between the sink and the range, and whether the kitchen feels like part of the house or a corridor behind a wall. We redraw a lot of older kitchens, and the pattern is familiar: a closed galley or a cramped U that was never planned for two cooks. This list ranks the layouts we recommend most often for compact footprints, with what each one needs in floor space and where it goes wrong. For the finishing moves that make a small kitchen feel bigger (ceiling-height cabinets, lighter colors, compact appliances, lighting), read our small kitchen remodeling guide . The clearances below are general planning guidelines, not code requirements; your actual room, doors and windows decide the final drawing. The list L-Shape Galley (Two Parallel Runs) One-Wall Peninsula (G-Shape) L-Shape Plus Island U-Shape One-Wall Plus Island Open Galley (Remove One Side Wall) 1 L-Shape Best all-around layout for small, open homes Two runs of cabinets meeting at a corner. The L is our default recommendation for small homes because it leaves two sides of the room open, so the kitchen reads as part of the living or dining area instead of a closed box. It naturally forms a tight work triangle with the sink on one leg and the range on the other, and it keeps traffic out of the cook&rsquo;s path. The weak spot is the corner. Without a lazy Susan or blind-corner pull-out, that inside corner becomes a dead zone, so plan the corner cabinet at the same time as the layout (our kitchen cabinets page covers the options). Keep the legs balanced if you can; one very long leg and one stub makes the triangle lopsided. Pros Open on two sides; feels larger Easy work triangle Room to add a small table or peninsula later Watch-outs Corner storage needs a real solution Less upper storage than a U 2 Galley (Two Parallel Runs) Best for long, narrow rooms and one main cook Two facing runs with an aisle between them. Galleys have a bad reputation because so many older ones are dark and closed at both ends, but the layout itself is one of the most efficient ever drawn: every step is short and there is counter on both sides of you. The key number on our small kitchen page is an aisle of at least 42 inches between the two runs so appliance doors can open and you can pass the person at the sink. Put the sink and range on opposite runs, slightly offset, so two people are not standing back to back at hot and wet stations. If one end of the galley is a wall you can open, that single change usually matters more than any cabinet upgrade (see item 8). Pros Very short walking distances Maximum counter and base cabinet run for the floor area Cheaper to plumb if you keep the sink wall Watch-outs Crowded with two cooks unless the aisle is generous Can feel tunnel-like if both ends are closed 3 One-Wall Best for studios, casitas and ADU conversions Everything on a single wall: refrigerator, sink, range and cabinets in one line. It uses the least floor area of any layout, which is why we use it in garage conversions and casitas (see garage conversion ADUs ). Plumbing and venting all live on one wall, which keeps the rough-in simple. The trade-off is counter space and walking. There is no triangle, only a line, so put the sink in the middle with the refrigerator at one end and the range at the other, and protect a clear stretch of counter between sink and range for prep. Run the upper cabinets to the ceiling, because you only get one wall of them. If the room allows it later, a one-wall kitchen plus an island (item 7) is the natural upgrade. Pros Smallest footprint Simplest plumbing and venting Leaves the rest of the room open Watch-outs Limited counter and storage Long walks if the wall is long 4 Peninsula (G-Shape) Best way to get seating without room for an island A peninsula is a counter run attached to the end of an L or U, open on three sides. It gives you most of what people want from an island (a seating edge, more prep space, a place for guests to land) while using less floor, because you only need walkway on the open sides. Our kitchen island guide says it plainly: if you can&rsquo;t hold 36 inches of clearance all the way around an island, a peninsula is usually the smarter call. For seating, the same island rules apply: about 12 inches of overhang and roughly 24 inches of width per stool. Pros Seating and prep space in a small room Needs less clearance than an island Adds base cabinets and drawers Watch-outs Can create a dead-end if it blocks the entry The inside corner still needs a storage solution 5 L-Shape Plus Island Best for small homes with an open great room If your kitchen opens to a family room and you have the floor for it, an L with an island is the most flexible plan there is: the L carries the appliances and the island becomes the prep, seating and serving surface. It only works if the clearances hold. Per our island guide , keep at least 36 inches of walkway on every side, 42–48 inches where two people pass, a dishwasher or oven door swings, or stools sit, and make the island at least 40 inches deep. If those numbers leave you a tiny island, drop back to a peninsula (item 4) or a cart. Pros Multiple people can work at once Island adds storage and seating Keeps the cook facing the room Watch-outs Needs the most floor area on this list Island plumbing or power adds cost and planning 6 U-Shape Best for storage in a small, enclosed kitchen Cabinets on three walls. A U gives you the most counter and cabinet run of any layout in a closed room, and the cook stands in the middle with everything within a turn. For a serious cook in a small house, it is hard to beat for storage. The risk is feeling boxed in. Two inside corners mean two corner cabinets to solve, and in a small U the opposite legs can end up too close together. Hold the same working aisle you would in a galley, and if anyone in the household uses a walker or wheelchair, plan around the turning space in the 2010 ADA Standards (&sect;304.3.1: a 60-inch-diameter circle) so they can turn around inside the U. Our accessible remodeling page covers that planning. Often we open the third wall into a peninsula to get the storage without the enclosure. Pros Most storage and counter in a closed room Keeps through-traffic out Watch-outs Two corners to solve Can feel cramped; hard for two cooks in a small U 7 One-Wall Plus Island Best for narrow open plans and condos A single appliance wall with a parallel island is really a galley with one side freed from the wall. It suits long, narrow open rooms, which are common in condos, townhomes and some newer builds. The wall keeps tall items (refrigerator, pantry, oven tower) out of sight lines, and the island supplies the counter a one-wall kitchen lacks. Treat the gap between the wall and the island like a galley aisle: at least 42 inches, more if two cooks share it. Putting the sink or cooktop in the island makes it a true work surface but adds plumbing or venting in the floor, so decide that early; it is one of the choices that locks in once the floor is closed up. Pros Open to the room on one side Tall storage stays on the back wall Watch-outs Island utilities add planning Needs a room long enough for both runs 8 Open Galley (Remove One Side Wall) Best upgrade for closed 1970s–1990s kitchens Not a new shape so much as a fix: keep the galley or U, but remove the wall that closes it off from the dining or living room and turn that side into a peninsula or island. The workflow stays efficient and the room gains light and sight lines. It is often the single highest-impact change we make in older homes. Two cautions. First, some of those walls are load-bearing; that is solvable with an engineered header, but it has to be assessed and permitted (in Avondale that goes through the city's Building Services Division; see our Avondale remodeling permits guide ). Second, walls hold cabinets, so you lose upper storage. Our open-concept vs. traditional kitchen comparison explains how a reach-in pantry elsewhere usually makes that up. Pros Big gain in light and openness Keeps an efficient working core Watch-outs Possible structural work and permits Less wall cabinet space Quick Comparison Layout Floor space needed Cooks at once Storage Feels open? L-shape Low–moderate 1–2 Good Yes Galley Low 1 (2 with a wide aisle) Very good Only if one end is open One-wall Lowest 1 Limited Yes Peninsula / G Moderate 2 Very good Mostly L + island Highest 2+ Excellent Yes U-shape Moderate 1 Excellent No One-wall + island Moderate–high 2 Good Yes How to Choose: The Work Triangle and Clearances The classic work triangle connects the sink, the cooking surface and the refrigerator. A widely used planning guideline from the kitchen design industry is that each leg of the triangle should run roughly 4 to 9 feet and the three legs together should total no more than about 26 feet, with no cabinet or island cutting through a leg. In a small home the more common problem is a triangle that is too tight, with no landing space beside the range or refrigerator. The clearances matter more than the triangle. The two numbers we check first on every small kitchen are the ones on our own guides: at least 42 inches between facing runs in a galley, and at least 36 inches on every side of an island, stepping up to 42–48 inches where people pass, sit or open appliance doors. We model the layout in CAD before anything is ordered so you can see those aisles, door swings and landing zones, which is part of how we run a kitchen remodel . Small-Home Notes for Avondale Most Avondale homes went up in the 1990s and 2000s — the city's median home was built in 2002, per Census Bureau survey data — and the city skews young and family-heavy, with a median age around 33. In a small kitchen in a busy household, that usually means planning for two people working at once: favor an L, a peninsula, or a galley with a wide aisle over a tight U, and give homework and snacks a seating edge away from the range. If you live in one of the older homes around Old Town or Cashion, have any wall you want to open checked for structure early (item 8). If you are planning to age in place, favor layouts with wider aisles and fewer dead-end corners, and put everyday items between hip and shoulder height. On permits: the City of Avondale's building code lets you replace cabinets and countertops without a building permit, but moving a sink or range, adding circuits, or removing a wall does need one, and the city inspects that work before it is covered up. We pull City of Avondale permits for our work. If your home is in an HOA community, check its rules before work starts; the city doesn't track HOA covenants. Frequently Asked Questions What is the most efficient kitchen layout for a small house? For most small houses an L-shaped kitchen is the most efficient all-around choice because it forms a tight work triangle and stays open on two sides. In a long, narrow room a galley is even more efficient per square foot, as long as you keep at least 42 inches between the two runs. If you want seating but lack room for an island, add a peninsula. How much space do you need for a kitchen island? Plan for at least 36 inches of clear walkway on every side of the island, and 42 to 48 inches on any side where two people pass, stools sit, or a dishwasher or oven door opens. The island itself should be at least 40 inches deep to be useful. If you cannot hold those clearances, a peninsula or a rolling cart is usually the better choice. Is a galley kitchen a bad layout? No. A galley is one of the most efficient layouts for one main cook because every step is short and there is counter on both sides. Most complaints come from galleys that are closed at both ends or too narrow. Keeping an aisle of at least 42 inches and opening one end to the dining or living area solves most of those problems. Should I choose a peninsula or an island in a small kitchen? Choose an island only if the room can keep at least 36 inches of walkway all the way around it. A peninsula needs clearance on fewer sides, so it fits smaller rooms while still giving you seating, prep space and extra base cabinets. In many small kitchens a peninsula is the better fit. Can I change my kitchen layout without moving plumbing? Sometimes. Moving from a U to an L, or opening a galley into a peninsula, can often keep the sink where it is. Moving the sink or range to an island means new plumbing, gas or venting in the floor, which adds planning, cost and a City of Avondale permit for the plumbing, gas or electrical work. We check which walls hold plumbing and structure during the free in-home consultation. # Best Kitchen Sink Types (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-kitchen-sink-types.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Ten kitchen sink types ranked for Avondale, AZ kitchens: undermount, farmhouse, workstation, composite, fireclay and more, and how each handles hard water.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Best Kitchen Sink Types Kitchen Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Kitchen Sink Types (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: For most kitchens, the best sink is a large single-bowl undermount in brushed stainless steel : it is easy to clean, fits sheet pans and big pots, and its satin finish hides the spots that Avondale's very hard water leaves behind. A workstation sink is the best upgrade for serious cooks, a farmhouse (apron-front) sink is the best statement piece, and granite composite is the best pick for a quiet, scratch-resistant bowl, as long as you choose a lighter or speckled color. The sink is the hardest-working spot in the kitchen, and in Avondale it has an extra job: living with very hard water. City well water averaged about 21 grains per gallon in the city's 2022 water quality report — about double the report's own 10.5 gpg line for &ldquo;very hard&rdquo; — and it leaves calcium and magnesium spots wherever it air-dries, so the finish and color of your sink matter more here than they do in soft-water towns. A glossy black bowl can look chalky within a week. The sink also has to be decided early. Undermount and farmhouse sinks shape the countertop cutout and the base cabinet, so we pick the sink during design, before the cabinets are ordered and the countertops are templated. Here are the ten sink types we install most, ranked for everyday use in Arizona kitchens. The list Undermount Stainless Steel (Single Bowl) Workstation Sink Farmhouse (Apron-Front) Sink Granite Composite Fireclay Double Bowl Integrated Solid-Surface or Quartz Sink Enameled Cast Iron Drop-In (Top-Mount) Copper 1 Undermount Stainless Steel (Single Bowl) Best overall for most kitchens An undermount sink mounts beneath the countertop, so there is no rim to catch crumbs; you wipe straight from the counter into the bowl. Paired with a single large basin, it fits roasting pans and sheet pans that never fit in a divided sink. It is the configuration we recommend most, and it is one that never looks dated. For hard water, choose a brushed or satin finish rather than mirror-polished stainless; the fine grain hides water spots and light scratches. A thicker-gauge steel with sound-deadening pads is quieter and resists dents. Undermount sinks need a stone, quartz, or solid-surface counter; the fabricator cuts and polishes the opening in the shop, which our countertop cost guide lists at $150–$300. Mount Under the counter Hard-water look Brushed finish hides spots Counter Stone, quartz, or solid surface Pros Easy to wipe crumbs in Fits large pans Timeless Watch-outs Not for standard laminate counters 2 Workstation Sink Best for serious home cooks A workstation sink has a built-in ledge that holds sliding accessories: a cutting board, colander, drying rack, or roll-up mat. You can prep vegetables, rinse, and drain in one spot, which effectively adds counter space in a smaller kitchen. Most are stainless undermounts, and they tend to be long, so they usually need a wider sink base cabinet. That is easy to plan in a new layout and harder to retrofit into existing cabinets. Keep the accessories in mind when you choose a faucet; a pull-down with enough reach to cover the full bowl is worth it. For a small kitchen, see our small kitchen remodeling ideas. Mount Usually undermount Cabinet Often needs a wider base Pros Adds usable prep space Accessories store in the sink Watch-outs Needs a wide base cabinet More parts to clean 3 Farmhouse (Apron-Front) Sink Best statement sink A farmhouse sink has an exposed front panel and a deep single bowl. It is the centerpiece of farmhouse, craftsman, and transitional kitchens, and the deep bowl hides a pile of dishes. Because you stand right against the sink, many people find it easier on the back than reaching over a counter edge. It requires a dedicated apron-front base cabinet, and heavier materials need extra support underneath, so this is a decision to make during cabinet design, not after. Farmhouse sinks come in fireclay, stainless, enameled cast iron, and composite. In hard-water homes, a white fireclay apron shows the least spotting of the bunch. Pair it with a two-tone look from our two-tone cabinet guide . Mount Apron-front base cabinet Materials Fireclay, stainless, cast iron, composite Pros Striking focal point Deep, roomy bowl Watch-outs Needs a special base cabinet Hard to swap later 4 Granite Composite Best for quiet, scratch-resistant bowls Granite composite sinks are made from crushed stone bound with resin. They are quieter than stainless, very scratch resistant, and handle heat well, and the color runs through the material so light scuffs do not show. The Arizona caveat is color. Hard water can leave a whitish mineral film on dark composite, especially solid black, and it takes regular wiping to keep it looking deep and even. Lighter grays, beiges, and speckled colors hide mineral residue far better. Match the sink to your counter for a calm, built-in look; a gray composite under a gray-veined quartz almost disappears. Mount Undermount or drop-in Hard-water look Choose light or speckled colors Pros Quiet Resists scratches and chips Heat tolerant Watch-outs Dark colors show mineral film 5 Fireclay Best for a classic white sink Fireclay is clay fired at very high temperatures with a glazed surface. The glaze is glossy, nonporous, and easy to clean, and white fireclay is the best-looking sink we know of for a hard-water home, because mineral spots barely show on white. Fireclay is heavy and can chip or crack if you drop a cast-iron pan into it, so a bottom grid is a good idea. It is most often sold as a farmhouse sink, and like any heavy sink it needs solid cabinet support. If you want a bright, traditional look that stays clean with a quick wipe, fireclay is hard to beat. Surface Glazed, nonporous Hard-water look White hides spots well Pros Easy-clean glaze Hides mineral spots in white Watch-outs Heavy Can chip from dropped cookware 6 Double Bowl Best for hand-washing and multitasking A double-bowl sink lets you soak in one side and rinse in the other, or keep dirty dishes out of sight while you prep in the second bowl. It suits households that hand-wash a lot or have two cooks working at once. The catch is that neither bowl fits a large pan lying flat. An offset double, with one larger bowl and one smaller prep bowl, or a low-divide design that lets water pass over the middle, keeps most of the flexibility of a single bowl. If you run the dishwasher daily, a single large bowl is usually the better choice. Layouts Equal, offset, or low-divide Pros Soak and rinse at once Good for two cooks Watch-outs Big pans do not lie flat 7 Integrated Solid-Surface or Quartz Sink Best seamless look An integrated sink is made from the same material as the countertop, or fabricated to join it with no visible seam. With no rim and no joint, there is nowhere for grime or mineral buildup to collect, which makes it one of the easiest sinks to keep clean in hard water. Solid surface is the classic choice here, and scratches can usually be sanded out. The drawback is that sink and counter are one unit, so if the bowl is ever damaged, repair is a fabricator's job rather than a simple sink swap. It is a great fit for modern and minimalist kitchens. Seams None or nearly invisible Repair By a fabricator Pros No rim to clean Clean, modern look Watch-outs Harder to replace the bowl alone 8 Enameled Cast Iron Best for durability with a vintage look Enameled cast iron is extremely durable and very quiet, with a glossy enamel finish that comes in white and a range of colors. A well-kept cast-iron sink can last for decades. It is very heavy and needs a reinforced base, and the enamel can chip if something heavy is dropped on it, exposing dark iron underneath. Abrasive cleaners can dull the finish, so use soft cleaners for hard-water spots. It suits a vintage or traditional kitchen and is available in both drop-in and undermount versions. Weight Very heavy Finish Glossy enamel Pros Very durable and quiet Classic look Watch-outs Heavy Enamel can chip 9 Drop-In (Top-Mount) Best for laminate counters and budget updates A drop-in sink sits into a cutout from above, with its rim resting on the counter. It is the easiest sink to install and replace, and it is the standard choice for laminate countertops, which usually cannot support an undermount. The rim is its weakness: crumbs cannot be wiped straight into the bowl, and the joint between rim and counter collects grime and hard-water crust. If you are replacing counters with quartz or stone anyway, most clients choose an undermount instead. For a quick refresh on existing laminate, a drop-in is a sensible, budget-friendly fix. Mount Rim on top of the counter Counter Any, including laminate Pros Easy to install and replace Works with laminate Watch-outs Rim traps grime and mineral crust 10 Copper Best for a living-finish look Copper sinks bring warmth to rustic and Southwest kitchens and pair well with warm-metal fixtures. Copper develops a patina over time that many people love. That patina is the point, and it is also the maintenance. Acidic foods and hard water change the surface color unevenly, and keeping copper bright takes regular polishing. If you want a sink that always looks new, choose something else. If you like a finish that changes with the house, copper is a characterful choice. Finish Develops a patina Upkeep Higher if you want it bright Pros Warm, distinctive look Watch-outs Patina changes unevenly Higher upkeep Sink Types and Hard Water: A Quick Comparison Sink Hides hard-water spots Noise Watch-out Brushed stainless Good Moderate (quieter with pads) Polished finishes show spots Granite composite Good in light colors, poor in black Quiet White film on dark colors White fireclay Very good Quiet Can chip Enameled cast iron Good in white Quiet Very heavy Integrated solid surface Good Quiet Repairs need a fabricator Copper Poor (patina changes) Moderate Ongoing polishing Planning Your Sink in a Remodel Decide before cabinets and counters. Farmhouse and workstation sinks change the base cabinet, and every undermount changes the countertop cutout. We choose the sink during design so the cabinet, counter, and plumbing all line up. Think twice before moving it. Relocating a sink means rerouting drain and supply lines, which in Avondale is plumbing work that needs a City of Avondale permit and inspection; our kitchen remodel cost guide budgets $800 to $2,500 for a sink relocation, depending on distance and access. Match the faucet to the water. Brushed and satin faucet finishes hide hard-water spots better than polished chrome or matte black. Wiping the sink and faucet dry at night does more against mineral buildup than any cleaner, and with water this hard, a softener or a filter at the kitchen tap is worth discussing during design. We install sinks as part of every kitchen remodel , along with the countertops they sit in. Frequently Asked Questions What type of kitchen sink is easiest to keep clean? An undermount or integrated sink is easiest, because there is no rim for crumbs and mineral crust to collect in. A brushed stainless or white fireclay bowl hides hard-water spots best. Drop-in sinks are the hardest to keep clean because of the joint between the rim and the counter. Is a single or double bowl kitchen sink better? For most households with a dishwasher, a single large bowl is better because it fits sheet pans and big pots. A double bowl suits people who hand-wash a lot or cook with a partner. An offset or low-divide double bowl is a good middle ground. Do granite composite sinks show hard water spots? Dark composite sinks, especially solid black, can show a whitish mineral film in hard-water areas like Avondale. Lighter grays, beiges, and speckled colors hide mineral residue much better. Wiping the sink dry after use helps any color. Can I put an undermount sink in a laminate countertop? Usually not. Standard laminate countertops are built for drop-in sinks, because the exposed edge of an undermount cutout would let water into the core. If you want an undermount, choose quartz, granite, quartzite, or solid surface for the counter. Does a farmhouse sink need a special cabinet? Yes. A farmhouse or apron-front sink needs a dedicated base cabinet with a cut-down front, and heavier fireclay or cast iron models need extra support underneath. That is why we choose the sink during cabinet design rather than after the cabinets are installed.
