# Best Kitchen Storage and Pantry Ideas (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-kitchen-storage-and-pantry-ideas.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Pull-out pantries, deep drawers, corner fixes, trash pull-outs and appliance garages: the kitchen storage and pantry ideas that earn their space in 2026.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Kitchen Storage & Pantry Ideas Kitchen Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Kitchen Storage and Pantry Ideas (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: The storage upgrades that pay off most are deep drawer banks instead of base cabinets with doors, a tall pantry cabinet with pull-outs , and a real corner solution such as a lazy Susan or blind-corner pull-out. After those, add a trash and recycling pull-out , vertical tray dividers and an appliance garage . Plan them into the cabinet layout from the start, because most of them are built into the boxes, not added later. Most kitchens do not lack space so much as usable space: shelves you have to kneel to reach, a corner cabinet nobody opens, a pantry where cans disappear behind other cans. A remodel is the best chance to fix that at the source, because storage is decided when the cabinets are laid out, not when the shelves are loaded. Here are the storage and pantry ideas we build in most often, ranked by how much everyday difference they make. Many are cabinet options, so the line you choose matters: our custom vs. RTA cabinets comparison explains which interior options are easier to get in semi-custom and custom lines. The list Deep Drawer Banks Tall Pull-Out Pantry Cabinet Reach-In Pantry Wall Walk-In Pantry Corner Solutions Trash and Recycling Pull-Out Appliance Garage Vertical Tray Dividers and Spice Pull-Outs Drawer Organizers and Inserts Cabinets to the Ceiling Island Storage 1 Deep Drawer Banks Best single upgrade for base cabinets Replace door-and-shelf base cabinets with stacks of wide, deep drawers. Instead of kneeling and digging, you pull the drawer out and look down at everything: pots, pans, lids, mixing bowls, even dishes. Our kitchen cabinets page calls deep drawers one of the most popular upgrades clients choose once they see them in the CAD layout, and we agree. Specify full-extension, soft-close slides so you can reach the back of the drawer, and good drawer boxes that will carry the weight of cast iron for years. If you store dishes low, a peg-board insert keeps plates from sliding. Pros Everything visible and reachable Easier on backs and knees Watch-outs Costs more than a door-and-shelf box 2 Tall Pull-Out Pantry Cabinet Best pantry for kitchens without a pantry closet A floor-to-ceiling cabinet with roll-out trays or a full-height pull-out frame. It fits a lot of food in a small footprint, and pull-outs mean nothing gets lost at the back. It is the answer for most small and mid-size kitchens that have no room for a walk-in. Roll-out trays inside a door are the most flexible; a full pull-out unit gives access from both sides. Place it at the end of a run, near the refrigerator or prep zone, and make sure its door can open fully without hitting an appliance or wall. Pros Big storage in a narrow footprint Nothing hides at the back Watch-outs Heavy pull-outs need quality slides Uses wall space you might want for counters 3 Reach-In Pantry Wall Best for open-concept kitchens that lost their uppers A wall of tall cabinets, or a shallow closet with doors, dedicated to food and small appliances. Shallow shelving is the secret: food one or two cans deep is visible and easy to reach, while a deep closet shelf becomes a black hole. This is the fix we most often recommend when a wall comes down to open a kitchen. Our open-concept vs. traditional comparison explains why: walls hold cabinets, and a reach-in pantry elsewhere makes up for the lost uppers. Pros Lots of storage with shallow, visible shelves Hides clutter behind doors Watch-outs Needs a full wall or closet 4 Walk-In Pantry Best for larger kitchens and serious bulk buyers A small room lined with shelves. It holds the most, and it can take small appliances, a second refrigerator or bulk goods that never fit in a cabinet. For households that shop in bulk, a walk-in is hard to beat. It also needs the most space, and it only works with good lighting and shelving no deeper than you can see into. If you have to borrow the space from another room, compare it honestly with a reach-in pantry wall; many homeowners find the reach-in holds nearly as much and is easier to keep organized. Pros Maximum capacity Room for appliances and bulk goods Watch-outs Takes the most floor area Deep corners become clutter 5 Corner Solutions Best fix for the most wasted space in the kitchen Every L and U kitchen has an inside corner, and a plain corner cabinet is a dead zone. The options are a lazy Susan turntable, a blind-corner pull-out that swings or slides contents out to you, or a set of corner drawers. Our small kitchen page calls a well-installed lazy Susan or blind-corner pull-out one of the most-used storage spots in a kitchen. Which one fits depends on the corner type and your cabinet line, so decide during layout, not after the boxes arrive. Pros Recovers space you already paid for Watch-outs Mechanisms add cost Some corners fit only certain units 6 Trash and Recycling Pull-Out Best everyday convenience upgrade Two bins on a slide-out frame inside a base cabinet, usually next to the sink or in the island where you prep. It keeps garbage off the floor and out of sight, and one pull sorts trash from recycling. Put it within a step of the sink and the main prep zone, and not next to the dishwasher door, where two people can&rsquo;t use both at once. A door-mounted pull-out or a full-height drawer front both work. Pros Out of sight, right where you work Sorts trash and recycling Watch-outs Uses a full base cabinet 7 Appliance Garage Best for clearing the counter of small appliances A countertop-level cabinet with a lift-up, pocket or tambour door that hides the mixer, toaster, coffee maker and blender. Plug them in inside and slide them out when you need them. Our 2026 trends guide lists appliance garages and coffee stations with integrated outlets among the features that are growing. Plan the outlets and the depth before the countertop is templated, and give heat-producing appliances enough clearance to be pulled out to use rather than run inside the cabinet. Pros Clean counters Appliances stay plugged in and ready Watch-outs Needs electrical planning Uses counter length 8 Vertical Tray Dividers and Spice Pull-Outs Best for baking sheets, boards and spices Vertical dividers in a narrow cabinet store baking sheets, cutting boards and trays on edge, so you can pull out one without lifting the stack. A narrow pull-out beside the range holds spices, oils and cooking tools exactly where you need them. Our cabinets page lists both as standard ideas we design in. They are a smart use of the filler-width spaces left at the ends of runs, which would otherwise be blank panels. Pros Uses narrow leftover spaces Keeps the most-used items at hand Watch-outs Only fits narrow items 9 Drawer Organizers and Inserts Best low-cost way to make drawers work harder Built-in utensil trays, knife blocks, spice inserts and adjustable dividers keep drawers organized so everything has a place. Custom-fit inserts use the full drawer instead of leaving gaps around a store-bought tray. They are inexpensive relative to what they add, and many cabinet lines offer them as options. Decide what goes in each drawer during design, and size the inserts accordingly. Pros Inexpensive Easy to add to most lines Watch-outs Fixed inserts are hard to rearrange later 10 Cabinets to the Ceiling Best for kitchens with tall ceilings If your uppers stop short of the ceiling, the gap above them collects dust and wastes space. Running cabinets all the way up, often with a second row of short cabinets on top, adds storage for seasonal and rarely used items and makes the room look taller. Our small kitchen page recommends pairing it with pull-down shelf systems for the highest cabinets. Keep a step stool handy, and put the things you use daily between hip and shoulder height, especially if you plan to age in place. Pros More storage, no extra floor Room looks taller Watch-outs Top shelves need a step stool 11 Island Storage Best for kitchens with room for an island Because you can reach an island from more than one side, it can hold storage that is awkward elsewhere: deep drawers on the working side, cookbooks or display shelves on the seating side, a trash center, or a charging drawer. Our kitchen island ideas guide covers the options. The rule that governs islands still applies: keep at least 36 inches of walkway on every side, and check that island drawers and nearby appliance doors can open fully at the same time. Pros Storage on more than one side Keeps prep tools in the prep zone Watch-outs Only if the room can hold the clearances How to Plan Kitchen Storage Start with an inventory, not a catalog. List what you store now, what never fits, and what lives on the counter that you would rather hide. Then assign zones: prep (knives, boards, bowls) near the main counter, cooking (pots, spices, oils) around the range, cleanup (trash, dish soap, dishes) near the sink and dishwasher, and food storage near the refrigerator. The storage ideas above slot into those zones. Two budget notes from our kitchen cabinet cost guide : every pull-out, drawer stack and specialty cabinet is priced as its own box, so when you compare bids, make sure they include the same accessories; and soft-close, full-extension drawer hardware is the upgrade homeowners notice every day, so it is usually worth prioritizing over fancier doors. Avondale Notes Avondale skews young and family-heavy — the median resident is about 33, according to Census Bureau survey data — so for many households here the priority is storage the whole family can use: a low drawer for everyday plates and cups, a snack pull-out kids can reach, and a trash and recycling pull-out right by the sink. If you plan to stay for the long haul or age in place, move everyday storage out of low cabinets and into drawers and pull-outs, keep high cabinets for rarely used items, and choose pulls that are easy to grip. Our aging-in-place remodeling page covers more. Two climate notes. Don't count on the garage as overflow pantry: the area averages about 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or hotter (National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals), and a closed garage in summer is no place for canned goods, drinks or paper goods, so plan enough pantry space inside the air-conditioned house. And monsoon season (June 15 – Sept. 30) pushes fine dust indoors, one more reason to run cabinets to the ceiling instead of leaving a dust shelf on top. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best way to add storage to a small kitchen? Replace base cabinets with deep drawers, add a tall pull-out pantry cabinet, fix the corner with a lazy Susan or blind-corner pull-out, and run upper cabinets to the ceiling. Those four changes usually add the most usable storage without adding floor space. Is a walk-in pantry better than a pantry cabinet? A walk-in pantry holds the most and can fit small appliances and bulk goods, but it needs a lot of floor area. A tall pull-out pantry cabinet or a reach-in pantry wall with shallow shelves holds a surprising amount, keeps everything visible, and fits most kitchens. For small and mid-size kitchens we usually recommend the cabinet or reach-in. Are drawers better than cabinets for base storage? For most base storage, yes. Deep drawers with full-extension slides bring everything to you, so you do not have to kneel and reach into the back of a cabinet. They cost more than a door-and-shelf cabinet, but they are the upgrade homeowners notice every day. What do you do with a blind corner cabinet? Install a corner mechanism: a lazy Susan turntable, a blind-corner pull-out that brings contents out of the corner, or corner drawers. The right option depends on the corner shape and your cabinet line, so it should be chosen when the layout is designed. Where should a trash pull-out go? Put it within a step of the sink and the main prep area, often in the base cabinet next to the sink or in the island. Avoid placing it where its door and the dishwasher door block each other. # Best Low-Maintenance Materials for Arizona Homes (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-low-maintenance-materials-for-arizona-homes.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: Ten low-maintenance kitchen and bath materials that stand up to Arizona hard water, dry air and sun: quartz, porcelain, LVP, groutless shower walls and more.

Home / Blog / Low-Maintenance Materials Remodeling Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Low-Maintenance Materials for Arizona Homes (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 10 min read Quick answer: The lowest-maintenance kitchen and bath materials for Arizona homes are the ones that give hard water nothing to soak into: quartz countertops, groutless solid-surface shower walls , porcelain tile with epoxy or urethane grout, and rigid-core LVP floors. Add brushed or satin fixture finishes and coated shower glass , and most of the weekly scrubbing that Avondale&rsquo;s very hard water causes simply goes away. Arizona is hard on interiors in ways that do not show up in national design magazines. Our water is very hard, so calcium and magnesium spots appear anywhere water air-dries. Our air is dry most of the year, which cracks wood and opens joints. Our sun is intense enough to fade finishes through a window, and the heat is relentless: National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals for the area average about 111 days a year at 100&deg;F or hotter. Then the monsoon arrives and blows fine dust into every textured surface and open joint. And almost nobody, whether they are raising kids or working long shifts, wants to spend a Saturday on their knees scrubbing grout. This list covers interior kitchen and bathroom materials only, ranked by how much work they save you in an Arizona home. None of it is exotic. It is what we reach for when a client tells us, "I never want to seal, scrub, or re-grout anything again." Where our site publishes a price, we link to it rather than repeat it; see our kitchen and bathroom cost guides for budgets. The list Groutless Solid-Surface Shower Walls Quartz Countertops and Vanity Tops Porcelain Tile Floors Rigid-Core Luxury Vinyl Plank Epoxy or Urethane Grout Cultured Marble or Solid-Surface Vanity Tops Coated Shower Glass Brushed and Satin Fixture Finishes Large-Format Porcelain Wall Tile Plywood Cabinet Boxes with Factory Finishes 1 Groutless Solid-Surface Shower Walls Best for ending grout scrubbing for good In a tile shower, grout is where the work is. Hard water deposits mineral scale on grout joints, and with Avondale&rsquo;s very hard water, grout usually discolors long before the tile wears out. Groutless shower systems replace tile with large solid-surface or acrylic panels bonded to the wall and sealed at the seams, so there are no joints for minerals, soap scum, or mildew to settle into. A wipe with a damp cloth is the whole routine. They also install fast: most groutless systems go in within one to two days, versus a longer tile schedule with setting and cure time. The trade-off is design range; panels cannot match every custom tile layout. Learn more on our groutless shower systems page, or compare the two honestly in groutless vs. tile showers . Grout lines None Install time Typically one to two days Cleaning Damp cloth wipe Pros No grout to seal or scrub Non-porous surface Fast install Watch-outs Less design range than custom tile Walls only; the floor is still tile or a base 2 Quartz Countertops and Vanity Tops Best countertop for zero upkeep Quartz is non-porous and never needs sealing, which makes it the lowest-maintenance stone-look counter for kitchens and vanities alike. Coffee, wine, and makeup wipe off, and hard-water spots sit on the surface where a damp cloth takes them away, rather than in the pores of the stone. Two cautions keep it maintenance-free: use a trivet for hot pans, and avoid putting light-sensitive colors under hours of direct sun. Mid-tone, lightly veined patterns hide water spots and crumbs far better than solid black or stark white. For prices by material, see our countertop cost guide ; for the service, see custom countertops . Sealing Never Hard water Wipes off the surface Pros No sealing Stain resistant Watch-outs Use trivets for hot pans 3 Porcelain Tile Floors Best floor for a lifetime of wear Porcelain absorbs almost no water (below 0.5%, the ANSI definition), resists stains without sealing, and does not move with Arizona's temperature swings. It will not fade in the sun or scratch from pet claws, and wood-look porcelain plank gives you the look of hardwood without its dry-air problems. For low maintenance, pick a matte or lightly textured finish (safer when wet and better at hiding footprints and water spots than polished tile), use larger tiles to cut down on grout lines, and choose a mid-tone grout. In a low-desert summer, a cool porcelain floor is a feature, not a drawback. See our tile flooring service and porcelain vs. ceramic guide. Water absorption Below 0.5% (ANSI) Sealing Tile: none; grout: depends on type Pros Extremely durable Does not fade Watch-outs Hard and cool underfoot Grout still needs the right type 4 Rigid-Core Luxury Vinyl Plank Best comfortable, waterproof floor Rigid-core (SPC) LVP is 100% waterproof through the core, softer and warmer underfoot than tile, and dimensionally stable in dry air, so it will not cup or gap the way solid hardwood can in our dry air. There is no grout at all, and a damp mop is all it needs. Choose at least a 12 mil wear layer for a household with kids or dogs, and 20 mil for heavy use. In rooms with big sunny windows, plan on window treatments, since strong sun can fade some vinyl over the years. LVP can often float over an existing floor, which keeps the project quick. More on our luxury vinyl flooring page. Water 100% waterproof core Wear layer 12 mil minimum; 20 mil for heavy use Pros No grout Comfortable Stable in dry air Watch-outs Some products fade in strong sun 5 Epoxy or Urethane Grout Best upgrade if you still want tile If you love tile, the single best low-maintenance decision is the grout. Standard cement grout is porous and needs sealing; hard water soaks in and stains it. Epoxy and single-component urethane grouts are non-porous, never need sealing, and resist staining, which is why we use them on shower floors and in hard-water areas. Color matters as much as type. Mid-tone grays and greiges hide hard-water staining best; bright white grout shows every mineral mark, and very dark grout shows a white haze. Our shower grout guide explains which grout belongs where and how to keep it clean. Sealing Never Best color Mid-tone gray or greige Pros No sealing Stain resistant Watch-outs Less forgiving to install than cement grout 6 Cultured Marble or Solid-Surface Vanity Tops Best seamless vanity top A cultured marble or solid-surface vanity top is molded with an integral sink, so the counter and bowl are one seamless piece with no joint at the sink edge. That joint is exactly where toothpaste, soap, and hard-water crust collect on an undermount or drop-in sink, so removing it removes the chore. These tops are also budget-friendly, which makes them a favorite in hall baths and guest baths. They are softer than quartz, so avoid abrasive cleaners. Our bathroom vanity guide compares tops and sink styles. Seam at sink None Cleaning Non-abrasive cleaners Pros No sink joint to scrub Budget-friendly Watch-outs Softer than quartz 7 Coated Shower Glass Best for clear glass in hard water Avondale&rsquo;s very hard water spots shower glass quickly, and frameless glass shows it most. A factory-applied protective coating makes the glass shed water so it stays clear with a quick daily squeegee or wipe instead of weekly scrubbing. Ask for the coating when you order the glass rather than trying to add it later. A simpler enclosure with fewer panels and minimal hardware also means fewer edges for mineral buildup. See frameless vs. framed shower doors for the full comparison. Upkeep Quick daily wipe When to order With the glass Pros Stays clear longer Less scrubbing Watch-outs Must be specified up front 8 Brushed and Satin Fixture Finishes Best for hiding water spots Faucets and shower trim are the first thing hard water marks. Brushed nickel, brushed stainless, and satin brass have a fine grain that hides spots and fingerprints between cleanings. Polished chrome shows every spot but wipes clean easily, and matte black looks striking but shows white mineral residue quickly in hard-water homes. Whatever you pick, keep one finish family per room so small differences in spotting are not obvious, and wipe fixtures dry at night. That habit does more against mineral buildup than any cleaner. Hides spots Brushed nickel, brushed stainless, satin brass Shows spots Matte black, polished chrome Pros Hides spots and fingerprints Watch-outs Still needs an occasional wipe 9 Large-Format Porcelain Wall Tile Best tile look with fewer joints If you want real tile on the shower walls, large-format porcelain cuts the number of grout joints dramatically compared with small subway tile or mosaics. Fewer joints means less grout to clean, and paired with epoxy or urethane grout, a large-format tile shower comes close to the upkeep of a panel system. Large tiles need a very flat wall and skilled setting to avoid lippage, so this is not a do-it-yourself job. Keep small mosaics for the shower floor, where the extra joints add grip. Our tile shower ideas page has layouts that keep joints to a minimum. Grout joints Far fewer than small tile Pros Tile look with less grout Non-porous porcelain Watch-outs Needs a very flat wall 10 Plywood Cabinet Boxes with Factory Finishes Best cabinets for leaks and dry air Cabinets are not usually on a maintenance list, but the wrong box turns one sink leak into a replacement. Plywood boxes resist water damage far better than particleboard, which swells when wet and never fully recovers. That matters most under kitchen and bathroom sinks. For the doors, a factory-applied, sprayed finish holds up far better in Arizona's dry air and sun than a brushed-on coat, and UV-resistant finishes help near south- and west-facing windows. Matte and satin sheens hide fingerprints better than high gloss. See kitchen cabinets and custom vs. RTA cabinets . Avondale&rsquo;s tap water is a blend of city well water and Colorado River (CAP) water, and the city&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report put city-produced water at an average of about 21 grains per gallon (357 mg/L), &ldquo;very hard&rdquo; on the report&rsquo;s own scale. It leaves mineral deposits wherever it dries. The best defense is surfaces with no pores and as few joints as possible. Dry air. Low humidity cracks wood and opens joints, which is why we favor LVP or porcelain over solid wood floors and plywood over particleboard. Sun and heat. Intense UV fades some finishes and flooring near big windows. Porcelain does not fade; for other materials, plan on window treatments. Dust. Monsoon storms, which officially run June 15 through September 30, push fine dust indoors. Smooth, sealed surfaces wipe clean; heavily textured tile and open grout joints hold onto it. Aging in place. For many of our clients, low maintenance is also a safety issue: fewer reasons to kneel in a tub scrubbing grout. We often pair groutless walls with a curbless or low-threshold shower. See our aging-in-place bathroom guide . We build these materials into every bathroom remodel and kitchen remodel we design. Frequently Asked Questions What is the lowest-maintenance shower for hard water? A groutless solid-surface shower is the lowest-maintenance option, because there are no grout joints for mineral scale and soap scum to settle into. A damp cloth wipe keeps it clean. If you want tile, choose large-format porcelain with epoxy or urethane grout and a mid-tone grout color. What countertop needs the least maintenance? Quartz needs the least maintenance of the stone-look countertops. It is non-porous, never needs sealing, and hard-water spots wipe off the surface. Use a trivet for hot pans and choose a mid-tone pattern if you want it to hide water spots and crumbs between cleanings. Which faucet finish hides hard water spots best? Brushed nickel, brushed stainless, and satin brass hide hard-water spots and fingerprints best. Polished chrome shows spots but wipes clean easily. Matte black looks striking but shows white mineral residue quickly in very hard water like Avondale&rsquo;s. Is LVP or tile lower maintenance? LVP is slightly lower maintenance day to day because it has no grout at all. Porcelain tile lasts longer and never fades, and with epoxy or urethane grout it needs very little care. Both are good low-maintenance choices for Arizona kitchens and baths. How do I keep hard water from staining bathroom surfaces? Choose non-porous surfaces with as few joints as possible, such as quartz, porcelain, solid surface, and groutless shower panels. Use epoxy or urethane grout, ask for coated shower glass, and wipe fixtures and glass dry after use. That habit does more than any cleaner. # Best Shower Niche and Bench Ideas (2026)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-shower-niche-and-bench-ideas.html
Section: Best-of lists — ideas & materials
Summary: The best shower niche and bench ideas for 2026: niche placement and sizing between studs, sloped tops that drain, floating, corner and fold-down benches.
==============================================================================

Home / Blog / Shower Niche & Bench Ideas Shower Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Best Shower Niche and Bench Ideas (2026) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated September 22, 2026 &bull; 9 min read Quick answer: The best shower niche is one recessed niche, built between the studs on a wall you do not face under the spray, with its bottom shelf pitched toward the shower so water drains out. The best bench depends on the room: a built-in tiled bench in a shower of about 36&times;60 inches or larger, a floating bench where you want an open floor, and a fold-down seat where space is tight. Plan both before demolition, because both live inside the waterproofing. See our walk-in showers page for how we build them. Niches and benches are the two shower details people touch every day, and the two that most often get improvised once the walls are open. A niche added as an afterthought ends up where the stud happened to be, not where your hand goes. A bench bolted on later means a seat that sits in the spray or blocks the door. Below are the niche and bench ideas we recommend most in our shower remodels, ordered roughly by how much they improve daily use. Each one notes where it fits and what to watch for. The dimensions we give are the same ones we publish on our tile shower ideas and aging-in-place bathroom guides, so the numbers line up across the site. The list One Large Recessed Niche Instead of Several Small Ones Niche on a Side Wall, Out of the Direct Spray Size the Niche to the Stud Bay Pitched Niche Floor So Water Drains Out Built-In Tiled Bench Floating Bench Corner Bench or Corner Shelf Fold-Down Shower Seat Accent-Tile or Lit Niche Niche Built Into a Groutless Panel Shower 1 One Large Recessed Niche Instead of Several Small Ones Best for most showers If you only do one thing, do this. A single niche of roughly 12&times;24 inches up to 16&times;32 inches holds more than two or three small ones, and it is easier to waterproof well because there are fewer inside corners to seal. Add a shelf inside the opening and you get two tiers of storage from one cut in the wall. Size it to what you actually keep in the shower. Tall pump bottles need a taller opening than bar soap and a razor. We usually ask clients to line up their current bottles on the counter during the consultation so we can size the niche to them rather than to a stock number. Typical size 12&times;24 in. to 16&times;32 in. (from our tile shower ideas guide) Shelves One shelf inside the opening doubles the tiers Pros More usable storage per square inch Fewer corners to waterproof and clean Watch-outs A wide niche may need a framed header (see #3) 2 Niche on a Side Wall, Out of the Direct Spray Best placement for keeping bottles clean The most common placement mistake is putting the niche on the wall directly across from the showerhead, where it catches the full spray. Bottles stay wet, soap residue builds up, and in Avondale&rsquo;s very hard water the mineral film on the niche floor shows up quickly. A side wall, or the valve wall offset from the head, keeps the niche reachable without soaking it. Set the bottom shelf somewhere between elbow and chest height for the main user so nobody bends to reach shampoo. If someone in the house sits to shower, add a second, lower niche within reach of the bench. Also avoid exterior walls where you can. Cutting into an insulated outside wall leaves a thin spot in the insulation right behind a wet surface, and that is not where you want a pocket of trapped moisture. Pros Bottles dry between showers Easy reach without bending Watch-outs Needs a check for plumbing and vent lines in that wall 3 Size the Niche to the Stud Bay Best for keeping cost and framing simple Most interior walls are framed with studs 16 inches on center, which leaves roughly 14&frac12; inches of clear width between them, and a standard 2&times;4 wall gives about 3&frac12; inches of depth. A niche that fits inside one bay needs only blocking at the top and bottom. That is why a 12-inch-wide niche is the easy default. Wider niches are fine, but they mean cutting a stud and framing a header, which is more work and must be done correctly on a bearing wall. It is worth doing for a long horizontal niche that runs the width of the shower. It is not worth doing for a few extra inches. Building the niche into the framing during the remodel is far cleaner than adding a surface caddy later. We confirm stud locations, plumbing, and wiring during demolition before we commit to a size. Stud spacing 16 in. on center is common framing practice Clear width About 14&frac12; in. between standard studs Depth About 3&frac12; in. in a 2&times;4 wall 4 Pitched Niche Floor So Water Drains Out Best for preventing hidden water damage A niche with a dead-flat bottom collects water. That water sits against the grout, soaks the edges of the tile, and slowly tests the waterproofing underneath. The fix is simple: pitch the niche floor slightly toward the shower, at least 1/8 inch per foot, so every drop runs back out. This is one of the details most often missed, and it causes water damage over time when it is skipped. The same logic applies to the top of a bench and to any shelf ledge. The shower floor itself gets a steeper slope to the drain (we build to a 1/4-inch-per-foot pitch), but horizontal surfaces up the wall need their own slope too. Ask any installer how they slope the niche sill. If the answer is a shrug, keep looking. Niche floor pitch 1/8 in. per foot minimum toward the shower Shower floor pitch 1/4 in. per foot to the drain 5 Built-In Tiled Bench Best for primary baths and long-term use A built-in bench is the sturdiest seat you can put in a shower, and when it is tiled to match the walls it looks like part of the architecture rather than an accessory. It is where you shave your legs, sit for a steam, or rest if your knees or balance change later. The comfortable range is about 17 to 19 inches high and 15 to 18 inches deep, and a bench typically takes 24 to 36 inches of one wall. In showers of about 36&times;60 inches or larger, a bench usually fits without meaningfully shrinking standing room. In anything smaller, look at #6 or #7 instead. The bench is framed or formed, then wrapped in the same waterproofing as the walls, with its top pitched toward the drain. Height About 17–19 in. Depth About 15–18 in. Wall length Roughly 24–36 in. Pros Very solid Looks integrated Easy to clean when tiled with few grout lines Watch-outs Permanent footprint Needs careful waterproofing on every face 6 Floating Bench Best for curbless showers and open floors A floating bench cantilevers off the wall with open floor underneath. The shower floor stays continuous, which is easier to clean and reads larger, and it pairs well with curbless, zero-entry showers where the whole point is an uninterrupted floor. The support has to be planned in the framing. Floating benches rely on solid blocking or a manufactured bracket system anchored into the wall structure before the waterproofing goes on. This is not something to add after the tile is set. Give the top the same slight pitch as a built-in bench so water does not sit on it. Pros Open floor under the seat Modern look Watch-outs Support must be built in before waterproofing Usually a bit less deep than a built-in 7 Corner Bench or Corner Shelf Best for smaller showers A triangular corner bench uses the one spot in the shower you rarely stand in. It gives you somewhere to prop a foot or set a bottle without eating a full wall, and in a tub-to-shower conversion it is often the only seat that fits. A corner bench is not as comfortable for sitting as a full bench, so be honest about how you will use it. If it is mainly a foot rest and a shelf, a corner unit is a smart use of space. If someone needs to sit to bathe, go with a built-in or fold-down seat that gives real support. Groutless panel systems also offer corner shelves that bond to the walls, which is a tidy alternative in a small panel shower. Pros Uses dead corner space Works in compact showers Watch-outs Smaller seat than a straight bench 8 Fold-Down Shower Seat Best for tight showers and aging in place A fold-down teak or thermoplastic seat adds almost no footprint when folded, but lets the shower be used standing or seated. It is the answer when a permanent bench would crowd the room, and it reads as a spa feature rather than a medical device. The key is what is behind the wall. A fold-down seat must be anchored into solid blocking installed before the walls close, rated for the load the manufacturer specifies. Pair it with a handheld shower on a slide bar within reach of the seat and a grab bar near it. Our aging-in-place bathroom guide covers seat, grab bar, and handheld placement together. Pros Near-zero footprint folded Flexible for every user in the house Watch-outs Needs in-wall blocking planned early Less of a design feature than tile 9 Accent-Tile or Lit Niche Best for a design focal point The back of a niche is a small, contained surface, which makes it a good place to splurge. A glass or stone mosaic, a metal-look tile, or a contrasting color frames the niche and signals intent. Because the area is small, a pricier tile barely moves the budget. More ideas are on our tile shower ideas page. Align the niche with your grout lines so it looks built-in rather than cut-in. That means locking the tile layout before framing the niche, not after. Built-in niche lighting is also popular, but any light in a wet location has to be rated for it and wired to code, so it gets decided during rough-in with the electrician. Pros High impact for a small amount of tile Watch-outs Lighting must be wet-rated and planned at rough-in 10 Niche Built Into a Groutless Panel Shower Best for the lowest-maintenance shower If you are choosing a groutless shower system , you do not have to give up a niche. Solid-surface and composite panel systems can include niche walls, niche inserts, and corner shelving that integrate with the panels, so the niche has the same smooth, non-porous finish as the rest of the shower. That matters here. The City of Avondale&rsquo;s 2022 water quality report put city-produced water at an average of about 21 grains per gallon, &ldquo;very hard&rdquo; on the report&rsquo;s own scale, and water that hard leaves mineral film on everything. A panel niche with no grout lines wipes clean in seconds. The trade-off is that size and shape follow what the panel system offers, so a niche sized to your exact bottles is easier to get in tile. Compare the two approaches on our groutless vs. tile shower page. Pros No grout to scrub in the niche Matches the panel finish Watch-outs Fewer size and shape options than a tiled niche Niches and Benches at a Glance Option Best for Plan before demo? Main watch-out Large recessed niche Most showers Yes Pitch the floor; check wall for pipes Built-in tiled bench Showers about 36&times;60 in. and up Yes Waterproof every face Floating bench Curbless showers Yes Support must be in the framing Corner bench Compact showers Yes Smaller seat Fold-down seat Tight showers, aging in place Yes (blocking) Anchor into solid blocking Groutless panel niche Lowest maintenance Yes Limited sizes How We Build Them Every niche and bench on this list lives inside the shower&rsquo;s waterproofing, so the order of work matters more than the finish. At Infinity Kitchens and Baths we lock the layout at design, frame niches and benches during rough-in, apply a continuous waterproofing membrane over every face, and only then set tile or panels. That sequence is the same whether it is a custom tile shower or a panel system. Frequently Asked Questions How big should a shower niche be? For most showers, one niche of roughly 12 by 24 inches up to 16 by 32 inches works better than several small ones. A 12-inch-wide niche fits inside a standard stud bay, which keeps framing simple. Add a shelf inside the opening for two tiers of storage, and size the height to your tallest bottles. Where is the best place to put a shower niche? On a side wall or offset from the showerhead, not directly across from the spray, so bottles do not stay soaked. Set the bottom shelf between elbow and chest height for the main user. Avoid exterior walls when possible, and check for plumbing and vent lines before cutting. Should a shower niche be sloped? Yes. The bottom of the niche should be pitched toward the shower at least 1/8 inch per foot so water drains out instead of pooling against the grout. A flat niche floor is one of the most common details that leads to slow water damage. Bench tops need the same slight pitch. How high and deep should a shower bench be? A comfortable built-in shower bench is about 17 to 19 inches high and 15 to 18 inches deep, and it typically takes 24 to 36 inches of one wall. In a shower of about 36 by 60 inches or larger, a bench usually fits without cramping standing space. Can I add a niche or bench to an existing shower? Only by opening the wall and redoing the waterproofing in that area, which in practice usually means retiling at least that wall. That is why we plan niches and benches before demolition during a shower or bathroom remodel. A fold-down seat also needs blocking inside the wall, which is far easier to install while the wall is open. # How to Pick the Best ADA Bathroom Remodeler in Avondale

Summary: How to choose the best ADA bathroom remodeler in Avondale, AZ: ROC license, CAPS experience, City of Avondale permits, HOA checks, and safe design.

Home / Blog / Choosing an ADA Remodeler Accessible Bathroom Guide — Avondale, AZ How to Choose the Best ADA Bathroom Remodeler in Avondale, AZ By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated November 11, 2026 &bull; 15 min read Part of our Choosing a Remodeling Contractor — see all 15 guides in this category. Quick answer: To choose the best ADA bathroom remodeler in Avondale, AZ: verify an active Arizona ROC license at roc.az.gov, confirm insurance, and favor a company with genuine accessible-remodeling experience — ideally a Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist (CAPS) on the team. Then look at what actually makes a bathroom safe and usable: proper grab-bar blocking and placement, a curbless or roll-in shower, a comfort-height toilet, adequate turning clearances, lever handles, non-slip flooring, and good lighting — all designed to ADA and ANSI A117.1 guidance. Confirm the remodeler pulls the City of Avondale permit and checks HOA rules before any exterior ramp, and add strong reviews, a detailed written estimate, and a workmanship warranty . Infinity Kitchens and Baths (AZ ROC #339999) designs and installs accessible bathrooms in-house and offers factory-direct pricing roughly 15-25% below retail. A bathroom is the most dangerous room in the house — wet, hard, and full of edges — and it's where accessibility matters most. Done well, an accessible bathroom lets someone bathe safely, keep their independence, and stay in the home they love for years longer. Done poorly, it's a set of grab bars screwed into drywall that pull loose the first time they're needed. The problem is that "best ADA bathroom remodeler in Avondale" is a crowded search full of ads, lead-generation directories, and general handymen who add a grab bar and call it "ADA." Telling a true accessibility specialist from a general remodeler takes more than a star rating. Drawing on our 35+ years of remodeling experience, including the accessible bathrooms we design and build, we wrote the honest checklist we'd use ourselves. It walks through how to verify a contractor, why certified aging-in-place experience matters, what real ADA and accessible bathroom design involves, the difference between true code compliance and general aging-in-place safety, what these projects typically cost, how funding might help (including a City of Avondale program worth asking about), and the local factors — multigenerational households, very hard water, City of Avondale permits, and HOA rules — that quietly shape the right approach. Use it to shop with confidence, whether or not you ever call us. 1. Verify the License and Insurance First In Arizona, bathroom remodeling contractors should hold an active license with the Registrar of Contractors (ROC). Before you talk price, ask for the ROC number and look it up at roc.az.gov — it's free and takes about a minute. Confirm three things: that the license is active , that it's in the correct classification for the work, and that there's no pattern of unresolved complaints. Then ask for proof of general liability insurance and, if the company has employees, workers' compensation. This matters more with accessible bathrooms than people expect. These projects often involve moving walls, relocating plumbing, and installing structural blocking for grab bars that must hold real weight in an emergency. If an uninsured worker is hurt in your home, or a plumbing change causes a leak behind the wall, you do not want to discover the coverage gap after the fact. A legitimate remodeler will hand over their ROC number and insurance certificate without hesitation. If someone dodges the question or claims they "work under someone else's license," walk away. (Infinity holds AZ ROC #339999 and is bonded and insured.) There's an Avondale-specific version of this check. The City of Avondale's permit application requires contractors to hold an ROC license unless the homeowner qualifies as an owner-builder under A.R.S. 32-1121. So if a bidder suggests you pull the permit as the owner while they do the work, that's a way around the license requirement — and it leaves you responsible for the job in the city's eyes. Ask every bidder: Who pulls the City of Avondale permit? The answer should be "we do." 2. Look for CAPS and Real Accessible Experience Anyone can screw a grab bar into a wall. Designing a bathroom that's genuinely safe for someone with limited mobility — or someone who uses a walker or wheelchair — is a different skill set. That's why the credential to look for is CAPS: Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist , a designation from the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) for professionals trained specifically in accessible home modifications. CAPS isn't legally required to remodel a bathroom, and it isn't a guarantee on its own — but it's a strong signal. A CAPS-trained remodeler understands how mobility limitations actually play out in a bathroom: where a grab bar needs to be to help someone rise from the toilet, how much clear floor space a walker needs, how a curbless shower keeps a wheelchair from catching a lip. Ask directly: Who on your team holds CAPS, and how many accessible bathrooms have you actually built? Photos of completed roll-in showers and reinforced grab-bar installations tell you more than any certificate. Experience with aging-in-place remodeling is what separates a specialist from a generalist who occasionally adds a safety bar. 3. ADA Compliance vs. Aging-in-Place Safety This is the single most important distinction to understand before you hire, because the two terms get used interchangeably and they don't mean the same thing. True ADA compliance follows the ADA Standards for Accessible Design and the ANSI A117.1 accessibility code — a set of precise, legally defined dimensions for clearances, grab-bar heights, roll-in shower sizes, and turning space. These standards are required in many public and commercial settings. A private home is generally not required to be ADA compliant, but some homeowners — especially wheelchair users — want their bathroom built exactly to those specifications. Aging-in-place safety borrows the same principles but tailors them to one household's real needs and budget. It might mean a curbless shower, grab bars, and a comfort-height toilet without hitting every ADA dimension to the inch. That's often the smarter, more cost-effective choice for a homeowner who's steady on their feet today but planning ahead. A good remodeler will ask about the actual person who'll use the bathroom — their mobility now and likely later — and tell you honestly which approach fits. Be cautious of anyone who slaps "ADA" on every quote without discussing whether you truly need code-level compliance or a well-designed accessible bath. If you want the deeper comparison, see our guide on how to choose the best aging-in-place remodeler in Avondale . 4. The Accessible Features That Actually Matter A safe, usable bathroom is a system of features working together, not a single grab bar. A remodeler who knows accessibility will walk you through each of these and explain the ADA/ANSI guidance behind them. Here's what to look for and what the standards generally call for. Feature Why It Matters What to Look For Grab bars & blocking Support to sit, stand, and steady Solid wood/steel blocking in the wall, mounted at code height Roll-in / curbless shower No lip to trip over or roll a chair across Zero threshold, proper slope to drain, wide entry Shower seat & hand-held Seated bathing, reach control Sturdy folding bench, hand-held sprayer on slide bar Comfort-height toilet Easier to sit down and rise Taller bowl (~17-19"), clear side space for transfers Turning clearance Room to maneuver a walker or chair 60" turning circle or T-turn per ANSI A117.1 Sink & faucet Usable seated, easy to operate Roll-under clearance, single-lever or touchless faucet Doorway & handles Getting in and out safely 32"+ clear width, lever handles instead of knobs Flooring & lighting Prevent slips, aid low vision Non-slip surface, low threshold, bright even lighting Grab bars and in-wall blocking This is where corner-cutting is most common and most dangerous. A grab bar is only as strong as what it's anchored to. Real accessible work means installing solid wood or steel blocking inside the wall before it's closed up, so bars can be mounted anywhere they're needed and hold significant force. ADA guidance calls for bars roughly 33–36 inches above the floor near the toilet and in the shower, but placement should also suit the actual user's height and reach. Bars screwed only into drywall anchors — no matter how nice they look — are a false sense of safety. Ask specifically how the grab bars will be backed. Curbless roll-in showers A curbless (zero-threshold) shower is the centerpiece of most accessible baths. Removing the curb eliminates a trip hazard and lets a wheelchair or shower chair roll straight in. It takes real skill: the floor must be sloped correctly to a linear or point drain so water doesn't escape, and the waterproofing has to be flawless. Pair it with a sturdy folding bench and a hand-held sprayer on a slide bar so bathing can be done seated. A tub-to-shower conversion is one of the most requested accessible upgrades — see our ADA and accessible bathroom page for options. Comfort-height toilets and clearances A comfort-height (or "right-height") toilet sits taller than a standard bowl, making it far easier to sit down and stand up. Just as important is the clear floor space beside and in front of it for a safe transfer from a wheelchair. ANSI A117.1 specifies side clearances for accessible toilets; a remodeler experienced in these details will lay out the room around them rather than squeezing fixtures in. Turning space, doorways, and reach For anyone using a walker or wheelchair, maneuvering room is everything. The standard target is a 60-inch turning circle (or a T-shaped turn) of clear floor space, a doorway with at least 32 inches of clear width — often meaning a wider door or a swing-clear hinge — and lever door handles and single-lever faucets that don't require gripping or twisting. These are the details general remodelers most often miss. Flooring, seating, and lighting Non-slip flooring with a low or flush threshold prevents the falls that send people to the ER. Good, even lighting — ideally with a well-placed night light — helps aging eyes and reduces missteps. A built-in bench or fold-down seat, accessible storage within easy reach, and contrasting colors that help low-vision users find edges all round out a truly usable bathroom. 5. The Accessible Remodel Process, Step by Step Understanding the sequence helps you spot a contractor who's cutting corners. A proper accessible bathroom remodel looks like this: Needs assessment & consultation — discuss the actual user's mobility now and later, current pain points, and whether the goal is true ADA compliance or aging-in-place safety. Design & specification — lay out clearances, grab-bar locations, shower type, and fixtures to ADA/ANSI guidance, and select finishes. Estimate & documentation — provide an itemized written estimate and any paperwork needed for grants or insurance. Permits — pull the City of Avondale permit through the Building Services Division; plumbing, electrical and framing changes typically need one, and a rebuilt shower gets pre-slope and shower liner test inspections before tile. Demolition & rough-in — remove old fixtures, reframe as needed, relocate plumbing, and install in-wall blocking for grab bars. Waterproofing & shower build — slope and waterproof the curbless shower base, then set tile or solid-surface walls. Fixtures & finishing — install the comfort-height toilet, roll-under sink, grab bars, seat, hand-held sprayer, lighting, and non-slip flooring, then final inspection. Note that in-wall blocking goes in before the walls are closed — anyone planning to add grab bars after the fact with surface anchors isn't building for real safety. 6. What an Accessible Bathroom Typically Costs Accessible remodels vary widely because the scope does — from a few safety upgrades to a full layout change with a roll-in shower. Actual numbers depend on how much plumbing and framing move, the fixtures and finishes you choose, and your bathroom's size, but these ranges reflect most of our projects and make a realistic planning guide: Project Typical installed range Grab bars + comfort-height toilet $300 – $1,500 Add-on shower seat & hand-held + non-slip floor $1,500 – $4,500 Tub-to-curbless-shower conversion $8,000 – $18,000 Full accessible bathroom remodel $18,000 – $40,000 Full wheelchair-accessible (ADA) remodel $35,000 – $60,000+ A useful cost-control tip: not every accessible bathroom needs to be gutted. If your layout already has enough room, focusing on a curbless shower, grab-bar blocking, a comfort-height toilet, and non-slip flooring gets most of the safety benefit at a fraction of the cost of moving walls. This is exactly the kind of guidance a good remodeler offers up front. Because Infinity buys factory-direct and installs in-house, our pricing typically runs roughly 15–25% below big-retail quotes. 7. Funding: Grants, Benefits, and Insurance Accessible remodels can be a significant expense, so it's worth understanding what help might be available — while remembering that eligibility and amounts are decided solely by the agencies and insurers involved, never by a contractor. Confirm every detail directly with the source before you plan around it. VA HISA grant. The Home Improvements and Structural Alterations (HISA) grant can help veterans pay for medically necessary bathroom modifications. Amounts and eligibility are set by the VA and typically require a physician's prescription. VA SAH / SHA grants. The Specially Adapted Housing (SAH) and Special Housing Adaptation (SHA) grants assist veterans with certain service-connected disabilities in adapting a home. These are larger programs with specific qualifying conditions determined by the VA. Long-term-care insurance. Some long-term-care policies include home-modification benefits. Check your specific policy language and pre-authorization requirements with your insurer. Medicaid waivers & local programs. Certain Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services waivers and area agencies on aging offer home-modification assistance. Availability varies, so contact the program directly. City of Avondale Home Repair Program. The city's Home Repair Program (Neighborhood & Family Services, (623) 333-2703) lists ADA work such as grab bars, wider doors and ramps for eligible owner-occupied homes on City of Avondale water. Ask the city about current eligibility and how the program works with contractors before you sign anything. We can't promise you'll qualify for any of these, and we won't pretend to speak for the VA or an insurer. What an experienced remodeler can do is provide the detailed estimates, scopes, and documentation these programs commonly request, so your application is easier to submit. For related help, see our notes on planning your project and getting an estimate . 8. Local Factors Avondale Homeowners Should Weigh A few things about Avondale are worth factoring into your choice: Multigenerational households, not a retirement market. Avondale is a young, family-heavy city — the Census Bureau's American Community Survey puts the median age at about 33. Accessible bathrooms here usually come from a parent moving in, several generations sharing one house, recovery from surgery or an injury, or a family member with a disability. The bathroom often has to work for a grandparent and a toddler at the same time, so look for a remodeler who designs for the whole household — a curbless entry and a hand-held shower on a slide bar serve everyone — rather than one who just installs "senior" products. Mostly 1990s–2000s homes, plus an older core. The median Avondale home was built in 2002, so most bathrooms are sound behind the walls and the work centers on layout: tubs you step over, narrow doorways, tight toilet alcoves. Houses in Old Town, Cashion and Las Ligas, the city's oldest neighborhoods, can hide more. If your only full bath is upstairs, a good remodeler will also talk with you about creating an accessible bathroom on the main floor. Very hard water. Avondale's tap water is very hard — about 21 grains per gallon for city well water in the city's 2022 water quality report. Non-porous shower surfaces, quality fixtures, and easy-clean finishes hold up better and stay safer than grout-heavy surfaces that get slick with buildup. City of Avondale permits. Residential permits come from the city's Building Services Division (Development Services Department, 11465 W. Civic Center Dr., (623) 333-4000) and are filed online through Accela. Tiling, cabinets and countertops don't need a building permit; plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC changes beyond minor repairs do. A remodeler who handles city permits routinely will build the inspections into a realistic timeline. HOA approval for exterior ramps. If your home is in an HOA community, check its rules early: the City of Avondale does not track HOA covenants and tells owners to check with their HOA before applying for a permit. If your project includes an entry ramp or a wider exterior door, ask who prepares the HOA submission and build that review into the schedule. Ramp surfaces also need thought here: National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals for the area put the July average high around 106&deg;F, so a ramp in full sun needs a material and finish that stays usable. 9. Reviews, Portfolio, Estimates, and Warranty Finally, vet the track record and the paperwork. Look for a real body of local reviews that mention specifics — whether grab bars felt solid, how clean and considerate the crew was, whether the finished bathroom actually made daily life safer — not just a star average. Ask to see photos of completed accessible bathrooms similar to yours, and look closely at the curbless shower thresholds and grab-bar installs rather than the wide "hero" shots. Then insist on a clear, itemized written estimate that breaks out demolition, plumbing, framing and blocking, the shower system, fixtures, flooring, and finishing, so you can compare quotes on equal terms. Vague one-line bids are impossible to compare and usually hide surprises. And confirm the warranty in writing: the fixture and material manufacturer warranties are separate from the remodeler's workmanship warranty — you want both, and you want to know exactly what each covers and for how long. Infinity Kitchens and Baths (AZ ROC #339999) is family-owned, factory-direct, and has been remodeling bathrooms since 2011. Search "best bathroom remodeler in Avondale" and you'll get ads, directories, and a dozen companies all claiming to be the best. So how do you actually tell them apart? After 35+ years of remodeling bathrooms, here's the honest checklist we'd use ourselves — the things that separate a contractor who builds a bathroom that lasts 25 years from one that needs repairs in five — along with the Avondale-specific questions about permits and water that belong on your list. 1. Verify the License and Insurance First In Arizona, remodeling contractors must hold an active license with the Registrar of Contractors (ROC). Before you talk price, ask for the ROC number and look it up at roc.az.gov — it's free and takes a minute. Confirm the license is active and in the right classification, and verify the contractor carries general liability insurance and workers' compensation. If a contractor can't or won't give you a current ROC number, walk away. (Infinity holds AZ ROC #339999.) 2. In-House Crews vs. Subcontractors Ask who actually does the work. Companies that run their own installation crews tend to deliver more consistent quality and accountability than those that hand your project to a rotating cast of subcontractors. When the same team that measured your bathroom comes back to build it, the hand-off errors that plague split projects simply don't happen. 3. Waterproofing Expertise (the Make-or-Break) This is the single most important — and most often cut — part of a bathroom remodel. Water intrusion behind tile is invisible for months or years until it isn't. A quality remodeler waterproofs the entire shower assembly before any tile goes up and can explain exactly how they do it. If a bid is suspiciously cheap, this is usually where the corners were cut. On a permitted shower rebuild in Avondale, the city's inspection list includes a pre-slope and shower liner test before tile — ask whether the remodeler builds that inspection into the schedule. 4. Reviews, Reputation, and a Real Portfolio Look for a substantial track record of reviews — not just a star rating, but specifics about communication, cleanliness, and standing behind the work. Ask to see photos of completed bathrooms similar to yours. A remodeler who specializes in bathrooms (not a generalist who does one occasionally) will have a deep portfolio to show. 5. Detailed Written Estimates and a Warranty The best remodelers give you a clear, itemized written estimate — materials, labor, scope, permits, and timeline — so you're comparing apples to apples. Vague one-number bids make it impossible to know what you're actually getting. Also ask about the warranty: what's covered, for how long, and by whom. 6. Avondale Know-How: Permits, Hard Water and Your House Permits. Avondale's building code lists tiling, cabinets, countertops and painting as finish work that needs no building permit, so new tile and a vanity swap usually don't. Plumbing is different: the code's exemption covers stopping leaks, clearing stoppages and resetting a toilet, but not work that replaces or rearranges valves, pipes or fixtures. Moving a drain, replacing a shower valve, adding a circuit or changing a gas line needs a permit from the City of Avondale's Building Services Division (11465 W. Civic Center Dr., 623-333-4000). Ask who pulls it — it should be the contractor, under their ROC license — and who schedules inspections, which the city runs Monday through Thursday. Our Avondale remodeling permits guide covers the details. Very hard water. Avondale's tap water blends city well water with Colorado River water, and the city's 2022 water quality report put city well water at about 21 grains per gallon — "very hard" on the report's own scale. That's tough on glass, fixtures and grout. A remodeler who works here should talk you through glass with a protective coating, fixture finishes and cartridges that handle mineral buildup, and surfaces that are easy to keep clean. Our guide to faucets and fixtures for hard water goes deeper. Your house. Most Avondale homes went up in the 1990s and 2000s — the median home was built in 2002 — so many bathrooms are original and reaching the age where valves, tub surrounds and vanities are due. Homes in the city's oldest areas, such as Old Town and Cashion, can hide older materials behind the walls; a renovation that falls under the asbestos rules needs a notice to Maricopa County 10 business days before work starts. City programs. If you're on City of Avondale water and replacing older fixtures, the city's Low Flow Plumbing Rebate pays $75 per toilet (1.6 gallons per flush or less) and $25 per showerhead (under 2.6 gallons per minute); apply within a year with a dated receipt. A good remodeler will mention it and give you the receipt you need. # Choosing a Cabinet Maker in Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/best-cabinet-maker-avondale.html

Summary: How to choose the best cabinet maker in Avondale, AZ: ROC license, box construction, wood species, finishes for desert sun and hard water, and warranty.
