# Bathroom Flooring Options for Arizona's Climate
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/bathroom-flooring-options.html
Section: Guides & ideas
Summary: Bathroom flooring options for Avondale, AZ homes — porcelain tile, LVP, natural stone, and more.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Bathroom Guides / Bathroom Flooring Options Bathroom Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Bathroom Flooring Options: What Works Best in Arizona's Climate By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Published May 20, 2026 &bull; 6 min read Part of our Bathroom Design & Planning Guides — see all 8 guides in this category. Bathroom flooring selection involves a short but unforgiving list of requirements: moisture resistance, slip resistance, durability, and comfort underfoot. Arizona's climate adds two more variables: extreme heat and hard water. This guide covers the flooring options we actually install in bathrooms and the considerations that typically drive the decision. Avondale Climate Factors Before comparing materials, a few climate factors that matter for bathroom flooring in Avondale: Heat: Avondale is low desert, about 1,000 feet. National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals for the area put the July average high near 106°F, with about 111 days a year at 100°F or hotter. Flooring materials that expand and contract significantly (some LVP products, hardwood) need proper acclimation and expansion gaps, especially near sunny windows. Hard water: Avondale's tap water is a blend of city well water and Colorado River (CAP) water, and it is very hard: the city's 2022 water quality report put city-produced water at an average of about 21 grains per gallon (357 mg/L). High calcium and magnesium content means mineral deposits (calcium scale) form on grout lines and light-colored tile surfaces faster than in soft-water regions. This affects both material selection (lighter grout shows scale more) and cleaning requirements. Dry climate baseline: Despite the monsoon season (officially June 15 through September 30), Avondale's baseline humidity is low most of the year. This works in favor of natural wood and some LVP products that could be problematic in high-humidity coastal markets. Material Comparison Porcelain Tile Porcelain tile is the most versatile and durable bathroom flooring option available. It's fully waterproof, doesn't expand or contract meaningfully with temperature change, resists staining without sealing, and is available in virtually every aesthetic (stone looks, wood looks, concrete, geometric patterns). Slip resistance varies by finish — matte and textured surfaces provide better grip than polished. For a wet shower floor specifically, select tile with a DCOF rating of 0.42 or higher. The trade-offs: it's the most labor-intensive to install (requires cement board underlayment, thinset, grout), it's the hardest underfoot (standing on tile for long periods is less comfortable than other options), and it's the coldest to step on first thing in the morning — an issue addressed by radiant heat under the tile. Cost range installed: $8–$20/sq ft for standard porcelain; $14–$30/sq ft for premium large-format or specialty tile. Luxury Vinyl Plank (LVP) LVP has taken significant market share in bathroom flooring over the past decade for good reason: it's 100% waterproof (core and all), comfortable underfoot (softer and warmer than tile), easy to install, and available in convincing wood-look formats. It's also significantly easier to replace than tile if a section is damaged. The considerations specific to Arizona: LVP has a thermal expansion coefficient that responds to temperature — in direct sun exposure or rooms that heat to 90°F+, some LVP products can buckle if installed without adequate expansion gaps. For an interior bathroom floor out of direct sun, this is rarely a problem. Choose a product rated for temperature range from 40°F–100°F and acclimate the planks in the room for 48 hours before installation. LVP is appropriate for bathroom floors outside the shower area (the main floor, around the toilet, under the vanity). We don't recommend LVP for shower floors — the shower floor needs tile with proper slope and drain integration. Cost range installed: $5–$12/sq ft for standard LVP; $8–$16/sq ft for premium thicker-core products. Natural Stone (Travertine, Slate, Limestone) Natural stone bathroom floors create a visual warmth and authenticity that no manufactured product fully replicates. Travertine, in particular, is extremely popular in Arizona homes — it reads warm and organic rather than cool and modern, and it's been used in the Southwest long enough to feel at home in desert architecture. The maintenance reality in a hard-water market: natural stone requires sealing at installation and annually thereafter. Travertine's open pores absorb water, soap, and calcium scale if left unsealed. In Avondale's very hard water, unsealed travertine in a bathroom will show white calcium staining within weeks. If sealed and maintained, it lasts for decades and looks better with age. Slate is more dense and less porous than travertine — a lower-maintenance natural stone option with a rougher texture that provides natural slip resistance. Cost range installed: $10–$25/sq ft for travertine or slate; $18–$40/sq ft for premium marble. Ceramic Tile Ceramic tile is a step below porcelain in density and water resistance (higher water absorption rate, more susceptible to cracking under impact), but it's significantly more affordable and appropriate for bathroom floors in lower-traffic bathrooms, guest baths, or areas where budget is the primary driver. Not suitable for shower floors, where porcelain's non-porosity matters more. Cost range installed: $5–$12/sq ft. Material Waterproof Sealing Required Hard Water Cost/sq ft (installed) Porcelain tile Yes No Excellent $8–$30 LVP Yes No Good $5–$16 Natural stone No (porous) Yes, annual Needs sealing $10–$40 Ceramic tile Mostly No Good $5–$12 Radiant Heat Under Bathroom Floors Tile's most significant comfort drawback — cold underfoot — is solved by electric radiant heat under the tile. A thermostat-controlled heating mat is installed below the tile during the bathroom remodel. The result is a warm tile floor that responds within 15–20 minutes of activation. Avondale's winters are mild, but January lows still average in the 40s, so tile can feel cold first thing on a winter morning. Here radiant heat is a comfort upgrade rather than a necessity, at a one-time installation cost of $600–$1,500 depending on floor area. Radiant heat works with tile and natural stone. It is not compatible with standard LVP (the heat can damage the vinyl core) — some specific LVP products are rated for radiant heat but require verification with the manufacturer. Grout Considerations for Avondale's Hard Water Grout color choice matters more with water as hard as Avondale's than in most places, because of the calcium scale it leaves behind. The practical guidance: Avoid white or very light grout on floors: Calcium deposits are white-ish. On a white grout floor, the buildup is nearly invisible until it's a thick layer. On medium grey grout, regular cleaning removes it before it accumulates. Epoxy grout is worth the premium: Epoxy grout is non-porous — calcium scale sits on the surface rather than absorbing in. Much easier to clean than cement grout in hard water areas. Sealed cement grout is second choice: If epoxy isn't in the budget, seal cement grout at installation and annually. Medium grey or tan colors hide buildup better than white. Frequently Asked Questions Can I put LVP in a bathroom with a shower? Yes — on the main bathroom floor around the shower, under the vanity, and around the toilet. Not inside the shower floor, where tile with proper slope and drain integration is required. The transition between the LVP bathroom floor and the tile shower floor is typically handled with a threshold or flush transition strip. Is heated tile flooring worth it in Avondale? It can be, if you spend meaningful time barefoot in your bathroom on winter mornings. Avondale's winters are mild, but National Weather Service 1991–2020 normals for the area still put January lows in the 40s, so tile can feel cold in the cooler months. Expect to use it a few months a year, not half the year. The installation cost ($600–$1,500) is modest relative to the comfort benefit and adds negligible electricity cost when used on a timer. We install it frequently and clients universally say they'd do it again. What's the best bathroom floor for resale value? Porcelain tile in a neutral color (white, grey, greige, or a warm wood-look) has the broadest appeal and the longest recognized lifespan. LVP is increasingly accepted and recognized by buyers as a quality choice in secondary bathrooms. Natural stone reads as premium but is noted by buyers as requiring maintenance. For maximum appeal at resale, porcelain in a neutral format is the consistent answer. How long does bathroom flooring installation take? Tile removal and new porcelain tile installation in an average primary bathroom (60–80 sq ft) takes 2–3 days including subfloor prep, setting, and grout cure time. LVP installation is faster — typically 4–6 hours once the subfloor is prepped. If radiant heat is added, add 4–6 hours for the mat installation and thermostat wiring before tile goes down. Not Sure Which Bathroom Flooring Is Right for You? We carry samples and can walk you through the options at a free in-home consultation. We'll assess your subfloor, layout, and goals before making a recommendation. # Bathroom Lighting Ideas & Layout Tips (Avondale, AZ)
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/bathroom-lighting-ideas.html
Section: Guides & ideas
Summary: Bathroom lighting ideas for your remodel: layered lighting, vanity sconces, color temperature, wet-rated shower lights, dimmers, and LED mirrors.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Bathroom Guides / Bathroom Lighting Ideas Bathroom Remodeling Guide — Avondale, AZ Bathroom Lighting Ideas for Your Avondale Remodel By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated June 19, 2026 &bull; 6 min read Part of our Bathroom Design & Planning Guides — see all 8 guides in this category. Quick answer: Good bathroom lighting uses three layers — ambient (recessed or ceiling), task (at the mirror), and accent. For the vanity, mount sconces at eye level on either side of the mirror, use warm 2700K–3000K bulbs with a CRI of 90+, and add dimmers. Showers need a wet-rated fixture. Backlit LED mirrors give soft, shadow-free light. Infinity Kitchens and Baths (AZ ROC #339999) designs code-compliant bathroom lighting as part of every bathroom remodel. Lighting is the most overlooked part of a bathroom remodel — and one of the highest-impact. The right plan eliminates harsh shadows at the mirror, makes the room feel larger, and sets the mood for a spa-like space. Here's how we approach bathroom lighting in our remodels. Layer Your Lighting Great bathrooms use three layers: ambient (overall room light, usually recessed cans or a ceiling fixture), task (at the mirror, for grooming), and accent (toe-kick lighting, niche lighting, or a statement fixture). Relying on a single overhead light is the most common mistake — it casts shadows on your face and flattens the room. Get the Vanity Lighting Right Vanity lighting is the part people notice most. The gold standard is a pair of sconces mounted on either side of the mirror at roughly eye level — this lights your face evenly with no shadows. If sconces aren't an option, a quality fixture above the mirror works, ideally paired with the layered lights below. Color temperature: aim for 2700K–3000K (warm white) for a flattering, comfortable light. Color rendering (CRI): choose bulbs rated CRI 90+ so makeup and skin tones look true. Brightness: don't under-light the vanity — it's the working zone of the bathroom. Shower & Wet-Area Lighting Showers need their own light, and it must be a wet-rated (damp/wet-location) fixture for safety and code. A single recessed wet-rated downlight transforms a dim shower; for larger or tiled showers, two lights keep things even. Add Dimmers Dimmers are inexpensive and make a big difference — bright for grooming, low for a relaxing soak. We recommend dimming the ambient and accent layers at minimum. LED Mirrors & Natural Light Backlit LED mirrors provide soft, even, shadow-free light and a modern look — a favorite in our recent remodels. Where possible, we also maximize natural light with windows or a skylight, which makes any bathroom feel bigger and fresher. Under Avondale&rsquo;s summer sun, that glass should be low-E, and a skylight or west-facing window needs to be placed so it brightens the room without baking it. Safety & Code Bathroom lighting and outlets must meet electrical code — GFCI protection, proper wet/damp-location ratings near water, and correct clearances. As a licensed contractor (AZ ROC #339999), we handle all of that as part of the remodel. In Avondale, only like-for-like swaps such as replacing a lamp or a receptacle are exempt from a building permit; new circuits, added fixtures and relocated boxes go through the City of Avondale&rsquo;s Building Services Division, and we pull that permit for you. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best lighting for a bathroom vanity? A pair of sconces mounted at eye level on either side of the mirror is ideal — it lights your face evenly with no shadows. Use warm-white bulbs (2700K–3000K) with a high color-rendering index (CRI 90+) so skin tones and makeup look true. What color temperature should bathroom lights be? 2700K to 3000K (warm white) is the most flattering and comfortable for bathrooms. Cooler 'daylight' bulbs can look harsh. Pair this with CRI 90+ bulbs for accurate color. Do showers need special lights? Yes. Any light in or directly over a shower must be a wet- or damp-rated (wet-location) fixture for safety and to meet electrical code. We install wet-rated recessed lights in showers as standard. Are LED mirrors worth it? For many homeowners, yes. Backlit LED mirrors give soft, even, shadow-free light at the vanity , look modern, and can reduce the need for additional fixtures. They're a popular upgrade in our recent remodels. Home / Guides / Bathroom Guides / Bathroom Remodel Mistakes Contractor Perspective — Avondale, AZ Bathroom Remodel Mistakes to Avoid (From an Avondale Contractor) By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Published May 27, 2026 &bull; 8 min read Part of our Bathroom Design & Planning Guides — see all 8 guides in this category. After 35+ years of bathroom remodeling, the same mistakes show up over and over — in projects we're fixing for other contractors and in consultations with homeowners who have already gone down a wrong path. Most of these mistakes share a common feature: they're expensive to undo once the remodel is complete. This guide covers the ones that cause the most real-world pain, with direct guidance on how to avoid each one. Mistake 1: Skipping the Waterproofing This is the most consequential mistake in shower construction. Tile is not waterproof — it's water-resistant at best. The waterproofing layer goes behind the tile: either a liquid-applied membrane (like Schluter Kerdi or Mapei AquaDefense) or a waterproof cement board system with taped seams. Without it, water penetrates the grout, reaches the cement board or drywall behind the tile, and begins deteriorating the substrate, the framing, and eventually the structure. We see this every year: a bathroom remodeled 5–10 years ago with beautiful tile that's now pulling away from the wall because the substrate behind it has rotted. The waterproofing adds $300–$600 to the cost of a shower installation. The repair cost when it's omitted is typically $3,000–$8,000 minimum — plus the same waterproofing that should have been installed the first time. How to avoid it: Ask any contractor bidding your bathroom remodel what waterproofing system they use. If they can't name the specific product (Schluter Kerdi, Mapei AquaDefense, Wedi, RedGard, Laticrete Hydro Ban, or similar), treat that as a red flag. Mistake 2: Choosing the Cheapest Bid In any market with many small contractors competing for business, the variance in bid prices for the same bathroom remodel is often 2:1 or more. The temptation to choose the lowest bid is natural — but the lowest bid almost always represents one of three things: cheaper materials, less experienced labor, or both. A bathroom remodel done incorrectly — plumbing not properly sloped, waterproofing skipped, tile set in the wrong mortar, grab bars anchored into tile instead of blocking — fails in 3–7 years. The fix costs as much as or more than the original job done correctly. We regularly get calls from homeowners asking us to fix a bathroom that was "just remodeled" by a lower-price contractor. How to avoid it: Get three bids and ask each contractor to walk you through exactly what they're including. A bid that doesn't explicitly include waterproofing and a specific tile adhesive is almost certainly leaving those out to keep the number low. Mistake 3: Starting Work Without All Materials on Order Tile, fixtures, vanity, and glass enclosure all have lead times. Tile from specialty suppliers: 2–6 weeks. Custom vanity: 4–8 weeks. Frameless glass enclosure: 7–14 days after final measurement, which happens after tile is complete. If a bathroom remodel starts before these items are ordered and confirmed, the project will stall waiting for materials — and the bathroom will be unusable in the interim. This also creates another risk: if a tile is discontinued or a fixture is backordered after demolition has already happened, you're either waiting indefinitely for the original selection or making a rushed substitution that you'll live with for the next 15 years. How to avoid it: Finalize all material selections and confirm order lead times before setting a demo start date. The contractor should be verifying this as part of project planning — if they're not, ask specifically about lead times for each item in the project. Mistake 4: Ignoring Ventilation Bathroom ventilation is frequently overlooked, especially in homes that still have their original builder-grade fan. Much of Avondale's housing went up in the 1990s and 2000s (the city's median home was built in 2002), so many of those fans are now more than 20 years old. An undersized or poorly positioned exhaust fan leads to persistent moisture buildup — which leads to mold, deteriorating grout, peeling paint, and warped cabinetry over time. Arizona's dry climate creates a false sense of security here: the bathroom still generates significant moisture from showers, monsoon season (officially June 15 through September 30) adds humidity on top of it, and that moisture needs to move out of the space. Avondale builds to the 2024 International Residential Code, adopted with city amendments effective Jan. 1, 2026, and under that code a bathroom without an operable window needs a mechanical exhaust fan. The fan should be sized for the bathroom's cubic footage (minimum 1 CFM per sq ft of floor area, or match the Home Ventilating Institute's bathroom fan calculator). It must vent to the exterior — not into the attic, which is a code violation and causes attic moisture damage. How to avoid it: During a remodel, the exhaust fan should be replaced or verified as adequate. Ask your contractor what CFM rating the existing fan is, whether it vents to the exterior, and whether it's being replaced as part of the project. A $150–$300 quality exhaust fan is not the place to cut costs in a bathroom remodel. Mistake 5: Setting Unrealistic Budget Expectations The national average figures quoted in most remodeling articles often don't match what a real project costs once labor, materials and permits are priced for your actual scope. Typical ranges across our 2025–2026 bathroom remodels: Cosmetic update (vanity, fixtures, flooring, no structural work): $6,000–$14,000 Mid-range full remodel (new shower, vanity, toilet, tile, flooring): $18,000–$35,000 Primary bath full remodel with custom tile shower: $28,000–$55,000 High-end primary bath (curbless shower, steam, custom tile, double vanity, heated floor): $50,000–$90,000+ Going into a remodel expecting $10,000 for what's actually a $25,000 project leads to cutting corners on materials and labor to hit a budget that wasn't realistic to begin with — which leads back to the earlier mistakes. How to avoid it: Get an honest consultation with at least two contractors before setting a budget. Ask them to estimate the scope you're describing and what it actually costs in this market, before you've committed to a number in your head. Mistake 6: Underestimating Hidden Conditions Bathrooms in older homes (in Avondale, about 12% of homes were built before 1980, with much of the older housing around Old Town and in Cashion) frequently reveal unexpected conditions once walls are opened: galvanized plumbing that's corroded and needs replacing, subfloor damage from a slow leak that was never addressed, outdated wiring that doesn't meet current code when a new light fixture or GFCI circuit is required, or mold behind the shower tile from years of inadequate waterproofing. The 1990s and 2000s homes that make up most of Avondale have their own version: two decades or more of very hard water on the original shower valves and supply lines, and slow leaks under a tub or toilet that went unnoticed for years. These aren't contractor surprises used to inflate the bill — they're the honest reality of opening walls in an older home. A 10–15% contingency budget (above the original project estimate) is standard advice for any remodel, and particularly important in bathrooms because water-related damage accumulates invisibly for years. How to avoid it: Build 15% contingency into your bathroom remodel budget before you start. If you don't need it, it goes back in your pocket. If the walls reveal corroded pipes or damaged subfloor, you have room to address it correctly rather than patching over it. Mistake 7: Choosing Style Over Maintenance Reality White grout throughout the bathroom looks crisp and clean in the catalog photo. Unsealed marble tile looks luxurious. Both require maintenance that most homeowners are not prepared to commit to — especially with Avondale's very hard water (the city's 2022 water quality report put city-produced water at an average of about 21 grains per gallon), where mineral deposits form quickly. The most common version of this mistake we see: white cement grout on a shower floor. Within 6–12 months, it's grey-brown from mildew and soap scum and nearly impossible to restore to white without a steam cleaner and aggressive cleaning. The fix is either re-grouting (messy and expensive) or accepting a permanently stained floor. How to avoid it: Before finalizing any material selection, ask: what does this look like in 2 years with normal maintenance? Use epoxy grout on shower floors. Choose a medium-grey or warm-tone grout color rather than white. Use porcelain in the shower rather than natural stone unless you're fully committed to annual sealing. Mistake 8: Guessing About Permits Permits trip up a lot of bathroom remodels. Plumbing or electrical work done without one tends to surface later, often in a buyer's home inspection, when the walls are already closed and fixing it means opening them again. The opposite mistake is assuming the whole job needs a permit and putting off a simple tile refresh that never needed one. In Avondale, the line is fairly clear. The city's building code says painting, tiling, carpeting, cabinets and countertops need no building permit, so retiling a floor or a shower wall, or replacing cabinets and countertops, is finish work. Plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC work beyond minor repairs is not exempt. The city's plumbing exemption covers stopping leaks, clearing stoppages, and pulling and resetting a toilet, but only when the work does not involve replacing or rearranging valves, pipes or fixtures. Move a drain, replace a shower valve, convert a tub to a shower, or add a circuit for a heated floor or new lighting, and the job needs a permit from the City of Avondale's Building Services Division. A permitted shower is inspected in stages. Avondale's residential inspections include a pre-slope inspection and a shower liner test, and inspections have to happen before the work is covered. A permit expires if no inspection is approved within 180 days, so a project that stalls can lose its permit. How to avoid it: Ask every contractor bidding your job which parts of the scope need a permit and who pulls it. Applications are filed online through the city's Accela portal, and the Building Services Division is at 11465 W. Civic Center Dr., (623) 333-4000. If you live in an HOA, check your covenants before you start; the city does not track HOA rules. We pull City of Avondale permits for our work and schedule the inspections. Our Avondale permit guide covers the process in more detail. Frequently Asked Questions How do I know if my contractor is cutting corners on waterproofing? Ask directly: "What waterproofing product do you use in the shower?" and "Can I see it before it's covered by tile?" A contractor doing it right will name a specific product and should have no problem showing you the installed membrane before tile goes up. If the answer is vague or they say "we use greenboard" (greenboard is moisture-resistant drywall, not waterproofing), that's a red flag. What's the difference between a $20,000 and $40,000 remodel? Usually three things: tile quality and installation complexity, shower system (custom tile vs. prefab or solid surface), and vanity (stock vs. custom or semi-custom cabinetry). The structural work (waterproofing, plumbing rough-in, electrical) should be done correctly at any price — if a $20,000 bid is skipping those, it's not a $20,000 remodel, it's a $20,000 mistake. Is it worth doing a bathroom remodel all at once vs. in phases? Almost always yes. Labor mobilization, demo containment, and coordination costs mean that a bathroom done in two phases typically costs 20–30% more than doing everything at once. More importantly, tile and fixture selections made years apart are hard to match — phased remodels often produce visually inconsistent results. If budget is the constraint, do fewer rooms at once, but complete each bathroom in a single scope. Do I need a permit for a bathroom remodel in Avondale? It depends on the scope. In Avondale, tiling, painting, cabinets and countertops need no building permit. Plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC work beyond minor repairs does, and that includes replacing or rearranging valves, pipes or fixtures, such as moving a drain, replacing a shower valve or converting a tub to a shower. Permits come from the City of Avondale&rsquo;s Building Services Division, and a new shower pan is inspected at the pre-slope stage and with a shower liner test before tile goes on. Home / Guides / Bathroom Guides / Bathroom Remodel Timeline Bathroom Remodeling Guide — Avondale, AZ How Long Does a Bathroom Remodel Take in Avondale, AZ? By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated June 19, 2026 &bull; 8 min read Part of our Bathroom Design & Planning Guides — see all 8 guides in this category. Quick answer: Most of our bathroom remodels take about 2–4 weeks of active construction. A vanity or cosmetic update can finish in 3–7 business days, a tub-to-shower conversion in 1–2 weeks, and a full master bath with custom tile and frameless glass in 3–4 weeks. Total elapsed time runs longer because of design, selections, and material lead times. Infinity Kitchens and Baths (AZ ROC #339999) provides a written week-by-week schedule before work begins and handles the City of Avondale permits and inspections when plumbing or electrical work is involved. One of the first questions homeowners ask is simple: how long will I be without my bathroom? The honest answer has two parts — active construction time (how long our crew is on site) and total elapsed time (which includes design, selections, and waiting for materials to arrive). This guide breaks down both so you can plan with confidence. Bathroom Remodel Timeline at a Glance Project Active Construction Vanity / fixture / cosmetic update 3–7 business days Tub-to-shower conversion 1–2 weeks Standard full bathroom remodel 2–3 weeks Full master bath (custom tile, glass, double vanity) 3–4 weeks Most of our bathroom remodels land in the 2–4 week range for active construction. Below is what happens during each phase. Phase 1: Design & Material Selection (1–3 weeks, before demo) This phase happens before our crew arrives. We measure, finalize the layout, and help you choose tile, vanity, fixtures, and glass. The more decisions that are locked in before demo day, the smoother — and faster — the build goes. Custom items like frameless glass and special-order vanities have lead times, so we order early. Phase 2: Demolition (1–2 days) We protect floors and set up dust containment, then remove the old shower, tub, vanity, flooring, and any failing drywall. This is also when hidden issues surface — outdated plumbing, soft subfloor, or past water damage — which we address before rebuilding. Phase 3: Rough-In Plumbing & Electrical (2–4 days) If your layout is changing or you're adding features (a curbless shower drain, new exhaust fan, additional lighting), this is when the behind-the-wall work happens. Keeping plumbing in its existing location shortens this phase considerably. Plumbing and electrical changes are permitted through the City of Avondale's Building Services Division, and an inspector checks the rough-in before the walls close. Avondale runs inspections Monday through Thursday, and a request made by 3 PM is scheduled for the next business day — so rough-in finished on a Thursday usually waits until the following week. Phase 4: Waterproofing (1–2 days) This is the most important step in any bathroom — and the one budget contractors rush. We waterproof the entire shower assembly before a single tile goes up. Done right, it's what separates a bathroom that lasts 25 years from one that fails in five. On a permitted tiled shower, the City of Avondale's inspection list includes a pre-slope inspection and a shower liner test before tile goes on, and we build that inspection into the schedule. Phase 5: Tile, Surfaces & Flooring (3–7 days) Tile setting, grouting, and curing take time and cannot be rushed — grout and mortar need to cure properly. Large-format tile and intricate patterns add days. Groutless solid-surface walls install faster than tile if speed is a priority — and with Avondale's very hard water (city well water averaged about 21 grains per gallon in the city's 2022 water quality report), fewer grout lines also means less mineral buildup to scrub later. Phase 6: Vanity, Fixtures & Glass (2–4 days) We set the vanity and countertop, install fixtures, mirrors, and lighting, and then template for frameless glass. Custom frameless panels are fabricated to exact field measurements and typically arrive 1–2 weeks after templating, so glass is often the final item installed. What Affects Your Timeline Scope: a cosmetic refresh is days; a full master bath is weeks. Material lead times: special-order tile, vanities, and custom glass can extend the calendar even when the build itself is quick. Plumbing relocation: moving fixtures adds rough-in time. Permits and inspections: a cosmetic update (vanity top, tile, paint) needs no City of Avondale building permit; moving plumbing or adding circuits does, and inspections run Monday through Thursday. Surprises in older homes: hidden water damage or outdated wiring discovered at demo. We provide a written, phase-by-phase schedule before work begins and keep you updated throughout, so you always know where things stand. See real numbers in our bathroom remodel cost guide . Frequently Asked Questions Can I use my bathroom during the remodel? Not the one being remodeled — it will be out of service for the duration. If it's your only full bath, we discuss phasing the work or accelerating specific trades to minimize downtime, and we plan that out before demo so there are no surprises. Why does the total project take longer than the construction time? Active construction is usually 2–4 weeks, but the full project also includes design, material selection, and lead times for special-order items like custom vanities and frameless glass. We order long-lead items early so they're on site when needed. What's the fastest type of bathroom remodel? A cosmetic update — new vanity, fixtures, mirror, flooring , and paint with the existing shower and plumbing in place — is the quickest, often done in 3–7 business days. Do delays happen, and how do you handle them? Occasionally, usually from hidden damage in older homes or a backordered material. We build realistic schedules, order early, and keep you informed if anything shifts — no silent delays. # Bathroom Tile Ideas: Floors, Showers & Walls — Avondale, AZ
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/bathroom-tile-ideas.html
Section: Guides & ideas
Summary: Bathroom tile ideas for Avondale, AZ: porcelain, ceramic, stone, glass and mosaic, sizes, layouts, and grout tips.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Shower & Tile Guides / Bathroom Tile Ideas Bathroom Design — Avondale, AZ Bathroom Tile Ideas: Floors, Showers & Walls By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated July 1, 2026 &bull; 12 min read Part of our Shower & Tile Guides — see all 4 guides in this category. Quick answer: The best bathroom tile choices come down to material and location. Use dense, water-resistant porcelain for floors and shower pans, prioritizing slip resistance (a matte or textured tile with a wet DCOF of 0.42 or higher). Reach for glazed ceramic on walls, where it's affordable and easy to clean, and save natural stone and glass mosaics for accent walls, niches, and feature areas. Pick a tile size and layout that suits the room — large-format tile opens up small baths, while classic subway, herringbone, and vertical-stack layouts add character. Then let the grout color and a professional, well-waterproofed installation tie it all together. Tile is the hardest-working design element in any bathroom. It shrugs off water and steam, wipes clean, and — done well — turns an ordinary bath into the room people compliment first. But "what tile should I use?" is really several questions at once: which material, what size, which layout, and where each belongs on the floor, walls, and shower. Get those right and the room looks intentional and lasts for decades. Get them wrong and you end up with a slippery floor, cracked grout, or a busy pattern that fights itself. This guide walks through the tile decisions we make with homeowners — the materials worth knowing, the sizes and trends shaping bathrooms right now, the layouts that never go out of style, and the practical details (slip resistance, niches, curbless showers, grout, and mixing tiles) that separate a polished result from a regretted one. Use it to plan with confidence whether you're refreshing a powder room or gutting a primary bath. 1. Bathroom Tile Materials and Where Each Fits Every tile decision starts with the material, because that determines how the tile handles water, wear, and cleaning. Here are the surfaces you'll actually be choosing between, and where each earns its place. Porcelain Porcelain is the workhorse of the bathroom. It's clay fired at a very high temperature, which makes it dense, extremely hard, and nearly impervious to water. That combination makes it the safest all-around choice for floors and shower pans, and it's just as at home on walls. Better still, porcelain comes in convincing wood-look planks and stone-look slabs, so you can get the warmth of oak or the drama of marble without any of the maintenance. If you only remember one rule, make it this: when in doubt on a bathroom floor, choose porcelain. Ceramic Ceramic is porcelain's more affordable cousin — also clay-based, but fired at a lower temperature, so it's a bit softer and more porous. Glazed ceramic is a fantastic value for walls, wainscot, and accent areas where it won't take heavy foot traffic. Classic white subway tile is ceramic, and it remains one of the most versatile, budget-friendly wall tiles you can buy. For a deeper comparison of the two, see our guide on tile and custom shower installation . Natural stone Marble, travertine, slate, and limestone bring texture and one-of-a-kind character no manufactured tile can copy. The trade-off is maintenance: natural stone is porous and needs periodic sealing to resist water spotting and stains — a real consideration with Avondale's very hard water, which the city's 2022 water quality report put at an average of about 21 grains per gallon for city-produced water. Polished stone can also be slick underfoot, so it's usually smarter on walls and accents than on floors, unless it's honed or textured. Love the look but not the upkeep? Stone-look porcelain gets you most of the way there with far less fuss. Glass Glass tile reflects light beautifully, resists water and staining completely, and adds a jewel-like shimmer that's perfect for accent bands, niches, and feature walls. It's typically too slick and too costly to cover an entire floor, but as a strip of color or a shower niche liner it delivers a lot of impact for a small quantity. Mosaic Mosaics are small tiles — often 2 inches or less — mounted on mesh sheets. Because they pack in so many grout lines, they grip better underfoot, which makes them the go-to for shower floors where traction matters and the tile needs to follow the slope to the drain. They also shine as accent inlays, niche backers, and decorative borders. Penny rounds, hexagons, and tiny squares all fall in this family. Tile Material Best Use Durability Maintenance Porcelain Floors, showers, walls Excellent Very low — no sealing Ceramic Walls, wainscot, accents Good Low Natural stone Accent walls, feature areas Good (varies by stone) Seal periodically Glass Accents, niches, borders Good Very low Mosaic Shower floors, accents Excellent (great grip) Low; more grout to clean 2. Tile Sizes and the Large-Format Trend Size changes the whole feel of a room as much as color does. Bathroom tile generally falls into a few buckets: mosaics (2 inches and under), standard field tile (roughly 4x4 to 6x6), rectangular subway (3x6, 4x12), and large-format tile (12x24, 24x24, and up to true slab panels). The clear trend right now is large-format. Big tiles mean fewer grout lines, which reads as a cleaner, more continuous, more contemporary surface — and, importantly, less grout to scrub over the years. In a small bathroom, large-format tile actually makes the room feel bigger because the eye isn't chopped up by a grid of joints. Running the same large tile from the floor up the shower walls, or extending floor tile straight into a curbless shower, blurs the boundaries and stretches the space visually. That said, size should follow function. Large tiles are wonderful on floors and walls but a poor fit for a shower pan, where the tile has to slope to the drain — that's where small mosaics still win. Match the tile scale to the surface, and don't be afraid to mix sizes on purpose (large on the walls, mosaic on the shower floor) for both looks and safety. 3. Popular Tile Layouts and Patterns Two homeowners can use the exact same tile and end up with completely different rooms based on layout alone. These are the patterns that consistently look great in bathrooms: Subway / offset (running bond). The timeless brick-style layout with each row offset by half. A safe, clean classic — traditional at a 50% offset, more modern at a 30% offset. Herringbone. Rectangular tiles set in a zig-zag for a dynamic, upscale look. Beautiful on floors and feature walls; it uses more material and labor because of the angled cuts. Vertical stack. Tiles stacked in straight columns rather than offset. Crisp, modern, and great for making a ceiling feel taller — vertical subway tile is having a real moment. Chevron. Similar to herringbone but the tiles are mitered so the zig-zag forms continuous, pointed rows. Bold and elegant, ideal for an accent wall. Straight stack / grid. Tiles aligned in a simple square grid — understated, contemporary, and perfect for large-format tile where you want the material, not the pattern, to star. A reliable approach is to keep the field tile calm and let one layout do the talking — a herringbone shower floor, say, framed by simple stacked wall tile. For a gallery of shower-specific combinations, browse our tile shower ideas . 4. Choosing Floor vs. Wall vs. Shower Tile Not all tile is rated for all locations, and the differences matter. Here's how to think about each surface. Floor tile Floors need to be hard, water-resistant, and — above all — slip-resistant. Porcelain is the standard pick. Look for tile specifically rated for floor use (wall-only tile is often too soft) and favor matte or textured finishes over high-gloss, which turns treacherous when wet. Wood-look porcelain planks are a huge favorite in bathrooms because they give a warm, spa-like feel without wood's vulnerability to water. Wall tile Walls take no foot traffic, so you have more freedom. This is the place for glossy finishes, delicate glass, and softer ceramics that wouldn't survive a floor. Wall tile can also climb higher than you might expect — a full-height tile wall behind the vanity or around the tub adds drama and protects the surface from splashes. Shower tile The shower is the most demanding zone in the house: constant water, steam, and the need for traction underfoot. Use porcelain or glazed ceramic on the walls and small textured mosaics on the pan. What lies beneath the tile matters even more than the tile itself — a properly waterproofed substrate is what keeps water out of your walls. If you'd rather skip grout maintenance entirely, our custom shower installation team can also walk you through groutless systems. 5. Slip Resistance: What COF and DCOF Mean Slip resistance isn't a design afterthought — it's a safety spec you should check before you buy floor or shower tile. Manufacturers publish a coefficient of friction (COF), and the number that matters for wet bathrooms is the dynamic coefficient of friction (DCOF) , measured under wet conditions. The widely used industry benchmark is a wet DCOF of 0.42 or higher for floors expected to get wet. A few practical takeaways: matte and textured tiles almost always outperform polished ones; smaller tiles and mosaics add traction because the extra grout lines break up the surface; and glossy stone or high-shine porcelain, however gorgeous, belongs on walls, not on a wet floor. On the shower pan specifically, small mosaics are the traction champion. If the tile's DCOF isn't listed, ask — a reputable supplier will have the number. 6. Accent Walls, Niches, and Curbless Showers The details are where a tiled bathroom goes from nice to memorable. Accent walls. Devote one wall — behind the tub, the vanity, or inside the shower — to a standout tile: a bold geometric, a natural-stone slab-look, or a shimmering glass mosaic. Keeping the accent to a single plane lets you splurge on a beautiful, pricier tile without overwhelming the room or the budget. Niches. A recessed shower niche is both practical storage and a design opportunity. Line it in a contrasting mosaic or the same tile as an accent wall, and align it with your grout lines so it looks built-in rather than cut-in. Building the niche between studs during the remodel is far cleaner than adding a surface caddy later. Curbless showers. A curbless (zero-threshold) shower — where the floor tile runs continuously into the shower with no step over a curb — looks sleek, feels spacious, and is a cornerstone of accessible, aging-in-place design. It requires careful sloping and waterproofing to keep water headed toward the drain, so it's very much a job for an experienced installer, but the payoff in both style and safety is significant. 7. Grout Color and Maintenance Grout is easy to treat as an afterthought, but it dramatically changes both the look and the upkeep of your tile. Two strategies dominate: Matching grout (close to the tile color) makes the surface read as one continuous plane, hides minor layout imperfections, and helps a small room feel larger. It's the go-to for large-format tile and calm, modern spaces. Contrasting grout (dark grout with white tile, for example) celebrates the pattern and gives subway or geometric layouts a graphic punch. Because it outlines every joint, though, the installation has to be precise. For maintenance, lean toward a slightly darker grout on floors and shower pans, where a bright white will show grime fast. Even better, choose a high-performance or epoxy grout in wet areas — it resists staining and water far better than standard cement grout and stays looking new with less scrubbing. Sealing standard grout periodically also goes a long way in Avondale's hard water. 8. Mixing Tiles Cohesively Combining several tiles is how designers create depth, but it's also where amateur jobs go sideways. A few rules keep a mix feeling intentional rather than chaotic: Vary the scale, not everything. Pair a large field tile with a small mosaic accent so the sizes contrast clearly instead of competing. Let one tile lead. Choose a single hero — the shower accent or the floor — and keep the rest quiet so the eye has somewhere to rest. Share an undertone. Tiles in different materials read as a set when they share a common color temperature (all warm or all cool). Limit the palette. Two or three tiles in one bathroom is plenty; beyond that, the room starts to feel busy. Sample in the actual room. Lighting shifts color dramatically — always look at samples on-site, in the bathroom's own light, before committing. Tile Selection Tips Buy 10–15% extra tile for cuts, waste, and future repairs — and keep the leftovers with matching lot numbers. Confirm floor and shower tiles are rated for those uses and meet a wet DCOF of at least 0.42. Order all tile for a room from the same production lot to avoid subtle shade variation. Favor matte and textured finishes underfoot; save glossy tile for walls. Choose large-format tile to open up a small bath, mosaics where you need grip. Pick your grout color deliberately — it's as much a design decision as the tile. Plan niches, accent walls, and curbless thresholds before demo, not after. Prioritize the waterproofing system in showers; it's what protects the whole installation. Why Professional Tile Installation Matters Tile is only as good as what's under it. Beautiful tile over a poorly waterproofed or uneven substrate will eventually crack, leak, or grow mold — and by the time you see the damage, it's usually behind the wall. Professional installation covers the parts you'll never see but absolutely feel over time: correct waterproofing membranes in wet areas, a dead-level and properly prepared substrate, consistent grout lines and spacing, precise cuts around niches and fixtures, and an accurate slope to the drain so water always leaves the shower. At Infinity Kitchens and Baths, we handle waterproofing and tile installation in-house — one accountable team from layout to final grout — for bathrooms in Avondale, AZ, and we pull City of Avondale permits when a tile project also moves plumbing or adds electrical work (tile on its own needs no building permit in Avondale). As a licensed contractor (AZ ROC #339999) with 35+ years of combined experience and factory-direct pricing that typically runs 15–25% below retail, we help you pick tile that fits how you actually live and install it to last. Explore our bathroom flooring options to round out the room, or request a free estimate to get started. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best tile for a bathroom floor? Porcelain is the best all-around bathroom floor tile: it's dense, nearly waterproof, and holds up to daily traffic. For floors, prioritize slip resistance — look for a textured or matte tile with a wet dynamic coefficient of friction (DCOF) of at least 0.42, and consider smaller tiles or mosaics where more grout lines add grip. Porcelain wood-look planks and stone-look tiles give you the warmth of wood or stone without the water and maintenance worries. What tile is best for a shower? Porcelain and glazed ceramic are the top choices for shower walls because they're water-resistant and easy to clean. On the shower floor, use small mosaic tiles (2 inches or smaller) or a textured tile — the extra grout lines create traction and let the tile follow the slope to the drain. Natural stone like marble looks stunning in a shower but needs sealing to resist water and staining. A properly waterproofed substrate matters more than the tile itself. Porcelain vs. ceramic tile — what's the difference? Both are made from clay and fired, but porcelain is fired hotter and denser, which makes it harder, less porous, and better suited to floors and wet areas. Ceramic is a bit softer and more affordable, making it a great value for walls and lower-traffic areas. For bathroom floors and shower pans, porcelain is usually the safer pick; for accent walls and wainscot, ceramic can stretch your budget without sacrificing looks. What tile size makes a small bathroom look bigger? Large-format tiles (12x24, 24x24, or bigger) make a small bathroom feel more open because fewer grout lines create a cleaner, more continuous surface. Running the same tile from floor up the walls, or extending floor tile into a curbless shower, blurs boundaries and stretches the space visually. Light colors and a grout that closely matches the tile also help a small room read larger and calmer. What grout color should I choose for bathroom tile? Matching the grout to the tile creates a seamless, expansive look and hides minor imperfections — ideal for large-format tile and small rooms. A contrasting grout highlights the tile pattern and is popular with subway and geometric layouts, but it draws the eye to every line, so installation has to be precise. On floors and shower pans, a slightly darker grout hides dirt better. Epoxy or high-performance grout resists staining and is worth it in wet areas. Are natural stone tiles a good idea in a bathroom? Natural stone like marble, travertine, and slate is beautiful and adds real character, but it's porous and needs periodic sealing to resist water spots and staining — something to weigh with Avondale's very hard water. Polished stone can be slippery underfoot, so it's better on walls than floors unless it's honed or textured. If you love the look but want less maintenance, stone-look porcelain gives you the aesthetic with far easier care. Should tile installation be left to a professional? Yes — especially in showers and wet areas. Tile is only as good as the substrate and waterproofing beneath it, and a hidden failure can lead to leaks, mold, and costly damage down the road. A professional handles proper waterproofing, dead-level layout, consistent grout lines, precise cuts around niches and fixtures, and correct slope to the drain. # Bathroom Vanity Sizes, Styles & Materials Guide
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/bathroom-vanity-guide.html
Section: Guides & ideas
Summary: How to choose a bathroom vanity for your Avondale home — sizes, single vs. double, and material options.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Bathroom Guides / Bathroom Vanity Guide Bathroom Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Bathroom Vanity Buying Guide: Sizes, Styles & Materials By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Published May 13, 2026 &bull; 7 min read Part of our Bathroom Design & Planning Guides — see all 8 guides in this category. The vanity is the most visible element in most bathrooms — and one of the most technically involved to get right. Size, mounting style, countertop material, sink configuration, and storage all interact. Get any one of them wrong and you have a functional or visual problem that's expensive to undo. This guide covers what actually matters when choosing a bathroom vanity for your remodel. Standard Vanity Sizes Bathroom vanities come in standard widths that correspond to common bathroom layouts. Height is typically 34"–36" (consistent with kitchen counters), and depth is typically 21"–22" for standard vanities and 18" for space-saving versions. Width Best For Sink Configuration 24" Half baths, tight powder rooms Single sink only 30" Small full baths, guest baths Single sink 36" Standard full baths Single sink, some storage 48" Primary baths, more counter space Single sink, ample storage 60" Primary baths, two users Single or double sink 72" and wider Spacious primary baths, his-and-hers Double sink standard The most common mistake in vanity selection is choosing a vanity that's too small for the space — or ordering a double sink vanity for a bathroom where the plumbing isn't centered. If you're doing a remodel, verify where the drain rough-in is before ordering, since moving drain locations adds $300–$600 to plumbing costs. Rearranging pipes or fixtures is also plumbing work that needs a City of Avondale permit, which we pull as part of the job. Freestanding vs. Floating vs. Built-In Freestanding Vanity Cabinets The most common type — a cabinet unit that sits on the floor with legs or a base. This is the simplest to install (no wall anchoring required beyond the countertop and plumbing), fits the most standard bathroom layouts, and offers the most storage in the base cabinet. The visual downside is that cleaning under and around the base requires moving the unit or mopping under it. Floating (Wall-Mounted) Vanities A floating vanity is anchored to the wall studs with no floor contact. The floor is fully visible beneath it, which visually expands small bathrooms, makes cleaning easier, and allows adjustable mounting height (useful for accessibility or taller users). The structural requirement is solid wall framing — we typically add a horizontal wood ledger or blocking between studs to distribute the load properly. Floating vanities also tend to look more contemporary and are often specified in modern and transitional bathroom designs. The trade-off is that they provide slightly less storage than a comparable freestanding vanity (no base to the floor), and installation takes longer. Custom Built-In Vanities A custom-built vanity is framed into the wall like kitchen cabinetry — fully integrated with the wall, floor, and adjacent elements (side walls, linen storage, medicine cabinet). This reads as the most finished, most "designed" option and allows sizes that don't correspond to any standard dimension. The cost premium over a stock or semi-custom freestanding vanity is $1,500–$4,000+ depending on size and material. Countertop Material Options Quartz Quartz is the most practical choice for bathroom vanities: non-porous (no sealing required), resistant to water and most cleaners, available in hundreds of colors and patterns, and consistent in appearance (unlike natural stone, there's no variation between slabs). This is what we recommend for most primary bathroom vanities, and with Avondale's very hard water, a top that never needs sealing is a real advantage. The main limitation is that harsh chemicals and heat can damage the resin binders — avoid drain cleaner and setting hot styling tools directly on the surface. Natural Stone (Marble, Granite) Marble vanities are beautiful and create a genuine luxury feel that no engineered material fully replicates. The realistic maintenance requirement for marble with Avondale's very hard water: seal at installation and every 6–12 months, wipe water and soap off the surface rather than allowing pooling, avoid any acidic cleaners. Granite is less porous than marble and easier to maintain. If the clients are willing to maintain natural stone correctly, the result is genuinely special. If not, the surface will etch and stain within a year. Cultured Marble Cultured marble is a polyester resin composite that's molded into a single vanity top and integral sink — one seamless piece with no seam at the sink joint. It's affordable, easy to clean, and eliminates the potential leak point at the sink cutout. The limitation is that it's difficult to repair when scratched or chipped, looks less premium than stone or quartz, and is harder to customize. Best suited for secondary bathrooms and lower-budget remodels. Porcelain Vessel Sinks Vessel sinks sit on top of the vanity surface rather than dropping in or undercutting. They create visual interest and work particularly well with floating vanities. The functional considerations: faucets must be selected for vessel height (tall body, typically 8"–12" spout height), the vanity counter height should be reduced by 3"–4" if a vessel sink is used (so the total height including the vessel lands at 34"–36"), and cleaning around the base of the vessel where it meets the counter requires attention. Single vs. Double Sink The decision between a single and double sink in a primary bathroom is practical, not just aesthetic. Two considerations that often resolve the question: Counter space vs. sink space: A 60" vanity with two sinks has roughly 8"–10" of counter space on each side of each sink — not much. A 60" vanity with one sink (offset or centered) has one full side with substantial counter space. For a household where one person uses the bathroom at a time, a single sink with more counter is often more useful. Plumbing cost: Two sinks require two drain connections and two faucet valve connections. If the plumbing isn't already roughed in for a double sink, adding the second drain and supply lines adds $400–$700. If you're doing a full remodel anyway, this cost is absorbed more easily than in a targeted vanity swap. Storage Planning Most standard vanities have a single open bay or two to four drawers. What actually serves bathroom storage best varies significantly by household. Ask yourself before selecting a vanity: Drawers (for everyday items, hair tools, makeup) vs. cabinets (for taller bottles, hair dryers, cleaning supplies) Need for a medicine cabinet (built-in or surface-mounted above the vanity — doubles usable storage) Linen tower or side cabinet if the width allows Organizational inserts: drawer dividers, pull-out shelves in base cabinets Frequently Asked Questions How much does a new bathroom vanity cost installed? A stock vanity with countertop, sink, and installation runs $800–$2,500. A semi-custom or higher-end stock vanity with quartz top runs $2,000–$5,000. A fully custom-built vanity with stone countertop runs $4,500–$12,000+. These ranges include the vanity cabinet, countertop, sink, faucet, and installation labor — they don't include plumbing rough-in modifications if the drain location needs to move. Can I keep my existing vanity and just replace the top? Yes, if the cabinet box is in good condition. Replacing just the countertop and sink is a good mid-range option for a bathroom refresh — it eliminates the largest cost item (the cabinet) while still updating the visual focal point. You'll need to verify the existing cabinet dimensions to ensure a standard top fits, or have a custom top fabricated. What height should my vanity be? Standard vanity height is 32"–34" (older) and 34"–36" for newer "comfort height" vanities. For most adults, 36" is more comfortable — it reduces the need to bend over the sink. For children's bathrooms, consider 32"–34". If you're incorporating aging in place features, confirm the height works for the user; ANSI/ADA accessible height for a forward-reach sink is 34" maximum. How long does vanity installation take? Swapping an existing vanity for a new prefabricated unit typically takes 4–8 hours (demo, plumbing adjustment, set cabinet, connect plumbing, caulk). If a custom countertop is being fabricated, add 1–2 weeks for templating and fabrication before installation day. If the existing plumbing needs to move, add 4–6 hours for rough-in modifications. # Curbless Shower Design Guide for Avondale Homes
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/curbless-zero-entry-showers.html
Section: Guides & ideas
Summary: Everything Avondale homeowners should know about curbless showers — benefits, build, cost, permits, and drainage.

Home / Guides / Accessibility Guides / Curbless Showers Bathroom Guide — Avondale, AZ Curbless & Zero-Entry Showers: An Avondale Homeowner's Guide By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated July 13, 2026 &bull; 7 min read Weighing shower types? Our complete shower guide compares walk-in, tub-to-shower, curbless and groutless side by side, with real installed costs. A curbless shower — sometimes called a zero-entry or roll-in shower — is a walk-in shower with no curb, step, or threshold to cross. The bathroom floor simply continues into the shower, with a gentle slope to the drain. It's one of the most-requested features in bathroom remodels right now, and for good reason: it looks clean and modern, makes a bathroom feel larger, and quietly future-proofs the home. But a curbless shower is only as good as its waterproofing and floor slope, which is why it's one project we always recommend leaving to an experienced remodeler. Here's what Avondale homeowners should know before committing. What Makes a Shower "Curbless"? In a traditional shower, a raised curb (usually 4–6 inches) keeps water in. A curbless shower removes that barrier entirely. Water is contained instead by a carefully sloped floor that channels everything to the drain — typically a modern linear drain set against a wall or at the entry — plus a properly waterproofed floor and, often, a single pane of frameless glass. Done right, not a drop escapes onto the bathroom floor. The Benefits It looks bigger and cleaner. With no curb and continuous flooring, the whole bathroom reads as one open space — a huge win in smaller bathrooms. It's easier to clean. No curb and (with a groutless wall system) fewer grout lines mean far less scrubbing — worth a lot in Avondale, where the city's 2022 water quality report put city well water at about 21 grains per gallon, "very hard" on the report's own scale. A single glass panel with a protective coating also means less glass to squeegee. It's safer and future-proof. Nothing to trip over now, and nothing to remodel later — a curbless shower is the cornerstone of aging-in-place design, letting you or a family member stay in the home comfortably for the long run. That combination of style and longevity is why it's the rare trend we recommend almost universally. How a Curbless Shower Is Built This is where craftsmanship matters. To keep water where it belongs without a curb, we (1) recess or slope the subfloor so the shower floor sits flush with the bathroom floor, (2) install a full waterproofing membrane across the shower and often a few feet beyond, (3) set the floor to a precise slope toward a linear or point drain, and (4) finish with tile or a solid-surface pan. Skipping or rushing any of these steps is how curbless showers leak — so this is not a place to cut corners or DIY. In Avondale this is permitted work. Moving the drain, replacing the shower pan and reworking the floor are plumbing changes that go through the City of Avondale's Building Services Division, and the city's residential inspection list includes a pre-slope and shower liner test, so the slope and the waterproofing are checked before any tile covers them. We pull the permit and meet the inspector. Before we recess any concrete, we also confirm how the slab was built: a post-tensioned slab has steel tendons under high tension that must never be cut, so on those floors we plan the drain and slope around them. Consideration What to know Drainage A linear drain along one wall handles water better than a center drain in a curbless design Floor prep The subfloor must be recessed or built up so the shower sits flush — easier on a slab, more work on a raised floor Waterproofing A continuous membrane is essential; this is the #1 thing that separates a good curbless build from a leaky one Glass A single frameless panel (or none) keeps the open look; full enclosures partly defeat the purpose Containment Correct slope plus the right drain keeps water in without a curb What Does a Curbless Shower Cost in Avondale? A curbless shower usually costs a bit more than a standard walk-in because of the extra floor prep and waterproofing involved. As a rough guide, expect a curbless shower to run in the ballpark of $6,000–$15,000+ installed depending on size, tile, glass, and whether the subfloor needs significant work — with slab-on-grade homes generally on the lower end. We'll give you an exact figure after seeing your bathroom. For a broader picture, see our bathroom remodel cost guide or try the cost calculator . Is a Curbless Shower Right for You? A curbless shower is a great fit if you want a modern, open, easy-to-clean bathroom, if you're planning to stay in your home long-term, or if accessibility is a current or future concern. It works in most homes, though slab-on-grade construction makes the floor work simpler. If you're weighing it against other options, our guides on walk-in showers and tub-to-shower conversions are good next reads. Frequently Asked Questions Do curbless showers leak? Not when they're built correctly. A curbless shower relies on a continuous waterproofing membrane and a precisely sloped floor to contain water — done right, it's completely watertight. Leaks happen when waterproofing is skipped or the slope is wrong, which is exactly why a curbless shower should be built by an experienced remodeler rather than attempted as a DIY project. Are curbless showers only for accessibility? No — accessibility is a major benefit, but most homeowners choose curbless showers primarily for the look and feel. Removing the curb makes a bathroom appear larger and more modern and makes it much easier to clean. The fact that it also supports aging-in-place is a bonus that adds long-term value to the home. How much does a curbless shower cost in Avondale? As a rough guide, a curbless shower typically runs about $6,000–$15,000+ installed, depending on size, tile selection, glass, and how much subfloor work is required. Slab-on-grade homes are usually on the lower end because the floor prep is simpler. We provide an exact written estimate after assessing your specific bathroom. Can any bathroom have a curbless shower? Most can, but the floor structure matters. In slab-on-grade homes, the concrete can often be recessed or the drain positioned to sit flush easily. In homes with a raised, framed floor, we recess the joists or build up the surrounding floor to achieve the flush transition. During a free consultation we'll tell you exactly what your home requires. Do I need a permit for a curbless shower in Avondale? Usually, yes. Tile on its own needs no building permit under the City of Avondale's code, but a curbless shower almost always means moving or replacing the drain, changing the shower pan and often reworking the floor — plumbing work that the city's Building Services Division permits and inspects, including a pre-slope and shower liner test before tile goes on. We pull the permit and meet the inspector. If you are in an HOA, check its rules first; the city does not track them. Want a Curbless Shower in Your Avondale Home? We build watertight, beautiful curbless showers — and we'll tell you honestly what your bathroom needs. Book a free in-home consultation — we come to your Avondale home. # Groutless Shower Walls: Pros, Cons & Cost
URL: https://www.infinitykitchenandbathllc.com/groutless-shower-walls.html
Section: Guides & ideas
Summary: Groutless shower walls explained — solid surface vs acrylic panels, real costs, and why they beat tile in Avondale&rsquo;s very hard water. ROC #339999.
==============================================================================

Home / Guides / Shower & Tile Guides / Groutless Shower Walls Bathroom Design Guide — Avondale, AZ Groutless Shower Walls: Pros, Cons & Best Materials By Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer at Infinity Kitchens and Baths Reviewed by Steve Hunt , Owner & Lead Designer &middot; AZ ROC #339999 Updated June 12, 2026 &bull; 6 min read Weighing shower types? Our complete Avondale shower guide compares walk-in, tub-to-shower, curbless and groutless side by side, with real installed costs. Grout maintenance is the number one complaint we hear from homeowners about their existing showers. Pink stains, discoloration, crumbling caulk at corners, and the near-impossibility of keeping white grout white — all avoidable with the right material choice. This guide covers the true groutless options, near-groutless options (large format tile with minimal joints), and the honest trade-offs of each. What "Groutless" Actually Means Strictly speaking, a truly groutless shower wall uses large-format panels with sealed seams rather than tile-and-grout construction. The seams (where panels meet at corners and transitions) are typically sealed with a color-matched caulk or silicone — not grout. This is a meaningful distinction: silicone is flexible and water-tight; grout is rigid and porous. Some homeowners use "groutless" loosely to mean "minimal grout" — large-format tile with tight (1/16") joints. This is a significant improvement over standard grouted tile but technically still has grout. Both are covered below. Groutless Shower Wall Options Solid Surface Panels Solid surface (brands include Swanstone, Corian, Wilsonart) is an acrylic or polyester-based material manufactured in large sheets — typically 30"×60" or custom-cut to fit. The panels are completely non-porous, with no grout joints, and the seams are sealed with a color-matched adhesive that bonds panel edges to create an integrated surface. Pros: Non-porous (mold/mildew cannot penetrate the material), easy to clean, no sealing required, available in marble and stone looks, repairable if scratched. Softer materials can be sanded and buffed. Cons: Not as hard as porcelain or natural stone; can scratch with abrasives. Color depth is less convincing at close range than actual tile. Fewer design options than custom tile. Price premium over standard tile. Cost installed: $2,500–$5,000 for a standard 3-wall tub surround or shower enclosure. Cultured Marble Cultured marble is a polyester resin mixed with limestone that creates panels with a gel-coat surface finish. It's been used in shower surrounds since the 1970s and remains a practical, cost-effective groutless option. Typically manufactured locally and installed in 3–4 panels. Pros: Non-porous, easy to clean, integrated with matching vanity top options, modest cost, fast installation. Cons: The gel-coat finish can yellow with age (particularly with harsh cleaners), can crack if impacted, and visually reads as a lower-tier product in most design contexts. Not recommended with abrasive cleaners. Cost installed: $1,500–$3,500 for a standard enclosure. Porcelain Slab (Gauged Tile/Panel) Thin, large-format porcelain panels — sometimes called gauged porcelain tile panels (GPTP) or slabs — are emerging as a high-end groutless option. These range from 48"×96" to full wall sheets with seams only at corners. The look is indistinguishable from stone at close range. Pros: Porcelain hardness (extremely durable, scratch-resistant), realistic stone aesthetics, truly minimal seam count, non-porous. The highest-end aesthetic in the groutless category. Cons: High cost, specialized installation requiring experienced tile setters, heavy and difficult to handle, requires proper substrate prep. Not all tile installers have the equipment and experience to handle gauged panels correctly. Cost installed: $4,500–$9,000+ for a shower enclosure, depending on panel size and complexity. Near-Groutless: Large Format Tile With Tight Joints For homeowners who want the look and feel of custom tile but minimal grout maintenance, large-format porcelain tile (12×24, 12×36, 24×48) with 1/16" grout joints using epoxy grout is a practical middle ground: Fewer joints = less grout surface area to maintain Epoxy grout is non-porous and highly stain-resistant — does not require sealing Porcelain tile is harder and less porous than ceramic Full design flexibility (colors, textures, patterns, accent strips) This is the approach we most frequently recommend for Avondale homeowners who want a custom tile look without traditional grout hassle. Epoxy grout costs 15–25% more than standard cement grout and is more labor-intensive to install, but the maintenance savings are significant over the life of the shower. Material Comparison at a Glance Material Grout Joints Cost (Installed) Maintenance Cultured marble panels None $1,500–$3,500 Very low Solid surface panels None (sealed seams) $2,500–$5,000 Very low Large format tile + epoxy grout Minimal (1/16") $3,500–$7,000 Low Porcelain slab panels Corner seams only $4,500–$9,000+ Very low What We Recommend for Avondale Homes Avondale's tap water is a blend of city well water and Colorado River water, and the city's 2022 water quality report put city well water at about 21 grains per gallon — "very hard" on the report's own scale. That makes grout maintenance more challenging than in soft-water regions: mineral deposits build up faster in grout lines, leave a white haze on dark grout, and are harder to remove. This tilts the calculus further toward groutless or minimal-grout options. Whatever wall you choose, glass and fixtures will still spot, so a protective glass coating, brushed fixture finishes, or a water softener are worth discussing at the same time. Most Avondale homes were built in the 1990s and 2000s (the median home dates to 2002, per Census data), so the shower we are usually replacing is an original builder-grade tub/shower combination. For most mid-range bathroom remodels, we recommend solid surface panels or large-format porcelain with epoxy grout, depending on the aesthetic goal. Solid surface is the right call when budget efficiency and minimal maintenance are the top priorities. Large-format tile with epoxy grout is right when design flexibility and a custom look matter more than installation speed. Porcelain slab panels are available through our suppliers and appropriate for premium bathrooms where budget is less constrained. Frequently Asked Questions Can I install groutless shower walls over my existing tile? Generally not recommended. Installing panels over existing tile adds thickness that can interfere with door frames, fixtures, and waterproofing. Any underlying moisture issues or adhesion problems get buried rather than resolved. Proper removal of existing tile and fresh substrate prep produces a longer-lasting result. In a tub-to-shower conversion, this is handled automatically during demo. How long do solid surface shower panels last? With proper installation and basic care (avoiding abrasive cleaners), solid surface panels commonly last 20–30+ years. The material is repairable — surface scratches can be sanded and buffed out, which isn't possible with tile. The main limitation is color availability; if you remodel the rest of the bathroom later, matching the panel color may be difficult. Is groutless the same as "one-day shower" systems? Some companies market one-day shower systems using prefab acrylic panels. These share the same concept but use lower-grade acrylic with a thinner wall section. Quality solid surface from manufacturers like Swanstone uses a thicker, denser material that is more durable. We install solid surface, not the thinner one-day systems, because the quality difference is significant over a 20+ year lifespan. Can I get a niche (recessed shelf) in a groutless shower? Yes — solid surface niches can be ordered pre-cut from the manufacturer or field-fabricated and sealed with color-matched adhesive. This is a standard feature request. Porcelain slab showers can also incorporate niches with a trim detail. The result is seamless and water-tight when done correctly. Done With Scrubbing Grout? We'll show you groutless and low-maintenance shower options that work for your bathroom and budget. Schedule a free consultation today.
